```bash
flui env adopt <token>
```

The CLI asks the installation to describe itself, writes a local
context pointing at it, then creates the SSH trust root **on this
machine** and registers only its public half with the
installation. That last part is the whole design: the private key
that opens those servers comes into existence on the owner's
workstation, at a moment the owner chose, and the installation
never had one to give away or lose.

`--skip-ca` rebuilds the context and stops there, leaving SSH
dormant — the right choice if you only ever intend to use the
dashboard.

Adoption rebuilds a connection, not somebody else's credentials.
The provider tokens the builder used stay on the builder's
machine; the adopted context knows where the installation is, and
you sign in to it as yourself.

## How the CLI shows which context is active

Every CLI command prints a small header before its output stating
which context it is acting on and which API it is talking to. A
forgotten switch does not produce silent damage on the wrong
installation: the header is the first thing you see. This is a
small piece of UX that prevents an entire class of "I just ran
that against production" mistakes.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/) —
  the layer below: one installation, many clusters.
- [Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/) — the vault, a
  first installation, and adoption, step by step.
- [CLI: Profiles & Configuration](/cli/profiles-and-config/) —
  the command-by-command reference for creating, switching and
  inspecting contexts.

sections.title: Observability as first-class
sections.body:
On most platforms, observability lives at the end of a long list
of "things to set up later". Flui inverts that ordering. Metrics
and logs are there from minute zero — the very same operation that
brings up a cluster also brings up the place where its metrics and
logs go — and they cover both the apps you deploy and the
platform's own components from day one. The surfaces you use to
read them on the first app are the same you will use on app number
two hundred.

This chapter is about the intent and the shape of that choice. The
detailed inventory of what runs inside the control cluster is the
[next chapter](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/).

## A pillar, not an add-on

Observability in Flui is not a separate tool you bolt on after
the fact. It is one of the pillars the rest of the platform stands
on, present from the first minute the installation is alive.

Three things make this concrete:

1. **It is part of the bootstrap.** The same operation that brings
   up the control cluster also brings up the backend that collects
   metrics and logs. The installation is not considered ready
   until that backend is. Workload clusters added later feed into
   the same backend — you do not stand up a second observability
   stack, you point the new cluster's agents at the one that
   already exists.
2. **It is modelled around the platform's own concepts.** The
   CLI and the dashboard expose metrics and logs in terms of
   clusters, servers and applications — the things you already
   reason about — instead of asking you to translate to namespaces,
   labels and query languages first.
3. **The platform itself relies on it.** Alerts evaluate against
   the metrics backend, and the suggestions the platform makes for
   scaling — when to grow a node, when an application is running
   close to the edge — read from the same data. Take observability
   away and those features have nothing to read.

The consequence: you cannot run Flui in a useful state without
observability. That is a deliberate constraint — it removes a
class of "I'll add monitoring later" decisions that, in practice,
never get made.

## What is in scope

Flui's built-in observability covers:

- **Metrics** — host-level metrics on every node, cluster-level
  metrics on every object, and the baseline per-application
  metrics (CPU, memory, restart count, replica health) that Flui
  surfaces for every app it manages.
- **Logs** — application logs from every cluster, indexed
  centrally and queryable per app, per cluster, per time range.
- **Dashboards** — the everyday path is Flui's own dashboard and
  CLI, which surface what is worth looking at — for a cluster and
  for an application — curated by Flui rather than left as a blank
  canvas. Grafana is also deployed on the control cluster,
  pre-wired to the metrics and log backends, but as an advanced
  tool for deep debugging and custom dashboards — not as the
  primary way to read metrics and logs.
- **Alerts** — conditions evaluated against the metrics
  backend, recorded as episodes and readable per
  application. See
  [alerts, below](#alerts-are-episodes-not-messages).
- **What your agents did** — once an agent holds a
  credential on this installation, the calls it makes are a
  register you can read. See
  [below](#what-your-agents-did).

Some classes of telemetry are not part of the built-in stack
today: end-to-end request tracing across services, application
performance profiling, and uptime checks from outside the
platform. Applications that need them add their own tooling on
top.

## No database storage for logs or metrics

Flui's database holds *state about the installation* — clusters,
nodes, applications, operations, releases, builds — and nothing
else. Logs and metrics live in their own purpose-built backends,
with their own retention and capacity policies.

Two records do live in Flui's own database, and neither is
telemetry: the alert episodes described below, and the
register of what agents did. Both are records of events
with a beginning and an end — much closer to an operation
than to a log line — and neither grows with your traffic.

When you query logs or metrics through Flui, the API acts as a
thin proxy: it resolves which application you are asking about,
scopes the query to that application's data, forwards the query to
the appropriate backend, and streams the answer back. No log line
and no metric sample is ever written to Flui's own database.

Three things follow from this:

- **The control plane stays small.** Flui's database does not grow
  with traffic; it grows with the number of resources you manage.
- **The backends are independently replaceable.** If a future
  release prefers a different metrics or log store, the change is
  contained — the user-facing surfaces stay the same.
- **Standard tools work.** Anyone with a background in the
  underlying query languages can drop into Grafana and run the
  same kind of queries Flui itself is running.

## Alerts are episodes, not messages

A metric you have to be looking at is not much use. Alerts
are the part of observability that comes to you instead.

Rules are evaluated on the control cluster against the
metrics already being collected, so there is nothing extra
to install and nothing to point at anything. What Flui adds
on top is the shape of the record.

**One row per episode.** A condition that stays true is
re-reported every few hours for as long as it lasts. Those
repeats update the same row rather than stacking up, so
`flui app alerts my-api` reads as a history of incidents
and not as a mailbox. Each row carries whether it is firing
or resolved, a severity, a one-line summary, and when it
started and ended.

**An end time can be a guess, and says so.** The notice
that a condition cleared is sent once. If it goes missing —
the API restarting at the wrong moment is enough — the row
would sit there as a permanent false alarm. So a firing row
that has gone quiet for six hours is closed, marked as
closed by timeout, and given the time it was last seen as
its end. The CLI prints those with an asterisk, and the
wording everywhere is *stopped reporting*, never *recovered
at*. Read it as the last moment the condition was known to
be true.

**Resolved history is kept for ninety days** by default and
then deleted. A firing row is never deleted, however old it
is — an old alert that is still firing is not archive, it
is the incident.

**Alerts belong to applications.** Each one is attributed
to the application it is about, and you see the alerts of
the applications you may read. Alerts about the machines
themselves are a separate list, for whoever runs the
installation, because their text carries host names and
internal identifiers a tenant should not be able to
collect.

Where to read them:

- `flui app alerts <app>` — newest first, `--firing` for
  only what is still firing, `--output json` for scripting;
- the **Alerts** section on the application in the
  dashboard;
- an agent, through the `app_alerts` tool.

Two honest limits. **Flui does not page anyone.** When an
alert starts or clears, the person the application belongs
to gets a live notice in the dashboard, and that is the
whole of delivery today — no email, no phone. And **an
empty alert list is not a clean bill of health**: it means
nothing was recorded, which is not the same as nothing
being wrong.

## What your agents did

Metrics and logs answer what your applications did. Once
you connect an agent to this installation there is a third
question worth being able to answer, and Flui treats it the
same way: **what the agent did**, kept per credential.

Every call an agent makes through the tool surface, or
through the assistant inside Flui, is a row: when, which
action, whether it was allowed, and what it started. Calls
made straight at the API — an agent driving Flui with plain
HTTP and no tool surface in front of it — are recorded too,
on the routes that stop and ask a person first. Those were
the quietest calls in the product and the least supervised,
which is a bad pair of properties to have together.

**The arguments are not kept.** A value only comes back as
it was sent when it is a member of a set written in Flui's
own source — a fixed choice, a number, a flag. Every
free-form string is withheld, because the answers to a
catalog install can carry an administrator password and
this is a table built to be read. What a call actually
touched is recovered instead from the operation it started,
which Flui wrote itself.

**You can read your own register with no management access
at all.** Deciding whether to disconnect an agent you
connected should not require being an administrator.
Somebody who administers access on the installation reads
the whole installation's register instead, and the page
says which of the two you are looking at. Somebody else's
rows read as absent rather than forbidden — a refusal would
confirm that the call it was hiding took place.

This is the one observability surface with no CLI. It is
the **Agents** page in the dashboard, or the API with your
own credential.

## How workload clusters feed the control cluster

The control cluster is the *consumer* of metrics and logs from
every workload cluster. The flow is push-based, not pull-based:
every node on every cluster runs a metrics agent and a log shipper
that send their data to the central backend over the cluster's
private network.

If the control cluster is unreachable, workloads keep running —
each cluster is autonomous in steady state — and the agents
buffer locally. When the link returns, recent data back-fills, and
the dashboard surfaces the brief gap rather than failing silently.

### Why push, not pull

The conventional model is pull, where a central scraper reaches
into each target. Flui pushes instead, for three concrete reasons:
the trust boundary points outward (workload clusters initiate, the
control cluster never reaches in), short outages back-fill from
the agent's local buffer rather than leaving holes in the time
series, and the control cluster does not need a registry of every
endpoint to scrape. Tracing, when it lands, is expected to follow
the same shape.

## What the user sees

Three surfaces, all backed by the same data:

| Surface | What it shows | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CLI | Single-app logs (filtered by level and full-text search), runtime status, recent crashes, and metrics | Debugging a specific app, scripting, CI |
| Dashboard | Per-app live charts and log streams, plus cluster-level views | Day-to-day operation; no Grafana needed |
| Grafana | Full query power against the metrics and log backends, custom dashboards | Cross-cutting analysis, custom monitoring |

The CLI and the dashboard share the same backend semantics;
Grafana is the always-there escape hatch. None of the three is
authoritative over the others — they are different views of the
same data.

The register of what your agents did is the exception to
that shape. It is not in the CLI and not in Grafana,
because it is not a query over telemetry — it is Flui's own
record of who asked for what.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/) —
  the detailed inventory: which components, in which role, at what
  cost.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — how the app
  surface is wired to the observability backend.
- [When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/) —
  answering a request, and reading the register of what
  your agents have done.
- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/) — why an
  agent's write stops and asks a person first.

sections.title: Anatomy of the control cluster
sections.body:
The control cluster is not "a cluster with monitoring on it". It is
the place where Flui itself runs, plus the observability backend
that every other cluster pushes into, plus the few platform pieces
that every Flui cluster needs to function. This chapter walks
through that inventory by role.

The components below are reconciled by the platform-components
catalog described in
[Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/),
restricted to the control cluster — except for the baseline ones
(certificates, ingress, in-cluster DNS) that every cluster carries.

## The platform itself

These are the components that make this cluster the *Flui control
plane*. None of them appear on workload clusters.

### Flui API

The service every CLI command, every dashboard request and every
third-party integration talks to. It runs *on the cluster it
controls*: there is no cloud-hosted Flui API tier — the API that
operates your installation is the one you installed yourself.
Reached at a public hostname through the cluster's ingress.

Not replaceable: it is the control plane.

### Flui dashboard

The visual surface of the installation: cluster lists, application
views, monitoring, deploy flows, identity, and the panel where you
answer an agent.

The dashboard and the CLI are equal citizens: they both call the
Flui API, and for most work either one will do. They are not
identical, though, and it is worth knowing where they part. The
control cluster is created from the CLI, because the dashboard
does not exist until that cluster is up. Answering an agent's
request for permission is done in the dashboard, or against the
API directly — there is no `flui` command for it. Assume the two
surfaces match everywhere and you will eventually go looking for
a door that is not there.

### Identity provider (Zitadel)

The OIDC authority for the installation. Issues the credentials
the CLI uses, the tokens the dashboard uses, and federates with
external identity providers when configured. Installed when the
installation runs in OIDC mode; in local-auth mode Flui falls back
to a database-backed admin user instead.

Replaceable in principle by any OIDC-compliant identity provider;
in practice Zitadel is the one Flui ships and tests.

### Database

The installation's state lives here: clusters, nodes,
applications, releases, builds, operations, encrypted credentials,
DNS zones, certificate metadata. Logs and metrics do not, by
design — they live in the observability backend below.

It also holds two newer records that are about agents rather than
about infrastructure: the action-cycle store and the agent
activity register. Both get their own section further down.

PostgreSQL is the engine Flui ships and tests against.

### Cache and queue backend

Every operation Flui drives — provisioning, deploys, builds,
lifecycle changes — flows through a job queue, and the same
component also serves caches that the API needs to keep small
pieces of state fast. Redis is the engine Flui ships and tests
against.

## What the control cluster keeps for agents

Two things were added to the control plane when agents arrived.
Neither is a service you can point at — both are records inside
the database above. They are listed here because they change what
the control cluster *is*. It used to hold the state of your
infrastructure. It now also holds the record of what your agents
asked for and what they did.

### The action-cycle store

When an agent asks for something that changes the installation,
the call does not run. It becomes a question waiting for a
person. That question has to be written down somewhere, because
nothing is holding a connection open while somebody thinks about
it. This is where it is written.

Two kinds of row:

- **Pending requests.** What was asked for, in one sentence,
  under which credential, and — when the action costs money —
  the price at the time of asking. A request expires after an
  hour, so nobody is ever offered a stale quote.
- **Standing permissions.** The "always" answers. Each one is
  tied to a specific action, a specific resource, and the single
  credential that asked. Each one can be taken back.

None of this grants anything. A standing permission only removes
a pause on something the person's own access already allowed. The
reasoning behind all of it lives in
[The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

### The agent activity register

Every call an agent makes leaves a row here. The register belongs
to the **credential**, not to any one surface: a call through the
agent tools, a turn of the in-product assistant, and a plain HTTP
call made with `curl` all land in the same place. That last one
is the point. An agent key presented straight to the API meets
exactly the same guards the tool surface meets, and until this
existed it left no trace at all.

A row records which credential acted, whether the call was
allowed, how the call ended, and the long-running operation it
started if it started one. Arguments are kept redacted: values
that come from a fixed set of choices are stored as they were,
anything else is withheld.

Reading it needs no special access. Anyone can read their own
rows — you cannot sensibly decide whether to keep an agent
connected if you cannot see what it has been doing. Someone who
administers access reads the whole installation. Somebody else's
row reads as *absent*, not as *forbidden*, because a register
that answers "you may not see this" has already confirmed that
the call it is hiding took place.

## The observability backend

The components that make this cluster *the place where every other
cluster sends its telemetry*. They are present on the control
cluster only; workload clusters push into them from outside.

### Metrics store

A time-series database that receives the metrics every node in
every cluster pushes. It exposes a query API in a well-known
dialect, which is what the CLI and the dashboard read from when
they show app metrics. Today it runs in a single-node shape; the
clustered variant is a future scaling step that does not change
the user-facing API.

### Log store

The central destination for application logs from every cluster.
Indexes them by label and serves a query interface that both the
dashboard and the CLI use through the Flui API, and that Grafana
queries directly when used as the deep-dive tool.

### Metrics scraper

The agent that collects metrics from cluster objects and
applications and pushes them to the metrics store. It runs on
every cluster — including the control cluster — so the control
cluster monitors itself with the same tools it uses on every
workload cluster.

### Alert evaluator

The component that watches the metrics store continuously and
turns raw data into useful signals. It fires alerts when a metric
crosses a defined threshold for long enough, and it pre-computes
heavier queries (rolling averages, per-app aggregates) so the
dashboard can read them straight from the store instead of
recalculating each time. A baseline set of alerts and aggregates
ships pre-defined; operators can extend it.

### Object metrics exporter

Surfaces the state of cluster objects — deployments, pods,
services — as metrics that the scraper picks up. This is what
powers the per-app baseline metrics (replica counts, restart
counts, health) the dashboard shows for every application.

### Grafana

The advanced exploration tool. Pre-wired to the metrics store and
the log store as data sources. Positioned as the deep-debug
surface; the everyday path is the Flui dashboard and CLI.

## The cluster baseline

These run on every Flui cluster — the control cluster and every
workload cluster. They are listed here because the control cluster
needs them too, but the full discussion lives with the cluster
concept itself.

### Ingress

The L7 entry point of the cluster: it terminates TLS, routes
requests by hostname and path, and exposes every public surface
the cluster offers — including, on the control cluster, the Flui
API, the dashboard and the identity provider.

### Certificate lifecycle

Issues and renews TLS certificates for every public hostname the
cluster serves, against the configured ACME endpoint (production
or staging — see
[Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/)).
When the provider exposes DNS as an API, an extension lets the
issuer solve DNS-based challenges through that API; other DNS
providers are added in the same shape as integration depth grows.

### In-cluster DNS

Service discovery inside the cluster. Ships with the cluster
runtime; Flui uses it as-is.

### Short-lived metrics source

The per-node and per-pod CPU and memory readings that some
in-cluster autoscaling decisions read from. Distinct from the
observability backend above: it is the cluster runtime's own
short-window source, not the place Flui's long-term metrics live.

### Default storage

A baseline storage class for cluster workloads. On a cluster with
shared storage enabled, applications can choose the shared volume
or a node-local fallback; on a cluster without shared storage,
the fallback is the only option.

## Optional cluster-side authentication gate

A small in-cluster service that sits in front of the ingress and
checks every incoming request against the installation's identity
provider before letting it through. With it enabled, any endpoint
on the cluster can be put behind OIDC login without the
application itself having to do anything about authentication.

Flui standardises this on a dedicated subdomain convention: an
endpoint published under `<app>.internal.<cluster-zone>` is
treated as gated and goes through the authentication check
automatically, while the same app on its plain `<app>.<cluster-zone>`
endpoint stays public. The full story lives in
[DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/).

It is off by default — not because it is rarely useful, but
because it adds an extra service on every request path and the
overhead is only worth paying on clusters that actually need
gated endpoints. Installing it on demand keeps clusters that
don't need it lighter. Flui-specific, not a replaceable
component.

## What is user-facing, what is internal

The cluster exposes a small public surface and keeps everything
else internal.

- **Public, through the cluster's ingress**: the Flui API, the
  dashboard and the identity provider. These are the addresses you
  put in a browser or call from the CLI.
- **Cluster-internal**: the database, the cache/queue, the metrics
  store, the log store, their agents, and Grafana. Reachable only
  from inside the cluster — or, for development, through a
  temporary tunnel that the CLI can open against the master.

This split is deliberate. The public surface is the contract you
sign with the platform; the internals are free to evolve underneath
without changing what you can call from outside.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Observability is not an afterthought](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/) —
  the *why* this anatomy looks the way it does.
- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) —
  when each of these components is installed.
- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/) — the
  identity provider's role in detail.
- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/) — why an
  agent's write stops and asks you first.

sections.title: VNets and subnets, abstracted
sections.body:
Every cloud that offers private networking models the concept its
own way: different names, different scoping rules, different
granularity. Flui's job is to give the *cluster* a coherent
"private network with one or more subnets" view regardless of what
the provider underneath is happy to call it.

This is one of the most concrete examples of the abstraction
described in
[How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/),
and it is where the rest of the platform stops caring about
provider-specific networking terminology.

## The Flui-side model

In Flui terms, a cluster's private network has just two ideas:

- A **VNet** — a private address space (an IP range) reserved for
  the installation.
- One or more **subnets** inside the VNet — each with its own IP
  range, into which nodes are placed.

That is the whole vocabulary. Nodes are attached to a subnet at
creation time and receive a private address inside it; everything
that needs to talk over the private network speaks through those
addresses.

Where providers disagree — on how the geographic scope is named,
on whether multiple subnets per network are a thing — Flui
normalises into this same shape. The rest of the platform reads
the same fields regardless of which cloud is underneath.

## One VNet per installation

Flui provisions **one VNet per installation**, shared by the
control cluster and every workload cluster the installation
creates. The reason is straightforward: a single fast, private
environment is what makes the control cluster and the workload
clusters talk to each other with low latency, and what makes
nodes within the same cluster talk to each other without ever
touching the public internet. One VNet across the whole
installation is the simplest shape that gives both of those
properties at once.

Clusters in the same installation share the VNet and reach each
other on their private interfaces; the provider firewall only
filters the public perimeter, not this private traffic.

This shape follows naturally from the single-provider-per-installation
choice covered in
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/): if
every cluster lives on the same provider, sharing one VNet is the
obvious move. That choice is enforced — a cluster on a provider
that requires a private network is rejected at create time with the
code `VNET_REQUIRED` when none is supplied — so the shared VNet is
something the rest of the platform can rely on always being there.

All of that assumes a provider with a private network to give.
When the machine is your own there is none, and the shape
changes — see
[When the server is your own](#when-the-server-is-your-own).

## Default IP ranges

A fresh installation comes up with a default private range for the
VNet and a default range for its first subnet. They are sized
generously enough that you do not have to think about them, and
because they are private addresses inside a single installation
they do not collide with anything outside it.

If you need to override them, the values are configurable through
environment variables read at bootstrap; the reference is in
[CLI: Environment variables](/cli/environment-variables/).

## What a node gets when it joins a cluster

When a node is created, the provider gives it two addresses:

- A **public address** on the provider's external network — used
  by the cluster's ingress (HTTP/HTTPS for applications) and by
  the operator's SSH access from outside.
- A **private address** on the VNet's subnet — used for everything
  intra-cluster and intra-installation: node-to-node, agents
  pushing to the central observability backend, the control plane
  reaching into a workload cluster.

The two addresses have distinct purposes: the public one carries
the traffic that has to come from outside, the private one carries
everything that stays inside the installation. They are not
alternatives — each handles its own kind of traffic.

The clearest example is the cluster's own Kubernetes API. It listens
on port 6443, but that port is never reachable from the public
internet. When Flui records how to reach a cluster, it writes the
master's *private* VNet address as the API endpoint, not the public
one — so every control-plane operation against a workload cluster
crosses the VNet rather than the open internet. The matching
firewall rule keeps 6443 closed at the public perimeter and scoped
to the subnet, the subject of
[Firewalls](/concepts/12-firewalls/).

## When the server is your own

Everything above assumes a provider that has private networks
to create. Bring your own server and there is nothing to
create: no network API, no address space to reserve, nothing
to carve into subnets. The machine already sits on whatever
network you put it on.

So Flui does not create one. It writes down the one that is
already there. At install it takes the address you gave the
installer, records the /24 around it as that cluster's private
network, gives that network a single subnet covering the whole
range, and attaches the machine to it. Same model, same
fields — filled in from what exists, rather than provisioned.

Three things said earlier in this chapter read differently in
this case.

**One network per cluster, not one per installation.** A
recorded network belongs to the cluster it was recorded for,
and two clusters do not land on the same one by themselves.
That matters in the shape people actually run: Flui on your
own machine, workload clusters on a cloud provider. Each of
those workload clusters gets its own private network at its
own provider, and the two are never joined. Clusters like that
reach each other over their public addresses, with each side's
firewall opened to the other's address, rather than over
shared private wire. The control-plane port still answers
nobody without the right certificate, which is what makes a
public address tolerable there.

**The range is yours to state.** The /24 Flui derives from one
address is a fair guess only when your machines really do
share that network. When you join another machine, say the
range out loud:

```bash
flui node connect --host 10.0.0.12 \
  --master-ip 10.0.0.11 --node-network 10.0.0.0/24
```

Flui stores that range on the cluster and opens the first
machine to it *before* the new one joins.

**Nothing filters at a provider edge.** There is no managed
firewall in front of the machine, so the rules are applied on
the machine itself, and everything is closed unless a rule
opens it. What is public stays public: web traffic on 80 and
443, and SSH for you. Everything the machines say to each
other is accepted only from the node network — which is why
that range matters more here than anywhere else. Name it wrong
and nothing fails loudly; the machines simply cannot see each
other. `flui env firewall status` shows what is applied on the
host, and `flui env firewall apply` puts it back.

One smaller consequence. On a single machine with a single
address, the public and private pair described above collapses
into one address doing both jobs. That is normal here, not a
misconfiguration.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Firewalls](/concepts/12-firewalls/) — what enforces isolation
  inside a shared VNet.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/) —
  the broader abstraction this chapter exemplifies.
- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) —
  when the VNet is set up during cluster creation.

sections.title: Firewall as a policy, not a resource
sections.body:
In Flui the firewall is not "a thing you create and edit". It is a
*derived view of the cluster's needs* — installed when the cluster
is created, applied to every node automatically, kept in sync as
the cluster's shape changes, and built around a policy the user
states rather than a rule list the user maintains.

This chapter is about that inversion of ownership: Flui owns the
firewall and its rules; the user states intent (which addresses
are allowed in for operator access), and the rest falls out.

## The default policy

Every Flui cluster comes up with the same baseline policy:

| Port | Source | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `22/tcp` (SSH) | a user-controlled allow-list (auto-detected operator IP, or values you pass) | Operator access for bootstrap and diagnostics |
| `80/tcp`, `443/tcp` (HTTP, HTTPS) | open to the world | Public ingress for the cluster's applications and platform components |
| Outbound | allow-all | Apps need to reach external services, registries, certificate authorities |

Everything else stays closed at the public perimeter. The cluster
runtime and the platform components keep talking to each other on
the private network without ever needing a firewall hole — see
[VNets and subnets, abstracted](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/).

The cluster's own control port is the clearest example. It is not
in the default rules at all, because the control plane reaches a
workload cluster over the private VNet using the master's private
address. If you do write a rule for that port, Flui makes sure the
subnet's own range is among its sources before applying it — it
adds the private range rather than replacing what you wrote, so a
deliberate exception survives while the cluster can never lose
reachability from inside its own network.

The default exists so the cluster comes up usable out of the box,
with the SSH allow-list bound to your workstation and everything
else closed. The everyday operation on this policy is updating
that allow-list — typically when your IP changes, or when more
operators need access — through `flui env update-firewall`, which
takes an IP, a comma-separated list of CIDRs, or no argument at
all (in which case it auto-detects your current public address).
`--add` and `--remove` edit the list instead of replacing it,
`--list` prints it and changes nothing, and the command refuses a
change that would leave the list empty. It touches only the SSH
rule; every other rule is left exactly as it is. It also talks to
the provider directly rather than through the cluster, so it still
works when your current address is the one locked out.

When the default policy is not what you need, the dashboard
exposes a full firewall editor: rules can be added, modified or
removed directly from the cluster's Firewall tab, and the API
accepts the same operations. The default is a sensible starting
point, not a fixed shape.

## The rules you cannot remove

The editor's existence is exactly why a few rules are held down
by the platform. A misconfigured firewall — a missing SSH rule,
a stray block on the certificate renewal path — is one of the
most common ways to lock a cluster out of its operator or out of
its own certificates. So three invariants are enforced on every
write, at cluster creation and on every later update alike:

- **Ports 80 and 443 always stay open inbound.** If a submitted
  rule set leaves one out, Flui puts it back, open to the world,
  and says loudly in the log that it did. Restrict the *source*
  of those ports if you need to; removing the port is not a
  thing you can do.
- **A workload cluster always admits the control plane on SSH.**
  Flui manages that cluster over SSH, so the control plane's own
  addresses are added to the SSH allow-list rather than
  replacing it.
- **A rule open to the whole IPv4 internet is opened to IPv6
  too.** Nodes have addresses on both, and a firewall drops what
  its rules do not match instead of refusing it — so a lone
  IPv4 wildcard turns every IPv6 host into a black hole that
  looks like a slow connection, not an error. Lists that name
  specific ranges are left alone: those are somebody narrowing
  a source on purpose, and widening them would undo the
  narrowing.

## One policy, two ways to enforce it

The policy above is the same everywhere. What changes underneath
is what there is to enforce it *with*.

Some providers run a firewall of their own in front of the
machine, and offer an API to drive it. Flui uses it. Others offer
no such thing — and a Linux machine you already own has nothing
in front of it at all. There Flui applies the rules on the host
itself, and the machine becomes its own perimeter.

Which of the two applies is read from the provider's declared
capabilities, never from its name. That is the same rule the rest
of the platform follows, and it is why nothing above changes
shape when you move to a provider with no firewall API:
`flui env firewall apply` is one command with one meaning, and
the mechanism behind it is a detail.

## The firewall on a machine you own

Installing onto your own machine is the case where this matters
most, because the window of exposure is real. A cloud cluster
gets its firewall before any node exists, so its host is never
reachable unprotected. A machine you already own is reachable
from the moment the cluster binds a port — unless something
closes it first.

So Flui applies the host firewall **before the cluster starts**,
as part of the install. Everything inbound is denied by default;
SSH, HTTP and HTTPS are opened; the ports the nodes use to talk
to each other, and the port range used for service traffic
inside the cluster, are reachable only from the cluster's own
private ranges and never from the internet. The ruleset is
written to the machine and re-applied when it restarts, so a
reboot does not undo it.

The installation is not reported ready until that is in place.
An install that leaves the machine open to the internet has not
succeeded, so Flui does not call it done.

**One rule is deliberately not narrowed: SSH stays reachable
from any address.** This looks like an omission and is not one. A
cloud machine has an out-of-band console you can fall back on
when a firewall change locks you out. A machine you own usually
does not, so a wrong SSH allow-list there is not an
inconvenience — it is permanent. Flui refuses to be the thing
that does that to you. Restrict port 22 at your provider's edge,
or in the machine's own SSH configuration, where you keep a way
back.

This is also why `flui env update-firewall` answers differently
here. There is no provider firewall to change, so instead of
failing it says so, and points at the two commands below.

## Applying and inspecting the host firewall

Two commands, both acting on the installation's own cluster:

```bash
flui env firewall apply
flui env firewall status
```

`apply` makes sure a firewall exists and then applies it. If the
cluster has none, it seeds the default rules for that kind of
cluster first. It is idempotent — re-running it is safe, and
re-running it is the fix for most of what can go wrong here.

`status` reads it back: whether a firewall is configured at all,
the reconciliation state, when it was last applied, and the
inbound rules in force. If there is none, it says so in plain
words — nothing is filtering inbound traffic — and tells you to
apply one.

It also reports **drift**. Drift means the rules Flui wants and
the rules it last managed to apply have parted ways: an update
that failed halfway, a provider call that did not land. It is a
comparison of Flui's own records, not a live scan of the
machine, and `flui env firewall apply` is the answer to it.

One failure worth knowing about, because it reads worse than it
is: if the install applies the firewall to the machine but
cannot register it with the control plane, the machine is still
protected — the rules are on it and active. What is missing is
Flui's record of them, without which it cannot reconcile the
firewall or report drift on it. Running `flui env firewall apply`
afterwards is what closes that gap.

When an agent asks for this, it stops and asks you first: the
firewall decides what can reach the cluster from outside,
including your own access to it. See
[The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

## How the firewall tracks the cluster

The firewall is born with the cluster and lives as long as the
cluster lives. Three moments matter:

- **At cluster creation**, on a provider that has one, the
  firewall is created before — or in the same step as — the
  master server, so the master is never briefly reachable on the
  public internet without protection. On a machine you own, the
  same guarantee comes from applying the rules on the host
  before the cluster starts.
- **When a worker is added**, the firewall is applied to it
  before the node carries traffic. There is no window in which a
  new node sits exposed.
- **When a worker is removed**, the server is deleted at the
  provider and the firewall's record of covered nodes is updated
  accordingly. The firewall itself stays in place for the
  remaining nodes.

The user never has to think about any of this: it is part of the
node add/remove flow described in
[Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/).

## The provider abstraction

The firewall is one of the dimensions Flui's provider abstraction
covers. Each integrated provider implements the same Flui-side
contract — create, update, apply, remove — and the differences
between providers in rule shape and direction semantics are
absorbed by the provider integration. The host firewall is simply
one more implementation of that contract, reached over SSH
instead of an API. The cluster above sees one neutral firewall
model either way.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) —
  where the firewall is born.
- [Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/) — installing onto a
  machine you already own, step by step.
- [VNets and subnets, abstracted](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/) —
  the private network the firewall does *not* filter.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/) —
  why firewall capability is one of the dimensions a provider can
  expose or lack.

sections.title: DNS integration
sections.body:
Deploying used to end with a wait. The application was up,
the address was decided, and then you sat on the one screen
that mattered — the link — while a brand new name made its
way around the world's resolvers. About a minute, usually.
Long enough to wonder whether something had gone wrong.

That wait had no reason to exist. Every application on a
cluster answers at the same address, and every one of their
names sits one label under the same subdomain. One record
can cover all of them, including the ones that do not exist
yet. That is what a Flui cluster publishes now.

## What an endpoint is

An endpoint is the address a browser, a service or a CLI
uses to reach an application from outside the cluster.
Endpoints are opt-in: an application that nothing outside
needs to reach can be deployed without one. When the
application does ask to be reachable, the rest — hostname,
record, certificate, routing — is on Flui. You do not
allocate hostnames or edit records by hand.

A certificate that makes the endpoint speakable over HTTPS
is provisioned alongside it, covered in
[TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/).

## One record for the whole cluster

When a cluster publishes under a zone, every application on
it is reachable at `<application>.<cluster>.<zone>`, and
every one of those names resolves to the same address — the
cluster's. So Flui publishes a single record, `*.<cluster>`,
pointing there.

Two things follow, and both are the point:

- **A new application answers immediately.** Its name is
  already covered before it is deployed. Nothing has to
  propagate, because nothing new was published.
- **Removing an application removes nothing from DNS.**
  There is no per-application record to leave behind, so
  there are no orphans to clean up.

The record is derived, never configured. Flui builds the
hostname rule itself, so it knows exactly which names it
would ever create, and the wildcard is scoped to the
cluster's own subdomain rather than the zone root. A zone
you also use for a website and a mailbox is untouched
outside `*.<cluster>`.

Two commands cover it:

- `flui dns wildcard status` says whether the record is in
  place, what it points at, and what the hostname pattern
  for this cluster is.
- `flui dns wildcard publish` writes it.

`status` reads the provider live rather than trusting a
stored value. That is deliberate: a record somebody deleted
by hand would otherwise keep reporting as fine, on the exact
screen you opened to find out whether it is.

Publishing **creates, and never overwrites.** If a wildcard
is already there pointing somewhere else, that is somebody's
decision, and taking it over would silently redirect
whatever it was serving. Flui says so and leaves it alone.
The status of that name is reported as its own thing, apart
from "not published yet", because one of the two is work
waiting to be done and the other is a button that would
refuse.

## When the wildcard does not answer

The per-application record is still there. It is the
fallback now, not the rule.

Every time an endpoint is reconciled, Flui looks in the zone
for a wildcard that covers this exact name. It counts as
coverage on two conditions, and both matter:

- **One label.** A DNS wildcard matches a single label.
  `*.production` answers for `app.production` and not for
  `a.b.production`.
- **The same address.** A wildcard pointing elsewhere is not
  coverage — it is a different answer, and skipping the
  per-application record would send visitors to the wrong
  host.

When both hold, the record would be redundant by
construction: with it or without it, the name resolves to
the same place. So Flui does not write it. When either
fails — no wildcard, a foreign one, a provider that could
not be read just then — the application gets its own record,
exactly as before, and waits its minute.

Nothing to configure either way. Publish the wildcard and
the per-application records stop being written. Remove it
and they come back on the next reconcile.

One quiet detail worth knowing if you go looking at your
zone: an application covered by the wildcard does not own
that record. Tearing the application down deletes what it
owns, and the shared record is not its to delete.

**How far this is proven.** Everything in this section was
read in the product's own source — the reconciliation path,
the coverage test, the two commands. It has not yet been
watched end to end on a live cluster. Treat it as the
described behaviour, and check `flui dns wildcard status`
on yours rather than assuming.

## Zones, and giving one to a cluster

A **zone** is a domain you already own, registered with
Flui, on a DNS provider Flui can talk to. You create the
domain at the provider; Flui detects it and registers it.
Registering a zone is done from the dashboard or the API.
`flui dns zone list` shows the zones an installation knows
about, along with each one's provider and TTL.

Assigning a zone to a cluster is what moves that cluster's
applications off a nip.io name and onto the domain:

```bash
flui dns zone assign example.com --cluster production
```

It is done once per cluster, and again after a rebuild,
which is why it does not live only on a screen. Useful
flags: `--acme-email` for the address registered with the
certificate authority, `--certificate-provider` to choose
between Let's Encrypt and its staging service, and
`--no-wildcard-certificate` if you want a certificate per
application instead of one covering them all.

A cluster can publish under more than one zone. When an
application's hostname could belong to several, the longest
match wins.

The command answers immediately. The work behind it — the
credentials the certificate flow needs, the issuers, the
wildcard record — runs in the background.

## Keeping the zone in line

Flui keeps a view of what a zone should contain. The
provider holds what it actually contains. The two drift: a
person edits a record in the provider's console, a delete
the provider accepted gets lost, a cluster is rebuilt at a
new address.

`flui dns zone status` shows where each assignment stands —
in sync, reconciling, drifted, pending, or in error, with
the reason when there is one, and how long ago it last
settled.

`flui dns zone reconcile` re-applies what the assignment
needs. Add `--wait` when a script needs the outcome rather
than the acknowledgement; it polls, with `--timeout` in
seconds, and the work carries on regardless of whether you
are still watching.

## A second provider for the same zone

A DNS provider is a single point of failure you do not
control. If it stops answering, every application under that
zone becomes unreachable, however healthy the cluster is.

A **replica** is the same zone, carried on a second
provider. The primary is untouched; a replica only ever adds
coverage. Flui writes each record to the replica as well as
the primary, and a scheduled pass brings the replica back in
line if a write was missed.

- `flui dns replica add --zone <id> --provider <name>`
  registers one. It must be a different provider from the
  primary, and one this installation is configured for.
  Pass `--provider-zone-id` to adopt a zone you already
  created there instead of having Flui create one.
- `flui dns replica populate` copies every record across and
  applies the changes.
- `flui dns replica verify` is the same comparison with
  nothing written — it reports what it *would* create,
  update and remove.
- `flui dns replica list` shows each replica's state:
  pending, populating, active, degraded or disabled. A write
  Flui could not make marks the replica degraded rather than
  failing your deploy.
- `flui dns replica disable` and `enable` pause and resume
  the copying without unregistering anything.
- `flui dns replica remove` removes Flui's registration
  only. Records already written at the provider stay where
  they are.

Two consequences worth planning for. Registering the first
replica **lowers the zone's TTL** from five minutes to one,
because a long TTL is exactly what makes a failover slow;
removing the last one restores it. And Flui does not make
the second provider authoritative for you — adding its
nameservers at your registrar is your step, and it is worth
confirming the replica answers correctly before you take
it.

## Names without a domain: nip.io

When a cluster has no zone assigned, Flui builds the
hostname from the cluster's address, through a public
service (`nip.io`) that resolves a name back to the address
written inside it. No record exists anywhere; resolution
happens at the resolver.

This exists so the very first cluster of a fresh
installation can come up without DNS as a prerequisite. You
get a working URL the moment the cluster is ready. It is
also fine for development and staging, where the hostname
does not have to be presentable.

It is **not** for production. It is a third party in your
request path, it shares rate limits with everyone else using
it, and the address of your cluster is written in every URL.

Moving to a real domain later is one operation: register the
zone, assign it to the cluster, publish the wildcard. New
endpoints use the new names, and existing ones are
reconciled across without redeploying the application.

## Public and gated endpoints

An application can be published for the public or kept
behind the installation's sign-in:

- `<application>.<cluster>.<zone>` — the public address,
  covered by the cluster's wildcard.
- `<application>.internal.<zone>` — the same application,
  behind the sign-in gate described in
  [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/).
  Note that this name sits under the zone directly, not
  under the cluster's subdomain.

The only differences are that pattern and whether the gate
sits in the request path. Everything else — the record, the
certificate, the routing — runs the same way for both.

## When the link appears

An application's URL is published only once the endpoint
actually serves. A hostname is decided when the endpoint is
created, minutes before anything answers on it, and if that
work then fails the name resolves nowhere forever. So the
URL is withheld until the record and the routing are in
place — and withheld a little longer while the certificate
is still being issued, because handing you an `https://`
link in that window means a browser security warning on the
one screen that matters.

While it is withheld, the endpoint's state and its reason
are shown instead. An absent link with a reason beats a link
that does not work.

## What Flui DNS does not do

Buying a domain, and moving its authoritative DNS to a
provider Flui integrates with, are steps you take at the
registrar. Flui does not act at the registrar level: it
works on a zone you have already created at a supported
provider.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) —
  where the cluster's own addresses come from.
- [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/) —
  the certificate lifecycle, and why the wildcard
  certificate and the wildcard record are two separate
  choices.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/) —
  why DNS is one of the capabilities a provider can have or
  lack.

sections.title: TLS and certificates
sections.body:
Every Flui cluster runs on HTTPS from the first minute. There is
no "now go set up certificate issuance" step: certificates are
part of the same operation that creates an endpoint, and they
renew themselves without anyone having to think about it.

This chapter is about *how* — which authority signs the
certificates, which shape of certificate the cluster asks for,
and what it does when it cannot get the shape it wanted.

## The three issuance modes

Underneath there are two authorities: Let's Encrypt
**production** and Let's Encrypt **staging**. Three modes compose
them:

- **Production.** Certificates come from Let's Encrypt
  production — real, browser-trusted, valid for every client out
  of the box. This is the mode for anything real users reach, and
  it is the default.
- **Staging.** Certificates come from Let's Encrypt staging. Same
  issuance flow, but signed by an authority browsers do not
  trust, so they will warn. In exchange the limits are not the
  ones that hurt, so you can re-issue as often as you like while
  iterating.
- **Preflight.** Start in staging, then move. A staging
  certificate is issued first — fast feedback that the whole
  challenge chain works end to end — and once it is valid the
  endpoint offers you the switch to production. The promotion is
  a decision you make, not something that happens on its own.
  This is the safer path when you are testing a new domain setup
  and the cost of tripping a production limit is high.

The mode is a property of the installation, not of one
application: it is set with
`flui config set certificateMode production|staging|preflight`
and written into the dashboard's configuration. A single zone can
still be pinned to one authority when it is attached to a
cluster, with
`flui dns zone assign <zone> --certificate-provider lets_encrypt_staging`.

The rate-limit background is in
[Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/);
this chapter only repeats the consequence. Production is the
default for real environments, staging is the sane default for a
tight loop of creating and destroying clusters, and preflight is
the bridge. A cluster that starts in staging can be promoted to
production later; the other direction is rarely useful and no
surface offers it.

## The three certificate shapes

Within either authority, the cluster does not always ask for the
same kind of certificate. The shape follows from what the cluster
knows about DNS.

### One wildcard for the cluster

This is the ordinary case. Attach a DNS zone to a cluster with
`flui dns zone assign <zone>` and you get it without asking for
it; `--no-wildcard-certificate` is how you decline.

One certificate covers every name one level under the cluster's
subdomain. Applications that do not exist yet are already
covered, so deploying one costs no issuance at all — which is the
whole point. The certificate is issued once, held in one place on
the cluster, and copied to wherever an application needs it.

The cluster proves it controls the zone by briefly writing a
record on it — a DNS-01 challenge. That needs a zone Flui can
drive, which today means a zone on **Hetzner** or **Scaleway**.
On any other DNS provider the wildcard is not available, and the
cluster falls back to the shape below.

One detail worth knowing, because it explains something you may
see: a wildcard is exactly one label deep. A certificate for
`*.apps.example.com` answers for `shop.apps.example.com` and not
for `eu.shop.apps.example.com`, and not for the bare
`apps.example.com` either. Names a level deeper get a wildcard of
their own over their own parent, and a bare domain gets its own
certificate. So one cluster can hold more than one wildcard. That
is normal, not a mistake.

### One certificate per endpoint

This is what a cluster falls back to: when it has no DNS zone and
addresses applications by IP, when the zone lives on a provider
Flui cannot write to, when the wildcard was declined, or when a
single endpoint asks for the HTTP challenge by name.

Here the cluster proves it controls each name by serving a small
challenge file from that application's own address — an HTTP-01
challenge. No DNS integration is required at all, which is why it
works everywhere.

The cost is that every new endpoint is a fresh issuance. On a
cluster where applications come and go, the count adds up against
the authority's limits. That is the reason the wildcard is the
default now rather than an option you turn on.

### One certificate listing several names

A single certificate can instead list up to twenty hostnames.
Proof of control is per name, the same HTTP-01 as above — or
DNS-01, when every name on it sits under one zone Flui can drive.

This shape is asked for deliberately: the certificate is created
first, and endpoints are attached to it as they are created.
Flui's own use of it is the clearest example. When a cluster's
addresses are set up without a wildcard, the platform's three
addresses — the API, the dashboard and the identity provider —
go into one certificate, so the setup pays for one challenge
instead of three. It suits a small, fixed set of names known up
front, and suits nothing else: the list is fixed when the
certificate is created. An endpoint whose hostname is not on the
list is refused, and a different set of names means a different
certificate.

## Which shape an endpoint actually gets

The cluster decides per endpoint, in this order:

1. If the endpoint was attached to a multi-name certificate, that
   one is used.
2. Otherwise the wildcard, if the wildcard is not switched off,
   the endpoint asked for a certificate at all, its hostname
   falls under a zone attached to the cluster, and the cluster's
   wildcard issuance is ready.
3. Otherwise a certificate of its own.

The important part is the word *otherwise*. A wildcard that
cannot be used is never an error — each failing condition simply
means "give this endpoint its own certificate", and the deploy
carries on. When both the production and the staging wildcard
issuance are ready on a cluster, production wins.

## The record and the certificate are two different things

A cluster serves all of its applications from one wildcard DNS
record *and* covers them with one wildcard certificate. These
are separate, and you can have one without the other.

`flui dns wildcard status` prints both, per zone: a `dns` line
for the record and a `certificate` line saying whether the
certificate covers everything or applications get one each. If
the record is missing, `flui dns wildcard publish` creates it —
and the difference you feel is propagation. With the record in
place a newly deployed application answers straight away; without
it, each new name publishes on its own and waits about a minute
for the world's resolvers to see it.

If a wildcard record already exists on the zone and points
somewhere that is not this cluster, Flui leaves it alone and
applications keep publishing their own names. Overwriting
somebody else's record would be the worse mistake.

## Renewal

In every mode and every shape, certificates renew themselves
ahead of expiry, with no action from anyone.

The renewal path matches the issuance path: a wildcard renews
through the DNS challenge against its zone, and multi-name and
per-endpoint certificates renew through the HTTP challenge served
from the cluster. A renewed wildcard reaches every application
covered by it on its own — nothing is redeployed and nothing has
to be reconciled by hand.

## Why an application's link is not there yet

An application's URL is published only once the endpoint is
settled *and* its certificate is no longer on its way. An address
is reachable minutes before a certificate is signed, and the link
Flui hands you is an `https://` one — showing it early would hand
a visitor a browser warning on the one screen that matters.

The link is withheld only while a certificate is pending or being
issued, which is a window that closes; a refresh resolves it. A
certificate that failed or expired does *not* hide the
application, because that is not a window — the link appears and
the browser says what is wrong, which is the more useful answer.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [DNS as part of the deploy contract](/concepts/13-dns-integration/) —
  where the zone, the wildcard record and the hostnames come
  from.
- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) —
  the rate-limit discussion behind production vs staging.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/) —
  why the wildcard depends on the provider exposing a DNS API
  Flui can write to.

sections.title: Identity and OIDC
sections.body:
Identity is the place where many self-hosted platforms quietly
install a user/password table and call it done. Flui takes a
different approach: it delegates identity to a real OIDC provider
running on the control cluster, with everything that comes with
that — sessions, federation, machine accounts, password reset,
MFA. There is no Flui-maintained user database; the authority for
who can sign in is the identity provider, and Flui uses what it
issues.

## The problem identity has to cover

The control plane of an installation needs to handle:

- Sign-in for the platform — the dashboard, the CLI, the API.
- Sign-in for the applications deployed on the platform.
- Long-lived access for automation: CI pipelines, scripts,
  third-party integrations.
- Eventually federation with corporate identity providers.
- Account lifecycle work that nobody wants to write: password
  reset, MFA, audit log of sign-in events.

Building any one of these is plausible. Building all of them and
keeping them maintained for years is not. So Flui delegates the
whole stack to an OIDC provider.

## How it works

The identity provider is installed on the control cluster
alongside the rest of the platform and serves as the single
sign-on authority for everything the installation runs.

What this gives the user out of the box:

- One login that covers the dashboard, the CLI and the API.
- Long-lived machine-to-machine keys for automation, scoped and
  revocable independently of any human user.
- A foundation that can later be wired to a corporate identity
  provider — federation is a configuration change on the
  identity provider, not a Flui code change.

The interactive login is a short, well-known dance: the CLI or
dashboard sends the user to the identity provider, the user
authenticates, and the result is a session the platform trusts.

On the roadmap, the same identity provider becomes the OIDC
authority for the applications deployed on the platform too: the
framework templates Flui ships, and any custom application that
wants it, will be able to plug into the installation's
identity provider with no per-app configuration on the
operator's side. The end state is "the user logs in once and
that login is good for every Flui surface and every app on the
installation".

Part of that end state is already here for catalog apps. When a
[composed catalog app](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/) is
installed in OIDC auth mode, Flui auto-provisions an OIDC web
client on the identity provider at install time — no manual client
registration — and records the created client and project ids
against the install so it can clean them up again when the app is
uninstalled. The app is wired to single sign-on without the
operator touching the identity provider directly.

### How `flui auth login` works

The CLI needs an authenticated session for every operation that
acts on a cluster — anything that reaches the Flui API of an
installation. Read-only local commands (managing contexts,
inspecting configuration) do not.

To get that session, the user runs `flui auth login`. The CLI
opens a browser to the installation's identity provider, the
user authenticates there, and the CLI receives the result back
through a local callback. At that point the CLI does not keep
using the short-lived OIDC bearer the flow produced: it
immediately exchanges it for a **long-lived machine-to-machine
key** identifying the workstation, and saves that key in the
active context. From then on the CLI authenticates with that
key, and the interactive login is run only when the user
explicitly logs in again.

The reason for the swap is straightforward: the OIDC bearer is
short-lived by design (minutes), and the CLI needs a session
that lasts as long as the user is working. A named M2M key
gives that, and can be revoked on its own without touching the
human user it was issued for.

## What a key is, once it is issued

A login lasts as long as somebody is at the keyboard. A key
does not. It goes into a configuration file on a workstation,
into a build pipeline, into the environment of an agent that
runs unattended for months.

That changes the two questions worth asking about it. What
happens if somebody reads the key where it sits? And how much
is it worth when it is presented?

### Flui cannot give a key back to you

What Flui stores for a key is a fingerprint of the key, not the
key. A copy of the database is therefore a copy of no live
credential: the stored value opens nothing, and sign-in still
works, because Flui fingerprints whatever the caller presents
and compares that.

The consequence is the part you have to plan around. The key
itself exists for one moment — the answer that creates it.
Nothing on the installation can hand it back afterwards. The
listing does not carry it: `flui auth api-keys` shows the name,
whether the key is revoked, when it was created, when it
expires, and the scopes it carries. Never the key.

So save it when you mint it. If it is lost it is lost — revoke
it with `flui auth revoke-api-key <id>` and mint another.
Revoking stops that one key immediately and touches nothing
else.

You rarely meet this by hand, because `flui auth login` mints a
key for you and writes it straight into the active profile.

### A key is worth its scopes, on every path

A key is issued *as* its person. Everything that person may do,
the key could do — unless the key declares scopes, which only
ever take away.

That rule used to hold in one place only: the agent toolbox.
The same key presented to the plain API with `curl`, or on a
live-updates connection, still carried its owner's whole
weight. A read-only key minted by an administrator was
read-only in the toolbox and nothing of the sort anywhere else.
It is now held to its scopes on all three paths.

A key that declares no scopes at all declares no ceiling and
loses nothing. That is the one `flui auth login` makes, and the
platform's own internal identities. Narrowing is the only thing
scopes ever do; no scope on any key can let anybody do
something they were not already allowed to do.

[Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/) is where
that rule lives in full, next to the other half of the
question: not what the key may do, but what its holder may
reach.

### Scopes come in groups, not a flat list

Choosing scopes one at a time is how least privilege dies. A
dozen checkboxes get granted whole out of fatigue, and the
person clicking cannot say afterwards what they agreed to.

So the unit somebody actually switches on is a **group**, and a
group is two decisions rather than a list:

- **the area** the agent is trusted with — applications,
  observability, backups, migrations, mail, access, or the
  infrastructure;
- **the depth** it may go to — **look**, **change** or
  **destroy**.

That is fifteen groups, and each one carries a single sentence
written for the person about to say yes. The sentence describes
what the group really carries rather than what its area is
called: "Deploy and operate applications" also reads logs and
metrics, because an agent that can deploy but cannot read why
the deploy failed is of no use to anyone.

A group is granted whole or refused whole. It never comes back
quietly smaller than it was asked for, so what somebody
consented to and what the key carries are the same sentence. A
group naming something the issuer does not hold themselves is
refused, and the refusal names *which* group caused it — which
is the only version of that message somebody can act on.

Three lines worth knowing before you pick:

- "Grant and revoke access" is a group of its own and appears
  inside no other. It can never ride along in "deploy my
  applications".
- No agent key can be given cluster deletion, however the
  groups are combined.
- Every scoped key also gets one thing nobody switches on: the
  ability to read the instructions for operating this
  installation. An agent that cannot read the rules cannot
  follow them.

**From the terminal, groups are not there yet.**
`flui auth generate-api-key` takes `--scope` (repeatable) or
`--unscoped`, and refuses if you name neither — omitting both
used to mean "my full weight", silently. Groups are an API and
dashboard concept today.

### The trap: agent scopes on a person's account

Because the identity provider is the authority, scopes can also
arrive from it, as roles on an account rather than on a key
Flui issued. That works, and it is a legitimate way to cap an
agent.

It has one sharp edge. Put those roles on a *person's* account
— meaning "these are for her agent" — and they cap every token
that account is ever issued. Her browser session included. The
dashboard turns read-only for no visible reason.

The behaviour is right: the credential *is* that account, and a
declared ceiling is a ceiling wherever it is presented. What
was missing was any way to find out. The refusal now says where
the scopes came from, so the answer is on the screen instead of
being guessed at.

Agent scopes belong on a machine account, not on a person. The
identity provider is good at machine accounts, and Flui will
mint one for an agent on request: a machine user carrying agent
scopes and nothing else — never a role from the access ladder,
because a scope narrows and a role would hand the agent
standing of its own. Its secret, like a key, is returned once.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/) — the
  second question, and the one a refusal is usually about.
- [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/) —
  the identity provider as a platform component on the control
  cluster.
- [CLI: Authentication](/cli/authentication/) — the
  command-by-command reference for logging in and generating
  machine-to-machine keys.

sections.title: The app concept
sections.body:
In Flui, "app" is a first-class concept. It is the unit you
deploy, observe, scale and retire — the object every CLI command
under `flui app *` and every Apps page in the dashboard operates
on. An app is not the same as a running process or a single
piece of cluster infrastructure: it is the bundle of name and
slug, source, runtime configuration, endpoints, certificates,
builds, releases, logs and metrics that together describe one
deployable thing and everything that surrounds it during its
life on the cluster.

This chapter is the conceptual definition. The manifest that
describes an app for Flui has its own chapter
([The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/)), and
the distinction between **Application** and **CatalogApp** has
its own chapter too
([Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/)).

## What an app carries

An app, regardless of where it comes from, carries the same set
of things:

- **A name and a slug.** A stable slug unique within the
  installation and a human-friendly name. The slug is what every
  other surface refers to.
- **A cluster.** Every app lives on one cluster at a time — the
  cluster whose dashboard you opened, or the one you pointed the
  CLI at. Moving it to another cluster is one operation now, not
  a second deploy you do by hand; see
  [Moving an app to another cluster](#moving-an-app-to-another-cluster)
  below.
- **A source.** Where the workload comes from. Today there are
  three: a container image pulled from a registry, a source
  repository that Flui builds for you against a `flui.yaml`
  manifest, or an entry picked from the Flui catalog of
  ready-made building blocks. The source decides what happens
  before the workload runs; the rest of the app shape is the
  same regardless of which one it is.
- **A runtime configuration.** Replica count and scaling
  limits, healthcheck, ports, volumes — the operational shape of
  the workload once it is up.
- **An endpoint, or none at all.** An app can declare that it
  should be reachable from outside the cluster, in which case the
  deploy flow gives it a hostname and a TLS certificate to match.
  An app that does not need to be reached — a background worker,
  a job — runs without one. The endpoint itself is its own
  concept, covered in
  [DNS as part of the deploy contract](/concepts/13-dns-integration/).
  How that reachability is shaped — public on its own domain, or
  internal behind the dashboard — is the *exposure* axis, below.
- **A release history.** Every deploy and every rollback is
  recorded as a new release entry, append-only. The current
  release is a pointer into that history.

The sections below take the points that need more than a line —
resources, configuration and secrets, moving, removal, scaling,
observability — and give each one a paragraph of its own.

## Resources: CPU and memory

Every app declares two numbers per instance: the **request** —
what the cluster reserves and guarantees — and the **limit** —
the ceiling the instance cannot go past. The scheduler places an
instance only if the node can honour the request; the runtime
enforces the limit at peak.

The dashboard shows both numbers and the current usage side by
side, and flags the app visually when the request is much higher
than what the workload uses (over-allocated, paying for capacity
that sits idle) or when the usage runs close to the limit
(under-allocated, one bad minute away from being killed). The
operator sees these signals without having to go looking for them.

There is also an automatic safety net for the very first launch
of an app: if the workload runs out of memory in its early
minutes, before its steady-state behaviour is even known, Flui
can nudge the allocation upward on its own so the app gets a
chance to start. The behaviour is meant for the bootstrap window,
not for routine operation.

## The capacity gate

Before an app is installed from the catalog, Flui adds up the
resource needs of the app — and of every component it brings, if
it is a composed stack — and refuses the install up front if the
cluster does not have room, keeping roughly a **10% safety
margin** in reserve. When it refuses, the message names the
shortfall: how much CPU and memory the install needs versus how
much is free.

The gate is deliberately **asymmetric**, and it is worth knowing
why:

- **CPU is gated on requests.** CPU is *compressible* —
  oversubscribing it only throttles a workload, it does not kill
  it — so the gate only needs the scheduling floor (the request)
  to fit.
- **Memory is gated on limits.** Memory is *incompressible* — an
  instance holds the RAM it touches up to its limit, and a node
  that runs past what it can allocate starts killing workloads —
  so the gate uses the peak (the limit, falling back to the
  request when a component declares no limit).

In short: CPU you can crowd, memory you cannot, and the gate
reflects exactly that. This is the same arithmetic the dashboard
deploy wizard runs, so the two surfaces agree on what will fit.

## Volumes and storage

An app that needs to keep data across restarts declares one or
more **volumes** — a name, a mount path inside the workload, a
size. Where the data physically lives — the cluster's shared
storage, where any node can reach it and the app can be moved
freely, or a node's local disk, where access is faster but the
app is pinned to that node — is decided by the cluster's
storage configuration. That choice carries implications for
placement and for what happens during cluster operations like a
node resize. The full story is in
[Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/).

Volumes are also the reason removal is a bigger decision than it
used to be. See
[Removing an app takes its data](#removing-an-app-takes-its-data).

## Port protocol

Every app's main port carries a **protocol** — `http` or `tcp`,
defaulting to `http`. It is a small field with one large
consequence: it gates observability. An `http` app is scraped for
the platform metrics like request rates; a `tcp` app — a
database, a message broker, anything that does not speak HTTP on
its port — is deliberately *not* HTTP-scraped, because there is
nothing meaningful to scrape and probing it would only add noise.
Declaring `tcp` is how you tell Flui "this is a wire protocol,
not a web service".

Readiness probes can also carry **HTTP headers** when the bare
path-and-port check is not enough — most often a `Host:` header,
so an app that only answers for a specific virtual host still
passes its health check during a rolling restart instead of
being failed by a request its router does not recognise.

## How an app is reached

Independently of *whether* an app has an endpoint, an app that
does is reached in one of two ways:

- **Public.** The app gets a public endpoint: a hostname, a TLS
  certificate, and routing from the open internet to the app.
  This is the default and the right answer for anything meant to
  be reached from outside.
- **Internal.** The app gets only a cluster-internal address — no
  public hostname, no certificate, no DNS record to manage. It is
  reachable solely through the dashboard's authenticating proxy.
