  This is the right answer for an admin tool or a console you want
  behind the platform's own login rather than on the public
  internet.

Apps the catalog marks **privatizable** can choose between the
two at install time; others are fixed at whatever their manifest
declares.

There is a third shape you do not choose, you inherit: a
**building block** installed from the catalog — a database, a
cache, a queue — is reachable only from inside its own cluster.
It has no public hostname and no proxy route at all. That is the
point of it: the thing that reads it is another app on the same
cluster, and nothing else should be able to knock on the door.
To reach one from your own machine, Flui opens a tunnel for you
([Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/)).

### Use the URL the app gives you

Each app's API representation carries the authoritative links it
should be reached by. A public app exposes a real `url` of the
form `https://<fqdn><entrypointPath>`; an internal app exposes an
`internalUrl` instead. The important rule — stated here because
it is easy to get wrong — is that any consumer of these (the
dashboard's "Open" button, the assistant) must use the value
**verbatim** and must **not** reconstruct a URL from the slug.
The slug is not the hostname; the real link accounts for the
endpoint's actual domain and path, and only the stored `url` /
`internalUrl` is guaranteed to be correct.

There is a second rule, and it is about timing. A URL is
published only once the endpoint really serves — reconciled, with
a valid certificate. Before that the app shows no URL at all,
which is honest: a link that is written down before it works
sends people to a browser error and teaches them not to trust the
next one.

## Configuration and secrets

Plain configuration reaches the workload as environment variables
and lives with the app. Sensitive values follow the same
name-value shape but are stored encrypted and **write-only**: the
surfaces show the names so you know what is set, and never the
values. A sensitive value can be overwritten at any time; it
cannot be read back once stored.

Three things want to own those values, and the order between
them is now settled.

**The manifest wins for the keys it declares.** This is a
reversal. A value pinned by hand used to beat the `flui.yaml`
forever, invisibly and with no way back. Now every deploy lets
the manifest reclaim every key it declares, and a hand-set value
only survives on a key the manifest does *not* declare. When a
reclaim overwrites a pin, the deploy says so rather than
swapping the value in silence.

**Explicit overrides still win over both.** A value passed at
deploy time with `--env` or `--env-file` is deliberate, and it
beats the manifest and the stored value alike.

**A linked value is never clobbered.** When a key points at a
building block's own credential — the password of the database
Flui installed for you — a plain manifest value does not
overwrite it. Replacing a live reference with a copied-out
literal is exactly how a credential leaks into a place nobody
remembers to rotate.

Two consequences are worth stating on their own.

**"Declared but not resolved" is not "removed".** A key the
manifest declares while getting its value from somewhere else —
from a person, from another service — keeps whatever is stored
for it. Only a key the manifest stops declaring altogether is
read as a deliberate removal.

**"Awaiting a value" is a real state.** A sensitive key that has
been declared but never supplied is listed alongside the others,
labelled `awaiting a value`. It is not blank, not missing and
not an error, and asking for the list does not fail because one
is outstanding. `flui app env list` shows the three states side
by side — plain values, which sensitive keys are set, and which
are still waiting — and `flui app env set <app> <KEY>` asks for
the value rather than taking it as an argument, so it never
lands in your shell history.

This matters most when an agent is involved. An agent can
declare that a key is needed; it cannot supply one. The pending
state is what lets it hand the job to you and stop, instead of
inventing a placeholder.

A changed value does not reach a running instance by itself. The
app receives it on its next deploy or restart — the CLI tells you
so when you set one.

The whole flow, on all three surfaces, is
[Set an application's configuration and secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/).

## How an app is classified

The dashboard groups apps along two orthogonal axes:

- **Category.** Two values: *system* and *user*. System apps are
  the components of the platform itself — the API, the dashboard,
  the identity provider, the database, the observability stack —
  installed and reconciled by Flui as part of the control
  cluster. User apps are everything you deploy. Both kinds live
  in the same table and are operated through the same surfaces;
  the difference is that system apps are protected from
  accidental deletion (a deletion command refuses unless forced).
- **Kind.** A coarser grouping by purpose: *database*, *tool*,
  *application*, *system*. Used by the dashboard to organise the
  Apps page in a way that matches how operators think about what
  is running. It does not change the lifecycle.

These two are distinct from the manifest's own `kind:` field
(`Application` vs `CatalogApp`), which describes where the app
comes from, not what it does. See
[Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/) for
that side.

## The lifecycle

An app sits in one of a handful of steady states:

- **Awaiting build** — for apps built from source, while the
  build is in flight and the platform is waiting for an image.
- **Running** — the app is up and serving its work.
- **Degraded** — the app is up but not at full health (some
  replicas down, a healthcheck failing intermittently).
- **Stopped** — scaled to zero on purpose; the configuration is
  still there, no instances are running.
- **Failed** — a terminal failure (the last build failed, the
  last deploy failed, an unrecoverable condition was hit).
- **Deleted** — the app has been torn down; the row remains for
  audit.

During an operation — a deploy, a rollback, a tear-down — the app
briefly passes through transient states that the dashboard
surfaces as progress indicators rather than steady values.

## Operations

The everyday operations on an app are these:

- **Deploy / redeploy.** Apply (or re-apply) the app's
  configuration. For image-based apps a redeploy can also pin a
  different image version; for source-built apps a redeploy
  reuses an existing build instead of building again. Every
  deploy appends a new release entry.
- **Rollback.** Move the current release pointer back to a
  previous entry. Importantly, this *adds* a new release entry
  (marked as a rollback) rather than rewinding history — the
  trail of what happened stays intact. Rollback is a dashboard
  action; the CLI lists releases but does not roll one back.
- **Start / stop.** Bring the app's replicas back from zero, or
  scale them to zero while keeping the configuration in place.
  Stopping is reversible without re-deploying.
- **Restart.** Replace the running instances without changing
  the release. See the rolling-restart section below for the
  shape of this operation.
- **Scale.** Set the replica count explicitly.
- **Move.** Take the app to another cluster in one operation.
- **Delete.** Remove the app from the cluster — and, now, the
  data it was keeping. Read the removal section below before you
  run it. System apps require an explicit force flag.

## Rolling restart

When the running instances of an app have to be replaced — to
pick up new configuration or new secrets, or just to clear a
wedged state — Flui rolls them: new instances come up first, and
only when they are healthy do the old ones go away. The replica
count never drops below the declared number, so the app keeps
serving throughout. The platform also triggers a rolling restart
on its own whenever a change it can apply in place needs to
reach the running instances.

## Moving an app to another cluster

This page used to say that moving an app was not a real
operation — that you deployed it again on the other cluster and
sorted out the address yourself. That is no longer true, and it
was the sentence most likely to talk somebody into a bad
afternoon.

Moving is now **one operation with a cutover in the middle**.
Flui builds the copy on the destination cluster while the source
keeps serving. When the copy is ready, the app is rebound to the
destination and its address follows it. You can let that happen
as soon as the copy is ready, or park it and cut over yourself
when you are watching.

Two properties are worth holding on to:

- **Before the cutover, nothing on the source has changed.**
  Aborting tears the destination down and leaves the original
  exactly as it was.
- **After the cutover, the source workload is still there,
  drained.** Destroying it is a separate, deliberate, irreversible
  step.

There are limits, and they are refusals rather than surprises. A
move of the app alone is for an app that holds no data of its
own: an app with volumes, an app pinned to a dedicated node, or
an app wired to another app's credential is refused with a
message saying which. Data moves through its own operation, and
an app together with its database moves through a third that
cuts both over at once. The full picture is
[Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/).

## Removing an app takes its data

Removing an app now removes the storage it was using. Before
this, a volume outlived the app that made it and simply sat
there — nothing listed it, nobody knew, and the bill kept coming.
That was never a decision anybody made; it was a default nobody
had ever looked at.

Because this is not recoverable, **every surface shows what will
be lost before it asks**. The confirmation names the volumes and
how much data they hold, and for a composed install it names the
whole install, because that is what the removal takes.

The important detail is what happens when Flui cannot read the
storage — an unreachable cluster, credentials it cannot open. In
that case it reports the loss as **unknown**, never as *none*.
A reassuring "no data will be lost" that turns out to be a
failed read is the worst sentence a delete prompt can print, so
it does not print it. When you see *unknown*, assume there is
data.

This repairs the future only. Every installation that has been
running for a while still holds volumes from removals that
happened before it landed, and `flui cluster volumes` is the
listing that finally shows them, with a way to remove them one at
a time. One honest limit: the scan errs by omission. It only
reports a volume when nothing mounts it and no existing app owns
it, so a volume created by something Flui did not write, and
carrying none of its labels, will never appear in it.

The removal flow on each surface is
[Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/).

## Automatic scaling

This page used to file automatic scaling under "roadmap". The
loop exists.

An app carries a scaling setting, and when that setting is on,
Flui applies a real autoscaler beside the app on every deploy.
It watches the app's own resource use and moves the replica count
between the app's declared floor and ceiling — 1 and 5 when the
app declares neither. What it watches is what the app asked to be
watched on: CPU utilisation, memory utilisation, or both, given
as target percentages. An app can also say how fast it is willing
to move in each direction — how many instances at a time, and how
long the autoscaler must be sure before it acts — which is how
you stop a spiky workload from thrashing.

Two boundaries keep this honest:

- **Building blocks are not autoscaled.** A database or a queue
  installed from the catalog runs as a single stateful workload,
  and no autoscaler is attached to it. Scaling a database by
  copying it is not scaling.
- **Setting a count by hand still works.** `flui app scale`
  sets an explicit replica count, and stopping an app is that
  same operation at zero.

Do not confuse this with a cluster buying itself more machines.
That is a separate decision, with its own written consent and its
own ceilings in money —
[What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).
One scales the copies of your app inside the room; the other
decides whether to rent another room.

## Logs and metrics

Every app has the same observability surfaces from day one, on
both the dashboard and the CLI:

- **Logs.** Streamed from every instance, queryable by level and
  free-text search.
- **Metrics.** CPU, memory, network and replica counts over time
  — the baseline Flui collects for every app it manages, with
  no setup on the app side.
- **Live status.** Replicas ready, current release, health at a
  glance.
- **Crashes.** A summarised view of recent crashes: exit codes,
  out-of-memory events, restart counts, last log lines before
  the crash.

All four read from the same central backend on the control
cluster — the position observability has in the platform is
covered in
[Observability is not an afterthought](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/).

## Going deeper when something is wrong

For the cases where the everyday views are not enough — a first
release that won't start, a sudden burst of crashes, a
configuration that subtly breaks the workload — the dashboard
groups two deeper tools under an **Advanced** menu on every app:

- **Diagnoses.** An automated read of recent failures that goes
  beyond the raw crash list: it correlates exit codes,
  out-of-memory events, healthcheck failures and the log lines
  around them, and surfaces a probable cause and a suggested
  remediation (a missing environment variable to add, a memory
  limit to raise). Unresolved diagnoses are also shown as a
  banner on the app's overview, so they cannot be missed.
- **A per-instance deep read.** An on-demand snapshot of every
  running instance of the app, with the low-level detail an
  operator needs when the higher-level views fall short.
  Refreshed on request rather than continuously, so the cluster
  is not paying for a constant detailed read of every app.

These surfaces are designed for the moments when the everyday
ones — logs, metrics, status, crashes — have stopped being
enough. They are not part of the routine flow.

## System apps are apps

A specific point worth being explicit about: the platform's own
components — the API, the dashboard, the identity provider, the
database, the observability stack — are themselves apps in this
model. They appear in the app list, they have releases, they
expose logs and metrics, they go through the same lifecycle as
user apps. What sets them apart is the *system* category and the
protection it carries: their delete operation refuses unless the
operator explicitly forces it. They are not special-cased in any
other way.

This homogeneity matters. Operators do not learn one set of
commands for "Flui's own bits" and another for "the apps I
deployed". The way you read the dashboard's logs is the way you
read your app's logs.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Set an application's configuration and secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/) —
  the precedence rules above, applied on each surface.
- [Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/) —
  the three kinds of move and the shape of a cutover.
- [Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/) —
  what the confirmation tells you, and the volumes older
  removals left behind.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/) — the
  declarative shape that produces an app.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/) —
  the two kinds of manifest that produce apps, and what
  distinguishes them.
- [Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/) —
  where an app's volumes physically live and how dedicated apps
  land on a worker.
- [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/) —
  multi-component installs and how the capacity gate sums them.

sections.title: The Flui manifest
sections.body:
A manifest is the thing you want, written down. It sits in
your repository, next to the code it describes, and it can
be read, reviewed and reverted like any other file. Flui
reads it. Flui does not own it.

That distinction is the whole point of this chapter, and it
is also why the vocabulary keeps growing: once people have
a file that says "this is what I want, apply it", they want
one for the next thing too.

## A spec, not a config format

The authoritative schema lives in its own repository —
[`flui-cloud/flui-spec`](https://github.com/flui-cloud/flui-spec) —
with its own versioning, narrative docs, JSON Schemas and
example manifests. The TypeScript types and the validator
are published to npm as
[`@flui-cloud/spec`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@flui-cloud/spec),
which Flui pulls in like any other dependency. Flui
consumes the schema; it does not maintain it.

This split is deliberate. A manifest that named a
Flui-internal concept, or that needed a Flui-specific
extension, would quietly tie you to one tool. Keeping the
spec outside and depending on it makes that impossible by
construction: the same file can be read by a different tool
tomorrow.

## Four kinds of document

Three kinds are published in the spec:

- **Application** — an application built from a source
  repository and deployed to a cluster. The one you write
  yourself.
- **CatalogApp** — a pre-packaged building block (a
  database, a queue, an admin tool) installed from the
  catalog with the configuration the catalog publishes.
- **AccessPolicy** — who may reach what. `flui iam export`
  writes one as a snapshot of every grant; `flui iam apply
  -f` reads it back.

There is a fourth kind, and it is worth being honest about
where it comes from:

- **ScalingGroup** — what a cluster may buy for itself and
  where it must stop. `flui scaling export` writes it,
  `flui scaling apply -f` reads it back. It is Flui's own
  document, not part of the published spec, and it carries
  no `apiVersion`. It borrows the shape — a `kind`, a name,
  blocks underneath — because a file that reads like the
  others is easier to review than a new format would be.

One rule on that file is unlike the others and catches
people out: a ScalingGroup file is the **whole** group. A
field left out is a field reset to its default, not a field
left alone. Several groups can live in one file, separated
by `---`. What the group is for is the subject of
[Scaling groups](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).

The rest of this chapter is about the **Application**
shape.

## What an Application manifest says

An Application manifest has exactly six things at the top:
`kind`, `apiVersion`, `metadata`, `build`, `deploy` and
`environments`. Under `deploy` there are nine: `port`,
`exposure`, `healthcheck`, `resources`, `scaling`,
`domain`, `env`, `volumes` and `startCommand`.

Each answers one operational question:

- **Name.** A stable identifier, under `metadata`. Every
  other surface — dashboard, CLI, observability — uses it,
  so the spec restricts it to a lowercase form that works
  in a hostname.
- **How to build the image.** A pointer to a Dockerfile in
  the repository, or a request to let the platform detect
  the framework and build accordingly. Also the build
  context and the build arguments. The block stays at the
  level of *what* and *where*, never *how* the build runs.
- **How to run it.** The port your code listens on, the
  healthcheck to probe, replica limits, CPU and memory
  (either explicit numbers or a t-shirt-sized preset), an
  optional start command.
- **How it is reached.** `exposure: public` means a public
  address, with a name and a certificate. `exposure:
  internal` means no public address at all: other
  applications on the cluster can reach it, and you can
  reach it through the dashboard. Public is the default.
  The `domain` block then says whether a hostname should be
  assigned automatically, which one to use instead, and
  which certificate flow to take.
- **Configuration and secrets.** A list of environment
  variables. An entry can carry a plain value, ask for a
  secret to be generated, point at an existing secret,
  point at a sibling application in the same project, or
  declare a value somebody must supply at install time.
- **Volumes.** Persistent volumes the application needs,
  each with a name, a mount path and a size.

The schema is **closed**: a key it does not name is an
error, not an extension. But closed is not frozen. The list
grows when the spec grows — `exposure` and `environments`
are both newer than the first version of this page — so
treat what is written here as today's vocabulary rather
than a final one. `flui app manifest` prints the field
reference straight from the schema Flui has installed, and
`flui app manifest --example` prints an annotated file to
start from. Both run offline.

## One file, several environments

`environments` is a map. You choose the keys —
`production`, `staging`, `preview` — and each entry names
the git **branch** it belongs to. Deploy that branch and
the entry is laid over the base: environment values first,
then resources, replica limits and domain.

Two details decide how this behaves in practice.

`build` cannot be overridden per environment. The spec
leaves it out on purpose, so what the file says about
building an image is the same everywhere, and only what
surrounds the image changes.

An entry that names no branch never matches anything. And
a validation that names no branch reports the base spec,
because there is no branch to pick an entry with.

## The composed CatalogApp surface

A `CatalogApp` can describe more than one workload. A
**composed** entry (`type: composed`) drops the
single-image body and carries a `components` list instead,
plus a few coordination blocks with no equivalent in the
Application shape:

- **`components`.** The workloads the entry bundles. Each
  has its own image, environment and resources, and runs as
  its own app. A component can declare `dependsOn` (other
  components that must be healthy first) and `when.option`
  (include this only when a named option is on).
- **`auth`.** Which sign-in strategies the entry supports —
  `auth.modes` lists them, `auth.default` names the
  fallback. The modes are `oidc`, `proxy`, `native` and
  `none`; the chosen one is an install-time answer, not a
  constant in the file.
- **`options`.** Install-time switches, each with a `key`,
  a `label` and a `default`. Components and post-install
  steps gate on them.
- **`postInstall`.** Steps that run once the components are
  up — an HTTP call, or a command inside a component — each
  conditioned on the chosen sign-in mode or on an option.

These blocks lean on a few **templating tokens** the
consuming tool resolves at install time rather than when
the file is written: a component's own public hostname
(`{{self.fqdn}}`) and, when OIDC is the chosen mode, the
provisioned client's `{{oidc.clientId}}`,
`{{oidc.clientSecret}}` and `{{oidc.issuerUrl}}`. The full
model is the subject of
[Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/).

## What the manifest deliberately omits

The exclusions matter as much as the contents:

- **Where it runs.** A manifest does not choose a cluster,
  a provider or a region. Whoever runs the deploy picks the
  target. The same file goes to staging on one invocation
  and to production on the next.
- **Credential values.** Secret values never live in the
  file. They are referenced by name, generated by the
  platform, or asked for at install time.
- **How the build runs.** The file says *what* to build,
  not where or how. The build runner belongs to the tool.
- **Runtime-specific resources.** The manifest describes
  the application, not the shape it eventually takes on
  whatever runs it.
- **Tool-specific extensions.** Internal identifiers and
  vendor tuning are not allowed. Additions go through the
  spec, where every implementation gets them on the same
  footing.

## Three fields that belong to the install, not the file

The same repository can be installed twice, and the two
installs cannot share a name or a hostname. So three fields
can be overridden when you deploy: `--name`, `--exposure`
and `--domain`.

These are stored on the application and re-applied on every
later deploy, which is what stops the next deploy from
anyone else's machine silently reverting an install to the
manifest's domain. When an override shadows something the
manifest says, the deploy prints both values rather than
quietly winning.

One of them is sharper than it looks. `--name` is part of
what identifies an application — cluster, repository,
branch and name together. Passing a new one installs the
same repository a second time instead of updating the
first, so once you have used it, pass it on every deploy
that targets that install.

## The manifest owns the keys it declares

For environment variables, the file wins. A key the
manifest declares is reclaimed by the manifest on every
deploy, even if somebody had pinned a value on it in the
dashboard. A key the manifest does **not** declare keeps
whatever was set. Values passed explicitly at deploy time
beat both.

Two exceptions are worth knowing. A key linked to a real
secret is never overwritten by a plain value from the file.
And a key the manifest declares but cannot resolve — one
whose value comes from somewhere else — keeps its stored
value. Only a key the manifest stops declaring at all is
read as a deliberate removal.

## Validation is two halves

Asking whether a file parses is not the same as asking
whether it would work here, and the second question is the
one that costs you eight minutes of a failed build.

**The first half is the schema.** It needs nothing: no
cluster, no login, no network. Flui validates against the
same published schema it deploys with, so the answer cannot
drift from what the deploy accepts.

**The second half asks this installation.** Seven
questions, none of which a schema can answer:

- the **target cluster** — does one answer to that id, and
  can it take a deploy;
- the **source repository** — is it connected to this
  account;
- the **build and registry credentials** — can this account
  build the image and push it;
- **room on the cluster** — do the CPU and memory it asks
  for fit what is free right now;
- **where it lands** — a workload cluster, or the control
  cluster that also runs the API, the dashboard and
  identity;
- **what this deploy does** — create a new application, or
  update one that already answers to this identity;
- **how it is reached** — internal, public under a name of
  yours, or public with no name bound yet.

Each answer is one of four: pass, warn, fail, or
**unknown**. Unknown is a real answer and never blocks: an
installation that could not be read has refused nothing,
and reporting that as a failure would send you rewriting a
manifest that was fine. Warnings are consequences to be
aware of, not problems to fix — deploying onto the control
cluster is supported, and says so as a warning.

The check also hands back the manifest **as it would
actually be applied**, with the branch entry and the stored
overrides already merged in. That is usually more useful
than the verdict, because it is the first time you see what
the file plus this installation actually amount to.

Two things follow from all this. A manifest can satisfy the
schema perfectly and fail every one of the checks. And when
the second half cannot run — not signed in, or no cluster
named — the output says which half ran, instead of letting
silence read as "everything was checked".

`flui deploy --validate-only` runs both halves and writes
nothing; add `--json` for a machine-readable answer. `flui
catalog validate <file>` runs the schema half only, and
takes any kind. Agents have the same check as a tool.

## The names are still moving

One honest caveat, because it will bite somebody.

The published spec package and the product currently
disagree about the names of the access roles. The spec
still lists `viewer`, `editor` and `manager`. The product
renamed that ladder and now accepts `viewer`, `operator`,
`maintainer` and `owner`.

They disagree in both directions. An AccessPolicy the
product accepts is rejected by `flui catalog validate`,
which validates against the published schema. A policy
written with the spec's names is refused by `flui iam apply
-f`. Neither tool is broken; they are reading two versions
of the same idea.

Do not treat either list as settled. For an AccessPolicy,
run `flui iam roles` — it lists the roles this installation
will actually accept, and which ones you are allowed to
hand out. The ladder itself is described in
[Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/).

## From manifest to running application

At deploy time Flui reads the file, lays the branch entry
over it, merges the overrides stored on the install, and
turns the result into whatever the target needs to host the
application. The manifest is the intent; what runs is the
realisation. Every deploy produces that realisation again
from the file, which is what keeps the file worth reading.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [`flui-cloud/flui-spec`](https://github.com/flui-cloud/flui-spec) —
  the authoritative spec: field-by-field schema, narrative
  docs, JSON Schemas and examples.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — what
  the manifest produces.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/)
  — the other kind and what distinguishes it.
- [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/)
  — the multi-component `CatalogApp` shape in depth.
- [Scaling groups](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/) — what the
  fourth document kind is for.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/) —
  the roles an `AccessPolicy` names.
- [Build pipeline today and tomorrow](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/)
  — what happens between a manifest and a running
  container.
- [DNS as part of the deploy contract](/concepts/13-dns-integration/)
  and [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/)
  — what the domain block triggers.

sections.title: Catalog vs Application
sections.body:
A `flui.yaml` declares one of two kinds: `Application` or
`CatalogApp`. They share the same outer envelope and the same
identity model, and they end up as the same kind of app inside
the platform — same lifecycle, same operations, same observability
surfaces. What separates them is one thing only: **where the
container image comes from**.

This chapter is about that distinction, and about how the two
combine.

## kind: Application — your code

An `Application` manifest describes an application built from a
source repository. The user owns the code and the manifest sits
in the repo's root. At deploy time the platform builds an image
from that source, pushes it to a container registry, and then
deploys the image to the target cluster. The manifest's `build`
block carries the *what* of the build (which Dockerfile, which
context, or "let the platform pick"); the rest of the manifest
describes how the resulting image should run.

This is the path for "deploy my own service" — a web frontend, a
backend API, a worker — anything the user authors and iterates
on.

## kind: CatalogApp — ready-to-install software

A `CatalogApp` manifest describes a pre-packaged application
whose image already exists on a container registry. The
manifest references the image by registry, name and tag, and
adds the installation parameters that make it usable: admin
credentials to generate, volume sizes, optional features. There
is no build step — picking a catalog entry produces the same
kind of running app as building one from source, just without
the build pipeline in front of it.

`CatalogApp` is not limited to entries Flui curates. **Any
container image — yours, someone else's, public or private —
can become a deployable application by wrapping it in a
`CatalogApp` manifest**: declare its registry coordinates, the
port it listens on, the healthcheck, the volumes it needs, and
you have a deployable manifest you can run through Flui the
same way the curated entries are. The curated catalog and a
user-authored manifest sit on the same path; the only
difference is who wrote the file.

## The same lifecycle on both sides

Once deployed, an application from source and an application
from the catalog behave identically inside the platform. The
same commands stop, start, restart, scale and delete them. The
same dashboard views show their logs, their metrics, their
status and their crashes. The same release history records
every deploy and rollback. The platform does not maintain "two
toolchains, one for your code and one for packaged software":
both kinds of app live in the same list and are operated the
same way.

This homogeneity is the point of having a single manifest envelope
and a single app model behind it.

## Three flavours of catalog entry

The catalog distinguishes three kinds of entries, by what they
are meant to do:

- **Standalone.** A complete application that runs on its own
  and serves its own purpose — an admin tool, a self-hosted
  service, anything you might install just to use.
- **Building block.** An application meant to back other
  applications rather than be reached directly — most often a
  database or a message queue. Building blocks are rarely the
  user's end goal; they are what a user `Application` is
  composed on top of.
- **Composed.** An entry that bundles several coordinated
  workloads installed together as a single unit — a database, a
  cache and an app tier, say, provisioned and torn down as one
  atomic install. Each bundled component is rendered as its own
  workload, the components are brought up in dependency order, and
  the whole stack shows up as a single bundle in your app list.
  This is covered in depth in
  [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/).

## Composing catalog entries

Catalog entries also compose with each other. A `composed`
catalog entry can declare that it needs a building-block entry
(typically a database or a queue) to function, and at install
time the operator picks how the dependency is satisfied:

- **A dedicated instance** is provisioned alongside the
  consumer, inside the same install operation: the building
  block is created first, the consumer on top once the building
  block is healthy, with the credentials the building block
  generates exposed to the consumer as injected configuration.
- **An existing instance** already deployed on the cluster is
  reused: the install only deploys the consumer and wires it to
  the existing building block. The building block's lifecycle is
  not part of the current operation.

Either way, consumer and building block end up side by side in
the application list, each with its own lifecycle and operations
once they are running.

## One manifest, more than one install

A manifest is a file. An install is a running thing on a
cluster. They are not the same, and the difference shows up
the moment you want one manifest running twice — production
and staging from the same repository, say, on the same
cluster.

Both installs read the same `flui.yaml`. They cannot both be
called what the file calls them, and they cannot both answer
on the hostname the file names. So three fields can be
overridden when you install:

- **name** — what this install is called;
- **exposure** — `public` or `internal`;
- **domain** — the hostname it answers on.

Everything else stays with the manifest. The file still owns
the build, the port, the resources and the configuration
defaults. The overrides are the short list of things that
belong to *this* copy rather than to the code.

### The name is identity, not decoration

On the `Application` path an app is identified by four things
together: the cluster, the repository, the branch and the
name. So changing the name does not rename anything. A deploy
carrying a name Flui has not seen installs that repository a
**second time**, next to the first.

That cuts both ways, and this is the part that surprises
people. Exposure and domain are remembered on the install and
keep winning over the manifest on later deploys — otherwise
the next deploy from anyone's machine would quietly drag an
install back to the manifest's hostname. The name is
deliberately not remembered, because it is what the lookup
uses to find the install in the first place. Pass it on every
deploy that targets that install; leave it off once and the
next deploy aims at a different application.

### The catalog side does not have that problem

Installing a catalog entry twice always produces two separate
installs, each with its own generated identifier. A second
install never lands on top of the first, whatever you call
it. There the name is a label you read in the app list, not a
key.

Exposure works differently too: an entry is only offered the
public-or-internal choice if it declares that it can run
privately. The rest run the way their manifest says.

## Where each side lives

A short summary of where the moving pieces sit for each kind:

| | `kind: Application` | `kind: CatalogApp` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manifest | In the user's repository | Curated by the catalog, or user-authored against the spec |
| Image | Built from source by the platform's build pipeline, pushed to a registry | Pulled from a public registry; no build step |
| Configuration | `build` + the runtime blocks | Installation parameters published by the entry |
| Install-time overrides | Name, exposure and domain; the name is part of the app's identity | Name and address; exposure only where the entry allows it |
| Lifecycle operations | The same on both sides |
| Observability | The same on both sides |

## Writing a custom catalog entry

Anything that runs as a container can be a `CatalogApp`. The
contract is light: the image must be reachable from the cluster,
the manifest must declare the port and the healthcheck the
runtime needs to know the app is up, and any persistent state
the app keeps has to be expressible as a volume. A user can
write a `CatalogApp` against any image they want and deploy it
through the same path as the curated entries.

The curated set of catalog entries is itself the result of this
contract — each entry is just a `CatalogApp` manifest, written
once, reviewed, and made available to everyone.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — what both
  kinds produce, regardless of where the image came from.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/) — the
  shared envelope both kinds sit under.
- [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/) —
  the composed flavour in depth: components, auth modes, options
  and the install-time templating.
- [Install an application from the catalog](/tasks/install-from-the-catalog/)
  — doing it: finding an entry, the answers it asks for at
  install time, and the name, address and exposure you can
  override.
- [Deploy an application from your repository](/tasks/deploy-an-application/)
  — the `Application` path end to end, including what `--name`
  does to identity.
- [Framework templates](/concepts/19-framework-templates/) — how
  templates accelerate the `Application` path.
- [Build pipeline today and tomorrow](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/)
  — what happens between an `Application` manifest and a running
  container.

sections.title: Framework templates
sections.body:
The hardest step for a new self-hosted application is not the
deployment — it is the gap between "I have an idea in a
framework" and "I have a repository that the platform can
actually build and deploy". Templates close that gap. One
command produces a repository that already contains everything
Flui needs to build, deploy and observe the resulting
application; from that moment on, it is the user's code.

## What a template gives you

A Flui template is a real, working starting point for an
application in a specific framework. When the platform creates
a new repository from a template, the result is not a skeleton
to fill in — it is a buildable, deployable application that you
can clone, change, push, and watch deploy without writing any
infrastructure file yourself.

In particular, every template repository comes with:

- A **Dockerfile** that builds a production-ready image of the
  framework, using the framework's idiomatic base.
- A **`flui.yaml`** that declares the application: its name, the
  port it listens on, the healthcheck path, sensible defaults
  for resources and scaling.
- A **healthcheck endpoint** wired in the framework's own way —
  an API route in JavaScript fullstack frameworks, an actuator
  in Spring Boot, a view in Django, and so on — so the
  healthcheck the manifest points at actually answers from day
  one.
- A **build pipeline** that the platform can drive end-to-end,
  triggered by a push to the repository.

The deploy from that point on is identical to any other
`Application`: `flui deploy` reads the manifest, the build
pipeline runs, the image lands on the cluster, the endpoint and
the certificate are wired in.

## The first deploy, and every push after it

A template's promise is that a push becomes a running
application. That is exactly what happens the first time.
What happens on the pushes after it is a separate decision,
and Flui now asks you to make it.

Every push still triggers a build. That part has not
changed. What changed is what a successful build does next.

- **The first deploy is unaffected.** The application is
  not live yet, so the build that finishes rolls straight
  out. The template flow that got you here works the way it
  always did.
- **After that, rolling out is opt-in, one application at a
  time.** It is off unless someone turns it on. With it
  off, a successful build is recorded as an **available
  version** and stops there. It waits for a deploy to be
  triggered.

Two commands cover the waiting versions:

- `flui app versions <app>` lists the image versions the
  registry holds for that application, and which one is
  deployed.
- `flui app redeploy <app> <tag-or-digest>` rolls one of
  them out, without rebuilding anything.

The reason for the split is that pushing a commit and
shipping to production are two different intentions. A
template repository is exactly where they get confused: the
first push is meant to go live, the fiftieth usually is
not.

One consequence is worth saying out loud. **Applications
that existed before this landed stopped redeploying on
push.** The setting starts off, so an application that used
to roll out on every green build now records the image and
waits instead. If you want the old behaviour, turn it on
for that application.

Today that switch lives on the application itself and is
set through the API. There is no CLI flag and no dashboard
control for it yet.

## The frameworks Flui covers

The set of supported frameworks spans the languages most
self-hosted applications are written in — JavaScript and
TypeScript fullstack and backend stacks, a frontend framework, a
JVM backend, two Python backends, a .NET backend — plus a
generic catch-all template for the cases none of the above
fits.

The list is deliberately small. Each template is a real
repository that someone has to maintain over time: the goal is
to cover the common shapes without growing a long tail of
variants. The exact set, with versions and command syntax,
lives in the CLI reference.

## What makes a repository Flui-compatible

A template is really just one example of a **Flui-compatible
repository** — a repository the platform can find, build and
deploy. The contract is small:

- a Dockerfile that produces a runnable image,
- a `flui.yaml` at the root that describes how the resulting
  application should run,
- a working healthcheck endpoint matching what the manifest
  declares.

Anything that satisfies those three requirements is deployable
through the same flow as a template-generated repository, even
if no one calls it a "template". A user who outgrows the
official templates can fork one, edit it freely, or write their
own from scratch — the platform does not care which path the
repository came from, as long as the contract holds.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — what a
  template produces, once deployed.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/) — the
  shape of the `flui.yaml` every template ships.
- [Build pipeline today and tomorrow](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/)
  — the build flow that the template's pipeline plugs into.
- [CLI: Templates](/cli/templates/) — the command-by-command
  reference, including the current list of supported frameworks
  with their versions.

sections.title: The build pipeline, today and tomorrow
sections.body:
For an application built from source, there is a step between
the user pushing code and a container running on the cluster:
**the build**. Where that build runs is not a detail — it shapes
the cost model, what fails when something breaks, and what
credentials need to live where.

This chapter is about the build pipeline that turns a `kind:
Application` manifest plus a source repository into a deployable
image — what it does today, what happens to the image once the
build succeeds, what the pipeline deliberately doesn't try to
do, and where the design is heading.

## Today: build at the source

Today's pipeline runs **alongside the user's source repository**,
on the CI service of the platform that hosts it. When a deploy
of a `kind: Application` is triggered, the platform writes (or
refreshes) a build workflow inside the user's repository, makes
sure the workflow has the credentials it needs to push the
resulting image to a container registry, and watches the run
through to completion.

The shape of the pipeline is the user's CI tool's shape — its
runners, its logs, its reruns, its UI. Flui drives it; it does
not host it.

## When the build succeeds

A finished build and a running application are two different
things, and Flui keeps them apart on purpose.

When the run reports success, Flui **records the image** against
the application, together with the commit and the branch it was
built from. Recording is the part that always happens. You can
read the list back with `flui app versions <app>`, which shows
the images available for that application and which of them is
deployed.

**Rolling that image out is a separate decision.** It happens
automatically only when the application has **deploy on push**
turned on. When it is off — which is the default — the new
image sits in the list as an available version, and nothing
changes on the cluster until somebody asks for it:

```
flui app redeploy <app> <tag-or-digest>
```

This used to work the other way round. Every successful build on
an already-live application rolled straight out. That is a fine
default for a hobby project and a bad one for anything a person
is on call for, because it means a commit is a deploy whether or
not the author meant it that way. Making it opt-in moves that
choice to the person who owns the application. Applications
created before the change do not have it turned on.

**An application's very first deploy is never gated by this.**
At that point the application is not live yet, so there is no
running version being replaced, and waiting for a second
instruction would only leave a half-created application sitting
there doing nothing.

When deploy on push *is* on, the roll-out is not a bare image
swap. Flui reads `flui.yaml` at the pushed commit first, so the
push applies what the committed file says — environment
variables, port, resources — and not only a newer image.

One honest gap: deploy on push is a setting on the application,
and today it is set through the application itself — when it is
created, or by updating it afterwards. There is no flag for it
on any `flui` command.

## Build arguments reach the image

Some values have to be present **while** the image is being
built, not when the container starts. The usual case is a
frontend framework that bakes a public API URL into the bundle
at build time: setting it as a runtime environment variable is
too late, because the value was already compiled into the
JavaScript.

The manifest has a place for those:

```yaml
build:
  strategy: dockerfile
  dockerfile: Dockerfile
  args:
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: https://api.example.com
```

Every entry under `build.args` is passed to the image build as a
build argument. Flui resolves them from the manifest and writes
them into the generated build workflow, so they stay in step
with the rest of the build description instead of being pieced
together by the CI run itself.

Two things follow from that, and both matter:

- **They are not secrets.** The values land in a workflow file
  inside your repository and are baked into the image. Anyone
  who can read the repository, or pull the image, can read them.
  A credential belongs in the environment variables of the
  running application, marked as a secret — never here.
- **They do not vary per environment.** The manifest's
  per-environment overrides deliberately leave the `build` block
  out, because the intent is that one built image moves between
  environments rather than being rebuilt for each of them.

## Why an external pipeline

Building images is heavy work — compilation, dependency
download, layer composition, image push. Doing that work on the
same cluster that is also serving production traffic creates a
noisy-neighbour problem at exactly the wrong moment. Running it
outside the cluster avoids that problem entirely.

The CI services Flui integrates with also bring three things for
free: a mature **build cache layer** that makes repeated builds
fast, **generous time budgets** that for a typical user mean the
build infrastructure is genuinely free, and a **standard
debugging surface** the user already knows — when a build
fails, there is a run page with logs, the user opens it and
reads. Flui does not have to reinvent any of that.

## The trade-offs

A few honest costs that come with this choice:

- **External dependency.** If the CI service is down, new
  deploys cannot land. Running applications keep running and the
  observability stack stays up — but the deploy path is gated on
  a service Flui does not control.
- **Credentials in the user's CI.** Pushing to the registry
  requires a credential, and that credential lives where the
  workflow runs. The user has to be comfortable trusting that
  surface with it.
- **Latency floor.** Running the build elsewhere puts a real
  lower bound on how fast the deploy loop can close. For tight
  inner-loop iteration, the build time on whichever runner the
  CI picks is the floor.
- **Coupled to one CI today.** The current integration is
  specific to one CI service; other CI services need a parallel
  integration, which is one of the directions the next section
  describes.

## Where the design is heading

Two directions are on the roadmap, both aiming at the same
property: the user's manifest never has to know which pipeline
ran the build.

- **Other CI/CD systems.** The current single integration is
  the first one, not the only one. The roadmap covers other CI
  services as additional backends, with the platform picking the
  right one for the installation without changing the
  application model or the manifest.
- **A self-hosted alternative.** For air-gapped or disconnected
  installations, for compliance environments where build traces
  cannot leave a controlled perimeter, and for teams that prefer
  to keep all their infrastructure on hardware they own, the
  build can run inside the installation itself — pipeline and
  optional registry, end-to-end inside the user's control plane.

Both moves are deliberate substitutions inside the build
pipeline, not a rewrite of the deploy contract. The user-facing
shape — `kind: Application` produces an image, the image
deploys to a cluster, the cluster runs the workload — is the
same regardless of which pipeline drew the lines underneath.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — what the
  build pipeline produces, once the image is on the cluster.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/) —
  the file the `build` block above lives in.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/) —
  why the build pipeline matters only for `kind: Application`,
  and not for `kind: CatalogApp`.
- [CLI: Applications](/cli/applications/) — the command-by-command
  reference for inspecting builds and managing image versions.

sections.title: Storage classes and dedicated placement
sections.body:
Most workloads do not need anything special from the disk under
them. They write the occasional file, they read it back later,
and they can move freely from one node to another whenever the
cluster needs them to.

Some workloads, though, depend on the disk behaving in a precise
way. They expect their writes to land in order, their locks to
be honoured, their "I saved this" to be a promise the kernel
actually keeps. Databases are the canonical example, but the
property is what matters, not the workload's name: anything that
relies on real filesystem semantics belongs in this second
group. Shared storage that fronts a network filesystem cannot
always guarantee those semantics, and the mismatch ranges from
"surprising performance" to "quietly losing the last seconds of
writes".

Flui ships two storage classes — one for each group — and lets
the application pick the right one.

## Two storage classes

Every persistent volume on a Flui cluster ends up in one of two
classes:

- **Shared.** The default, NFS-backed class. A single volume on
  the master is exposed to every node as a network filesystem,
  fronted by a local cache on each node. Any pod on any node can
  read and write through the same address. This is the right
  answer for stateless apps, log directories, and any workload
  that occasionally writes a file and re-reads it later.
- **Dedicated.** The node-local `flui-local` class, backed by a
  node's own disk. Writes hit that disk directly — there is no
  NFS hop in the path — and the pod that uses it is pinned to the
  node hosting the disk; once placed, it does not move. This is
  the right answer for databases and anything that depends on the
  disk behaving like a real disk.

The choice is on the application side: a catalog manifest
declares whether it needs dedicated placement, and Flui takes
care of the rest. An application that does not declare anything
gets shared placement.

## Where dedicated workloads live

When an application asks for dedicated placement, Flui has to
decide which node hosts its disk. The default target is a
**worker node**, not the master. At deploy time Flui looks at
every worker's free capacity and auto-pins the app to the one
with the most room — recording that choice as the app's
dedicated node name, so subsequent operations know exactly where
its disk lives. Keeping dedicated workloads off the master keeps
the control plane free of stateful, node-locked tenants and lets
their hosts grow independently.

There is one thing this default needs and cannot invent: a
worker has to exist. If a cluster has no worker at all and an app
asks for dedicated placement, the deploy does not silently fall
back — it **fails loudly** with the code
`NO_WORKER_FOR_DEDICATED_APP`, telling you to add a worker (or to
use the escape hatch below).

### The master escape hatch

For the genuinely small case — a single-node cluster, or a
deliberate choice to keep one dedicated app on the control plane
— an app carries an `allowMasterPlacement` flag (a boolean,
default `false`). It exists on both the application itself and on
the catalog-install input, so you can opt in either when
installing or later. When it is set, a dedicated app is allowed
to schedule on the master even though no worker is available;
when it is not, the missing-worker case is the loud failure
above. The default is deliberately the safe one: dedicated work
lands on a worker unless you say otherwise.

## A locked node

A node hosting at least one dedicated workload becomes a
**locked** node from Flui's point of view: the node-removal flow
refuses to delete it as long as those workloads live there, and
explains exactly which applications would lose their disk if it
went away.

Unlocking the node is a deliberate operation: move the dedicated
workloads off it (to another worker, or to the master via the
`allowMasterPlacement` escape hatch), then the node-removal flow
accepts. The platform does not migrate
dedicated data between nodes automatically — that step belongs
to the operator, who knows whether a downtime window is
acceptable and whether a backup-and-restore is the right way to
move the data.

## A pre-flight check before deploy

Before a dedicated workload is deployed (or re-deployed after a
configuration change), Flui sanity-checks the target node: it
asks the cluster how much CPU and memory the node has free, and
compares that against what the workload needs. If the node
cannot fit the workload, the deploy fails up front with a clear
error pointing at the gap — and at the operations that can close
it: resize the node, or move the workload to one that has the
room.

This check is run at deploy time, not just at install time, so
adding a new replica or growing the resource request of a
dedicated workload either succeeds because the room is there, or
fails with a useful diagnosis instead of leaving the workload
stuck in a degraded state.

## Vertical scaling: giving the host more

Once a workload is pinned, the only way to give it more CPU or
memory is to give *the host node* more CPU or memory. There is
no horizontal "add another replica" path for a dedicated
workload — there is only one disk it can speak to, so the
answer is always to grow the machine underneath it.

Resizing a node is a planned-maintenance operation. The cluster
powers the node down, asks the provider to change the server
type, powers it back up, and waits for the cluster to report it
healthy before declaring the operation done. The workload is
unavailable for a few minutes — this is unavoidable on the
providers Flui integrates with — and the platform makes that
window explicit in the operation's plan before doing anything.
The command-level reference for resize lives in
[CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/).

## Growing the shared storage

The shared storage layer also runs out of room over time, as
the apps using it accumulate state. Flui exposes a direct
operation to grow it: the underlying volume on the provider is
resized, the filesystem on top is extended, and the new space
is immediately visible to every node that mounts it. The
operation is online — no downtime, no pod restarts — but it is
one-way: the providers Flui integrates with let volumes grow,
not shrink. Plan the target size; the smallest reversible step
is "fresh cluster".

## When an application goes away

A volume that outlives its application is the quiet kind
of waste. Nothing is running, nothing looks broken, and
the bill does not change. That used to be exactly what
happened: removing an application left its disks where
they were.

Removing an application now takes its volumes with it.
The same holds for a catalog install with several parts —
uninstalling the install removes the storage of every
part, not only the one you named.

Because that cannot be undone, every surface says what
will be lost before it asks. `flui app delete` lists each
volume with its size, then makes you type the
application's name to confirm. The dashboard's delete
dialog shows the same list. An agent can read the same
removal preview before it proposes anything.

All three read one answer from the API, so they cannot
disagree with each other — and the removal then deletes
exactly what that answer named. What you were warned
about is what goes.

One honest detail: when Flui cannot reach the cluster to
read the volumes, it reports the loss as **unknown**. It
never reports "none". A blank where somebody's data
should be is safer than a reassuring guess.

## Storage left from before this changed

Deleting on the way out only repairs the future. Any
installation that has been running for a while may still
hold volumes from removals that happened before this
landed — and nothing ever listed them, so nobody knew
they were being paid for.

`flui cluster volumes` is that listing. It reports each
abandoned volume with its size, the application it
belonged to when that is still known, and a plain
sentence saying why it is considered abandoned. The
dashboard shows the same list on the cluster's Storage
tab.

Removing one is `flui cluster volumes --remove <ref>`,
using the reference the listing prints next to it. It is
permanent, so it asks you to type the volume's name back
first, and the server re-runs the whole check before it
deletes anything — the list you read may be minutes old,
and something may have started using that volume since.

An agent can read this list and cannot act on it. There
is no agent permission that deletes one; the most an
agent can do is tell you what it found and hand you the
command.

### The scan errs by omission

A wrong answer here is not symmetric. Missing a volume
leaves you paying for a disk. Naming the wrong one offers
to delete somebody's data. So the scan is built to miss
things rather than to find them.

Nothing is called abandoned unless every one of these
holds: no running workload is using it, no application
that still exists owns it, it is not sitting in a place
the platform reserves for itself, and it has been there
long enough — fifteen minutes — that it cannot be
something still being created.

On top of that it needs a positive reason. There are
four: Flui's own mark on it names an application that is
gone; its name matches an application Flui removed; its
name could only have been made for a workload that no
longer exists; or every application that ever lived
beside it has been deleted.

A volume with none of those — no mark from Flui, a name
that matches nothing, sitting next to applications that
are still alive — is never reported. An unlabelled volume
created by a third-party chart can land in exactly that
gap. So an empty list means "nothing found by these
rules", not "nothing is left". The same is true when the
cluster cannot be read at all: the listing says so
instead of showing you a clean, false zero.

There is a second, coarser level of leftover, at the
provider rather than inside a cluster: a block volume
that survived a cluster being destroyed.
`flui env orphan-volumes` lists those, and `--cleanup`
removes them.

## What is not in this story today

Moving a dedicated workload from one host to another is not an
automatic data migration: Flui re-pins the placement, but the
underlying disk does not follow. The workload has to be stopped,
its data copied to the new host explicitly (typically a backup
followed by a restore on the target), and then re-deployed with
the new placement. This is the main caveat to know about; it
does not break the common path of "install a database,
eventually resize the host, optionally grow the shared volume".

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — the
  application surface that declares storage, exposure and
  placement, and the home of the install-time capacity gate.
- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/) —
  the nodes a workload can be pinned to.
- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/) —
  the first-party tooling for the databases that most often want
  dedicated, node-local storage.
- [CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/) —
  the command-by-command reference for resizing nodes and
  growing the shared volume.
- [CLI: Applications](/cli/applications/) —
  removing an application, and finding the storage of
  applications that no longer exist.

sections.title: Composed catalog apps
sections.body:
Some software is not a single container. Nextcloud wants a
database, a cache and a background worker. WordPress wants a
database next to its web tier. Immich wants several services that
only make sense together. A **composed catalog app** is a single
`CatalogApp` manifest that bundles all of those workloads and
installs them as one atomic unit — provisioned together, torn down
together, and shown as one thing in your app list.

This chapter is about that shape: how a composed entry is put
together, how its pieces are wired, and the install-time choices
it exposes. The broader distinction between `Application` and
`CatalogApp` lives in
[Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/);
this is the deep dive on the composed flavour.

## What a composed app is

A composed entry sets `type: composed` (`CatalogSpecComposed` in
the schema). Instead of a single `image`/`ports`/`env` body like a
standalone entry, it carries a `components` list. Each component is
rendered into its own running app — its own workload, its own
internal address, and its own storage volume if it declares one —
exactly as if it had been installed on its own. The composed
manifest is the coordination layer on top:
it decides what gets created, in what order, and how the pieces
find each other.

The point is atomicity. You do not install a database, then a
cache, then the app, then wire three sets of credentials by hand.
You pick one entry, answer a few prompts, and the whole stack comes
up wired and healthy — or none of it does.

## The component model

Each entry under `components` has a `name`, an `image`, and the
same runtime blocks a standalone app would have (`ports`,
`volumes`, `env`, `resources`, `scaling`, `healthcheck`). Two extra
fields turn a flat list into a coordinated stack:

- **`dependsOn`** — names of other components that must be healthy
  before this one starts. The installer brings components up in
  dependency order, so a web tier marked `dependsOn: [db]` waits for
  the database to pass its healthcheck first.
- **`when.option`** — a gate that includes the component only when a
  named install-time option is enabled. A component without a `when`
  is always included.

Components reference each other through templating in their `env`.
A web component reads its database host and credentials straight
from the `db` component:

```yaml
components:
  - name: db
    image:
      registry: docker.io
      repository: library/mariadb
      tag: "11"
    env:
      - name: MARIADB_USER
        value: wordpress
      - name: MARIADB_PASSWORD
        valueFrom:
          generate: secret
          length: 32
    # ...ports, volumes, resources, scaling, healthcheck

  - name: web
    dependsOn:
      - db
    image:
      registry: docker.io
      repository: library/wordpress
      tag: "6.5-apache"
    env:
      - name: WORDPRESS_DB_HOST
        value: "{{components.db.host}}:3306"
      - name: WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD
        value: "{{components.db.env.MARIADB_PASSWORD}}"
        secret: true
    # ...ports, volumes, resources, scaling, healthcheck
```

The `{{components.db.host}}` and `{{components.db.env.*}}` tokens
resolve at install time to the database's in-cluster service host
and the value the database generated. The generated password is
created once on the `db` side and injected into `web` as a secret
(`secret: true`), so it never appears in plaintext.

## Auth modes

A composed entry declares which authentication strategies it
supports under `spec.auth`:

- `spec.auth.modes` is the list of supported modes.
- `spec.auth.default` is the one chosen when the installer is not
  told otherwise.

At install time you pick one mode via the install's `authMode`,
which must be one of `oidc`, `proxy`, `native` or `none`. `native`
leaves the app's own login in place; `none` disables auth wiring;
`proxy` puts the app behind a header-injecting proxy; `oidc` wires
the app to Flui's identity provider.

### OIDC auto-provisioning

When you choose `oidc`, Flui does the SSO plumbing for you. It
registers a **web OIDC client** against Flui's own Zitadel-backed
identity provider, scoped to the install's resolved hostname, and
records the resulting `oidcAppId` and `oidcProjectId` on the install
record. Those IDs are what let Flui clean the client up again when
you uninstall, so an SSO registration never outlives the app it was
created for.

The client's credentials reach the app through whatever channel the
manifest declares under `spec.auth.oidc`:

- **`envMapping`** — the issuer URL, client ID and client secret are
  injected as environment variables the app reads natively.
- **`configFile`** — a rendered config file is written into the
  container at a declared path.
- **A `postInstall` exec step** — the app is configured through its
  own CLI. Nextcloud, for instance, runs
  `php occ user_oidc:provider Flui` to register Flui as an OIDC
  provider after the container is up.

Whichever channel is used, the credentials arrive through the
templating tokens described below, never hard-coded in the manifest.

## Install-time options

`spec.options` is a list of boolean feature toggles. Each option has
a `key`, a human `label`, an optional `description`, and a `default`:

```yaml
options:
  - key: office
    label: "Office editing (Collabora)"
    description: "Adds a document-server component."
    default: false
```

At install you pass an `options` map (`key` → `true`/`false`); any
key you omit falls back to its `default`. Options gate two things:

- **Components**, via `when.option` — enabling `office` on Nextcloud
  pulls in the extra Collabora document-server component; leaving it
  off skips that component entirely.
- **Post-install steps**, via the same `when.option` — so the step
  that configures the optional component only runs when the option is
  on.

This is how one manifest can describe both a lean install and a
fully-featured one without forking into two entries.

## Multi-endpoint

A composed stack can expose more than one component to the outside
world. Any component with a port marked `expose: true` gets its own
endpoint and FQDN, resolved by Flui's endpoint-mode resolver the
same way a standalone app's endpoint is. Components with no exposed
port stay internal — a database or cache is reachable only from the
other components over the in-cluster service, never published.

## Post-install steps

`spec.postInstall` is a list of actions that run **after** the
components are deployed and healthy. Each step is either:

- **`http`** — an HTTP call (`method`, `path`, optional `headers`,
  `body`, `expectStatus`) against the running app.
- **`exec`** — a command run inside a component's container (the
  `occ` calls above are exec steps).

Steps can be conditioned with `when.authMode` and `when.option`, so
the OIDC-provider registration only runs in `oidc` mode and the
office-config step only runs when `office` is enabled. This is where
work that can only happen against a live, configured app lives —
trusting the public hostname, registering the SSO provider, enabling
an optional feature.

## Templating tokens resolved at install

Beyond the cross-component references already shown, two families of
token are resolved at install time and are specific to the composed
flow:

- **`{{self.fqdn}}`** — a component's *own* public hostname, made
  available before the component boots. Because the install slug is
  deterministic, Flui knows a component's final FQDN up front, so a
  component that needs to advertise its own public URL (Collabora's
  `server_name`, for example) can be handed it at create time rather
  than reconfigured after the fact.
- **`{{oidc.clientId}}`, `{{oidc.clientSecret}}`,
  `{{oidc.issuerUrl}}`** — the credentials of the web OIDC client
  Flui provisioned for this install (see above). These appear in
  `envMapping`, in a rendered `configFile`, or in a `postInstall`
  exec command, and are populated only when `authMode` is `oidc`.

## How a composed install appears

In `flui app list` a composed install shows up as a **single
bundle** — kind `composed`, as opposed to `standalone` — rather than
as a loose pile of unrelated apps. The bundle reflects the whole
stack, so you reason about Nextcloud as one thing, not as
`nextcloud`, `nextcloud-db`, `nextcloud-redis` and a worker side by
side.

To see what is inside, pass `-x`/`--expanded`:

```bash
flui app list --expanded
```

That reveals the individual components, each with its own slug,
status and exposure. Without the flag, the list stays at the bundle
level and tells you a composed app has components you can expand.

## Idempotency

Re-running an install is safe. The installer looks up the components
that already exist for the install and **reuses** them rather than
creating duplicates, so a re-entry after a partial failure or a
retried job continues from where it left off instead of standing up
a second copy of the stack. The same property is what makes the
post-install steps and the OIDC wiring safe to reach more than once.

## A note on capacity

Before a composed install starts, Flui sums the resource requests of
every component that will be included and checks them against what
the cluster has free, refusing the install if there is not enough
room (a safety margin is kept). This is the same capacity gate that
guards any install; the exact CPU-vs-memory accounting is covered in
[The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/).

## Where to read next

- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/) — the
  shared envelope, including the composed-manifest surface.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/) —
  the three flavours of catalog entry and where composed sits.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) — what each
  component becomes once it is running, and the capacity gate in
  full.
- [`flui deploy`](/cli/deploy/) — the command-level reference for
  installing and deploying.

sections.title: Inference and bring-your-own-model
sections.body:
Flui has features that need a large language model: the assistant
that drives the platform in natural language, and the AI assist in
the database console. Those features should not care *where* the
model comes from. So Flui draws a clean line: anything that wants
inference asks for a single, normalized endpoint, and a resolver
behind that line works out how to produce it.

That endpoint is always the same shape — an OpenAI-compatible
`{ baseUrl, apiKey }`. No Flui abstraction sits over the model
itself; the model ids, the request format, the streaming are all
plain OpenAI-compatible. The only thing Flui owns is *how the
endpoint is sourced and credentialed*, and that is where the two
ways below differ.

## Two ways to get an endpoint

There are exactly two sources of inference, and they are
deliberately different things.

### Native — inference as a provider capability

Some cloud providers also run an OpenAI-compatible inference
service. When they do, Flui models that as a capability the
provider declares, just like firewalls or DNS — an
`InferenceCapability` carrying a `baseUrl`, an optional curated
`models` list for display, a `euDataResidency` flag, and a
`sharesComputeCredentials` flag.

The interesting flag is `sharesComputeCredentials`. For Scaleway it
is `true`: the provider's inference service authenticates with the
**same IAM secret** Flui already holds to provision your
infrastructure. So when you point Flui at a Scaleway account, you
get inference for free — there is no separate AI key to create,
paste or rotate. Flui reuses the existing compute credential as the
inference bearer token.

A provider that *only* did inference — that you would never use for
compute — would not have a compute credential to borrow. For that
case Flui supports a dedicated credential whose purpose is
inference rather than compute, kept under the same credential model
as everything else. Scaleway just doesn't need one, because its one
credential already covers both.

The curated `models` list on the capability is only a placeholder
for display before a key exists. Once Flui has a working
credential, the **live** model list is read straight from
`{baseUrl}/models` — so the models you can pick are always the ones
the provider actually offers right now, not a list baked into Flui.

### A connection you bring yourself

The second source is a connection *you* configure: any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint — OpenAI, Mistral, a Claude-compatible
gateway, or a server you run yourself. This is **not** a provider.
It declares no capabilities and provisions no infrastructure. It is
pure connection config: a `base_url`, an API key (stored
encrypted), an optional list of `models`, and an `is_default`
flag.

These live behind their own small API under `inference/connections`
— you can list them, create one, validate it against its endpoint,
and delete it. Validation actually calls the endpoint, so a bad
key or wrong URL is caught when you save it, not the first time the
assistant tries to answer a question.

The split matters: native inference is something a provider *has*,
and you get it by virtue of connecting that provider; a connection
you bring is independent of any provider, and it works the same
whether or not you run any Flui-managed infrastructure at all.

## Two levels: the installation's, and your own

A connection you bring used to be one flat list for the whole
installation. It is now two levels, and which level a connection
sits on is the whole of its privacy.

**The installation's connection** is visible to everyone and
usable by everyone. It is the instance's own credential to a model
provider: one key, spent by every assistant on the installation.
Whoever manages integrations plugs it in and unplugs it. Every
connection made before this change is one of these, unchanged —
nothing was rewritten and nothing behaves differently.

**Your own connection** belongs to one person. Nobody else sees it
in a list, and — the part that matters more — nobody else can
spend it. You may connect one and disconnect it again with no
permission at all, because a person who may bring a key and may
not take it back is in the worst state a credential model can be
in.

Today the dashboard's settings screen manages the
installation's connections, and it hides those controls from
anyone who may not manage integrations rather than letting
them press a button that answers with a refusal. A private
one is made through the API — `POST` to
`inference/connections/mine`, and a `DELETE` on the same
path to take it away again.

### The privacy is enforced where the key is spent, not on the list

Hiding a private connection from other people's lists would have
protected nothing. Almost nothing that uses a connection reads the
list: the assistant's chat, the agent loop and each console
assistant take a connection **id** out of a request and turn it
straight into a live key. So the question "whose connection is
this?" is asked at that point — the one place every one of those
paths has to pass through.

The practical effect: a colleague who somehow learns the id
of your connection still cannot use it. Their attempt is
answered as an **absence**, in exactly the same words as an
id that never existed, so guessing ids teaches nobody
anything.
