Validating a connection goes through the same door, because
validating one *spends* it — the check calls the model
provider with the key. So a colleague cannot even test your
private connection, let alone chat with it.

### Nothing is promoted quietly

A private connection stays private. Flui has no path that
turns one into the installation's — not on the way in, not
later, not when the person who brought it stops using Flui.
It goes with the person who brought it, and nobody inherits
it. If the installation should have a shared model, somebody
connects one at the installation's level, deliberately.

### Defaults do not cross levels

Marking your own connection as the default makes it the default
**for you**. It does not unseat the installation's default for
anyone else, and it is never handed to a colleague who asked for
no connection in particular. That last one is the leak that
arrives without an id at all, and it is closed.

### One person can see everything, and still cannot spend it

Someone who may manage users — the `owner` rung — sees every
connection in the list, private ones included, because somebody
has to be able to answer "what is plugged into this instance?".
They can also remove one. What they cannot do is *use* it: seeing
a colleague's row is not a licence to charge their model account,
and the resolver refuses it as an absence like anyone else's.

### An empty list is not proof

Because private connections are listed to nobody else, an empty
list does not mean nothing is connected. It means nothing is
connected *that you can see*. This matters most for an agent
reporting on the installation, and the product says it out loud
rather than leaving the agent to conclude the wrong thing.

## How the default endpoint is chosen

Most of the time the assistant doesn't name a specific source — it
just asks for "the" inference endpoint. The resolver answers that
with a fixed preference order:

1. **A configured native provider**, EU-first by the order
   providers are declared. If an inference-capable provider has a
   usable credential, that wins.
2. Otherwise, **a connection flagged as default that you can
   use** — your own first, then the installation's.
3. Otherwise, **the most recent connection you can use** — when
   nothing is flagged, a usable connection is better than failing
   for lack of a flag.

If none of those produce an endpoint, resolution fails cleanly with
"no inference endpoint configured" rather than guessing. The
ordering favours native providers first because, when one is
present, it usually means inference is already paid for and
credentialed through the same account you provision with — the
lowest-friction path.

## What an agent may do with a model connection

An agent connected to Flui speaks *through* the model. That makes
the connection an odd thing to hand it authority over, so two
rules apply.

**An agent cannot unplug the installation's model.** Deleting that
connection asks for the permission to manage integrations, and no
agent scope carries that permission. An agent that could take away
the endpoint every assistant on the installation runs on is one
bad turn from a silent outage.

**An agent can ask a person to connect one.** There is a
tool for exactly that, `inference_connection_request`. It
has no argument that could carry an API key, and it never
sees one. It reports the connections it can see, says in as
many words that private connections are not counted, and
hands back the settings screen where a person picks a
provider and pastes the key themselves.

## EU data residency is first-class

`euDataResidency` is a property of the capability, surfaced
alongside each native provider, not a footnote. For a self-hosted
platform that may be running under European data rules, *where the
prompt goes* is part of the decision, so Flui makes it visible at
the point you choose a provider — Scaleway's inference, for
example, declares EU residency. A connection you bring points
wherever you configure it, so residency there is your call by
construction.

## Recommended models

Picking a model id from a raw `/models` list is not obvious — names
are version-pinned and not portable across providers, and some are
a bad fit for tool use or cost more than you'd want for a first
run. Flui ships an opinionated, **overridable** recommendation
policy to smooth that.

The policy is a config file at
`assistant/config/recommended-models.json`. It names a
`recommendedProvider` to get started with — currently **Mistral**,
with the model `mistral-small-2506`, called out for its generous
free tier — and then, per provider, a curated list of
version-pinned model ids with short descriptions. Some entries
carry a caveat `note` (for instance, a stronger model marked "not
recommended on free plan") so the trade-off is visible before you
switch. The whole file can be replaced via an environment override,
so an operator can re-point the recommendations without a code
change.

These recommendations are read at startup, validated, and exposed
through the assistant API so the dashboard can preselect a sensible
default instead of dropping you into an unfiltered model list.

## Who consumes inference

The resolved endpoint is the single seam every AI feature sits on:

- **The Flui Assistant** — the natural-language layer over the
  platform — runs against whatever the resolver returns. See
  [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/).
- **The database console's AI assist** — the helper that turns a
  question into a query — uses the same resolved endpoint, in
  every console family that has one. See
  [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/).

Every one of them asks for the endpoint *as the person on the
other end of the conversation*, which is what makes a private
connection stay private in a chat as well as in a list.

Because they all go through one resolver, configuring inference
once lights up every AI feature at the same time, with the same
data-residency and credential story.

## Where to read next

- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/)
  — why inference is modelled as a provider capability, like
  firewalls or DNS, rather than a special case.
- [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/)
  — the primary consumer of the resolved endpoint.
- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/) —
  the other consumer, where AI assist turns questions into queries.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/) — the
  role ladder the `owner` rung above belongs to.

sections.title: The Flui assistant and MCP
sections.body:
Most platforms bolt a chatbot on at the end and hope it
doesn't say anything embarrassing. Flui treats its assistant
as a real surface of the product, with the same care the rest
of the platform gets: it answers from a compiled knowledge
base rather than free-associating, it can actually *do*
things through a shared tool registry, and every action it
can take is governed by the same rules whether a person is
driving it in the dashboard or an external agent is calling
it over MCP.

This chapter is about the shape of that choice and — more
importantly — the safety model underneath it, because the
load-bearing part of an assistant that can deploy and
uninstall your apps is *what stops it doing the wrong one*.

## Two surfaces, one tool registry

There are two ways into the same capabilities:

- **The in-product assistant** — the chat surface inside
  Flui's dashboard. You ask a question or a request in plain
  language; it answers from the docs, and when you ask it to
  *act* it runs a tool-use loop on your behalf.
- **The MCP server** — a [Model Context
  Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) endpoint that
  offers the *same* tools to external agents: your own
  scripts, an agent in your editor, another LLM application.

The point of sharing is that a tool is written once. One
registry backs both the in-process assistant loop and the MCP
server, so there is no second, divergent surface to keep in
sync — and, more to the point, no second place where the
safety checks could drift apart.

The registry is large. It holds **a little over a hundred
tools**, in about twenty families: applications, the catalog,
observability, manifest validation, infrastructure and the
operations that change it, scaling, DNS, the gateway,
backups, migrations, scheduled jobs, mail, repositories,
access, how this installation is run, and a family whose
whole job is asking a person for a credential. Nobody sees
all of them at once; the next section is why.

Both surfaces get their model from Flui's inference layer
rather than holding a hard-coded provider — see
[Inference and bring-your-own-LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/)
for how that endpoint is resolved.

### A tool has no private door into the product

This is worth stating on its own, because it is the sentence
the rest of the safety model rests on.

**A tool reaches Flui only by calling Flui's own API, as the
caller's own principal.** It does not hold the services
underneath. It does not mint a token for itself. It sends a
request, over the same route your browser would use, carrying
the very credential the agent presented.

The reason is that every guard Flui has sits on the request
path — who may reach this application, which sections you
hold, what a guest is fenced off from. A tool that called the
code directly would walk past all of them while a real
request could not. So it makes a real request.

The practical consequence is short: **a tool call meets
exactly the checks a person clicking would meet.** An agent
cannot be handed a shortcut that a person does not have.

## The assistant answers from a knowledge base, not from memory

The assistant does not reach into a general-purpose model's
training data to answer questions about Flui. Instead, Flui's
documentation is compiled into a **knowledge base** — a
single versioned artifact (`kb.json`) built by a script from
the concept docs, the CLI prose, a generated CLI reference,
the `flui.yaml` schema, and a hand-authored *guardrails*
file. The assistant answers strictly from this corpus.

This grounding is a deliberate choice to keep answers tied to
the facts. The guardrails make the contract explicit: the
assistant's knowledge *is* exactly the corpus it is handed —
it is asked not to invent commands, flags, manifest fields or
version numbers, and if the answer isn't in the corpus it
says so and points you at `flui <command> --help` or the docs
rather than guessing. The knowledge base is also stamped with
the CLI, platform and schema versions it was built against,
so the assistant can tell you which version it is reasoning
about.

**This is why keeping these docs accurate matters.** The page
you are reading is one of the sources compiled into that
knowledge base. An inaccurate doc is not just wrong on the
website — it becomes a wrong answer the assistant gives with
confidence.

### A scope gate that also routes

Sending the whole corpus to the model on every message would
be slow and expensive. Flui avoids that with a single cheap
model call — a *guard* step — that does two jobs at once:

1. **Scope gate.** It decides whether your message is
   on-topic for Flui at all. A genuinely off-topic question
   (the weather, philosophy, general trivia) is refused with
   a short, warm message *in your own language* that says the
   assistant only helps with Flui — it does not answer the
   off-topic question. The bias is strongly toward answering:
   greetings, follow-ups and anything that plausibly concerns
   running apps on Flui are treated as on-topic.
2. **Router.** For an on-topic message, the same call returns
   the ids of the one-to-four most relevant knowledge
   sections. Only those are injected into the answering
   prompt, keeping it small.

So one inexpensive call refuses the irrelevant and narrows
the relevant, before the more expensive answering call ever
runs.

### The tool-use loop

When you ask the assistant to *do* something, it runs a loop:
the model can call tools, see their results, and call more
tools, up to a bounded number of rounds, before it writes a
final answer. In the dashboard this is streamed, so you watch
the text and the individual tool steps appear live rather
than waiting for a wall of output.

The loop is built defensively, so it stays reliable on
medium-to-small models rather than depending on a large one.
A few of those safeguards:

- **A URL guard.** Application endpoint URLs are passed
  through only when they actually came from a tool result;
  anything else is stripped before it reaches you. So a link
  you get is one the platform produced, not one assembled in
  the answer.
- **Doc-link surfacing.** The sections the router grounded
  the answer in are turned, deterministically, into links to
  the published docs.
- **Parameter recovery and rate-limit handling.** If a tool
  call comes back malformed, or a provider's per-minute limit
  is hit, the loop recovers and retries rather than failing
  the whole turn.

Taken together, these are also why the assistant does not
need a large frontier model. The corpus is already narrowed
by the router, the answers are grounded in it, and the guards
above are code rather than something left to the model — so a
**medium-to-small model is enough**, which is exactly what
Flui's inference layer recommends by default.

## The safety model

Everything above is convenience. This section is the
contract.

### Scopes, ordered into tiers

Every tool declares a scope, and scopes are ordered into four
**tiers** by blast radius:

```
read  →  plan  →  write  →  destructive
```

- **read** — list and inspect: applications, the catalog,
  logs and metrics, backups, migrations, mail, who can reach
  what.
- **plan** — analysis that changes nothing, such as
  validating a `flui.yaml`.
- **write** — state-changing operations: install, deploy,
  scale, restart, stop, connect a repository.
- **destructive** — delete and uninstall.

A grant at a tier implies every lower tier, so granting
*write* also grants *read* and *plan*.

Two areas are deliberately **in no tier at all**: operating
the machine room, and granting or revoking someone's access.
A tier is what a credential falls back to when it names
nothing of its own, so anything inside a tier can be acquired
by silence. Stopping somebody's cluster, or handing out
access, has to be a gesture. Those scopes are only ever held
by being named — see
[Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/).

### Default-deny, with three exceptions worth knowing

The system is **default-deny**. A tool runs only if its scope
is in the calling principal's set, and an explicit grant on
the credential always wins: a scoped key stays least
privilege even when the person who minted it is an
administrator.

What a principal gets when its credential names *no* scopes
depends on who it is, and the honest version has three
branches:

- **An ordinary authenticated principal** gets the safe
  default — **read and plan only**.
- **A platform administrator** driving the assistant from
  their own dashboard session gets the full tier. That is
  capability, not a bypass: writes still stop for a person,
  and destructive tools are still gated by the switch below.
- **A guest in the demonstration sandbox** gets one group
  instead — "deploy and operate applications" — because the
  platform default spans backups, migrations and mail, areas
  a guest would only ever be refused in.

So "no explicit grant means read and plan" is the ordinary
case, not a universal rule.

### Everyone is handed a different toolbox

`tools/list` is **filtered to the calling key's scopes**. A
tool this credential could never run is not advertised at
all, on either surface. Two agents connected to the same
installation with different keys see different toolboxes, and
neither sees the whole registry.

The reason is not tidiness. An offered tool costs the agent
context, invites a plan built around it, and pays that back
with a refusal. Hiding it is cheaper and produces better
behaviour. Execution is still gated separately — the filter
only trims what is offered, it never decides what is allowed.

When a refusal does happen, the two kinds are worded
differently on purpose. **"Missing required scope"** means
the tool was never handed to you: a grant problem, fixed by
reissuing the credential, and no resource will make the call
work. **"Refused by Flui access control"** means you hold the
tool but not this resource: a permission problem, fixed by
changing who can reach what. An agent that cannot tell them
apart tells you the wrong thing.

### Arguments are strict

An invented argument name is **rejected**, and the error says
both what was sent and what is accepted.

That sounds pedantic and is not. A permissive schema quietly
*drops* an unknown key, which is the worst possible failure
for a model-driven caller: the plausible-but-wrong argument
disappears, the real parameter is left empty, the tool runs
unfiltered, and the agent is handed a confident, successful
answer to a question it never asked. Rejecting costs one
turn. Accepting silently poisons the whole chain.

### Long work hands back a receipt, not a result

Installing, deploying, uninstalling, migrating and scaling do
not finish when the call returns. They hand back an
**operation id** and a status, and the tool result says so.

**Nothing polls it for the agent.** On the MCP surface the
agent is told, in as many words, that it must follow the
operation itself with `operation_status` until it is done,
and never claim it finished before then. In the in-product
assistant the dashboard shows a live progress panel, so there
the assistant is told the opposite: don't wait, don't
re-check, just say it started.

### Secrets never pass through an agent

An agent that needs a credential — an API key, the token that
pulls container images, a mail provider, a backup
destination, provider credentials, a model connection, an
invitation for a new user — does not ask you to paste it into
the chat. There are **seven tools whose entire job is to ask
a person instead**, and their shape is the point:

- **none of them has an argument that could carry a value.**
  Not optional, not "for automation": an argument is context,
  and context is transcript.
- **each answers *whether* a thing is configured, never
  *what*.**
- **none performs the privileged write.** They hand back
  either a command for you to run in your own terminal, or
  the screen you should open. The write stays yours.

An invitation link is itself treated as a credential and is
never returned to an agent.

### The destructive gate

Deleting and uninstalling are special. A destructive tool
needs **two independent yeses**:

1. the credential carries a **destructive scope**, *and*
2. a server-wide switch, `MCP_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE`, is on.

The switch is **off by default**. And when either condition
fails, the tool is not refused at call time — it is **not
offered at all**. An agent looking for a delete tool and not
finding one is looking at the answer, not at a glitch.

Where the tool is offered and the switch is off, the refusal
is deterministic — never negotiated, never retried — and it
is recorded.

### And there is a person in the loop

The switch above is a decision an operator takes once, at the
server. It is not the checkpoint. **The checkpoint is a
person, and it is per action.**

Flui declares more than forty write routes as being **inside
the action cycle**. When the caller is an agent, the call
does not run: it comes back as a request addressed to a
person, carrying one plain sentence describing what was asked
for and a link to the page where they answer *once*, *always*
or *no*. The agent learns the answer by making the identical
call again.

Two things about it belong here rather than in its own
chapter.

**The in-product assistant is inside the same cycle**, on the
same person's own session. That looks redundant — the human
is right there — and it is not. The question that decides the
pause is not *whose credential is this* but **who wrote the
arguments**. A dashboard form and a `flui` command carry what
a person typed. A tool call carries what a model chose.
Confirming the second is not theatre, because **what is
confirmed is not what they wrote.**

**A pause is not an error.** It is handed back in the shape
the protocol has for waiting, so a client that understands it
shows you a decision to make, and one that doesn't still
reads a sentence saying what is being asked. An agent that
mistakes it for a failure either gives up or starts varying
its arguments to get around it — and varying them just raises
a second question instead of answering the first.

The full argument, including why "always" is much narrower
than it sounds and why a standing permission can never widen
what anyone may do, is in
[The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

### Why this shape

The thinking is blast-radius first. The most useful thing an
assistant can do is also the most dangerous, so rather than
rely on every proposal being correct, the design makes a
wrong one cheap and recoverable instead of catastrophic —
defence in depth, not a verdict on the model.

Reads and plans flow freely, because they change nothing.
Writes go through the product's own front door, with the
caller's own permissions, and stop for a person before they
take effect. The irreversible operations need a destructive
scope *and* an operator's switch, and until both exist the
tool is not even in the box. No single mistaken token, and no
single bad turn, should be able to quietly destroy your data.

## Getting an agent connected

Three task pages walk the whole path:

- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/) — minting the
  credential and pointing an agent at `POST /mcp`. The first
  tool an agent should call is `get_started`, which returns
  the instructions for operating *this* installation and
  records that the credential has spoken.
- [Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/) —
  the permission groups a person picks from, and what each
  one honestly carries.
- [When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/) —
  answering a request, and taking a standing permission back.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/) — why an
  agent's write stops and asks, and what "always" really
  means.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/) —
  the access model every one of those tool calls lands on.
- [Inference and bring-your-own-LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/) —
  how the assistant and MCP get their model endpoint.
- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/) —
  where the authenticated principals, and the machine keys
  the MCP surface accepts, come from.
- [Observability is not an afterthought](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/) —
  the logs and metrics the read tools surface when you ask
  the assistant to debug an app.

sections.title: The database console
sections.body:
A database you run on Flui has no address on the internet.
That is the right default, and it leaves you with a
question the first time a row looks wrong: how do you look
inside it? The usual answers are all bad. Open the database
up and you have created the exact thing you were avoiding.
Host a second web tool in front of it and you now run, patch
and secure that tool as well. Reach for a native client and
you are hand-rolling a tunnel every time.

The console is Flui's answer. It is a data browser built
into the dashboard and served through Flui's own backend.
Nothing is exposed, and there is nothing extra to install.

This chapter is the picture behind it: what it opens, who
may open it, how it connects, and which limits are there on
purpose.

## It is not only databases any more

It started as two kinds of console. It is now about ten.
The list follows the building blocks Flui's catalog installs,
and they all have the same shape: a panel of connection
details, a way to browse what is in there, and a way to run
something by hand.

- **Relational** — Postgres and MariaDB. A query editor, a
  schema browser that reads tables, columns, primary keys
  and foreign keys, and the connection details.
- **Key-value** — Redis and Valkey. A keyspace summary
  (counts, not contents), a key scan, a value reader and a
  command runner.
- **Cache** — Memcached. Read a key, set one, delete one,
  flush.
- **Document** — FerretDB, driven with the shell statements
  a MongoDB user already knows, plus a browser for
  databases, collections and fields.
- **Full-text** — Meilisearch. The indexes, a search box,
  and a raw call for anything the box does not cover.
- **Kafka** — the cluster, its topics and its consumer
  groups, plus a command shell.
- **Messaging** — NATS and RabbitMQ. Streams, publish, and a
  peek at what is waiting.
- **Object store** — Garage, which speaks S3. Buckets and
  objects, upload and download, and signed share links that
  expire and can be revoked. Even a share link streams
  through Flui's backend, so the store itself is never
  reachable from outside.
- **Search** — OpenSearch. Indexes, mappings, queries and
  counts.
- **Secrets** — OpenBao. Browse a path, read a version,
  write one, undelete one.

You do not configure which one you get. Flui reads the
engine the catalog manifest declared when the service was
installed. Where no engine was declared — an install older
than the declaration — it falls back to what it can
recognise from the image name, and then from the settings
the install carries.

### Backup, disk and going back in time

Three more panels sit alongside the consoles, on the
database side:

- **Backup** — a logical dump produced by the engine's own
  tool and streamed to you, and a restore that runs that
  dump back into the live database. The restore overwrites
  what is there; it says so before it asks.
- **Disk** — how full the storage under the database is,
  with a near-full warning. The number is for the filesystem
  hosting the volume, because that is the boundary where the
  database actually stops.
- **Point in time** — where continuous backup is on, the
  window you can recover to, and a restore *as of* a moment.
  That restore never touches the source: it builds a fresh
  install and recovers into it, and you connect to the copy.

The same three have CLI equivalents — `flui db dump`,
`flui db restore`, `flui db disk`, `flui db backup-status`
and `flui db pitr-restore`.

## Who may open one, and that changed

This part used to be simple and wrong. Opening a console was
decided by one fact: is this row yours. If the application
belonged to you, the console opened.

It now asks the same access engine every other route in the
product asks. Four things follow from that, and the first is
the one to read twice.

**Owning an application is no longer enough on its own.**
Ownership is what a grant *selects on*, not permission by
itself. If nothing grants you access to that application,
its console does not open, even though the row is yours.

**A grant taken away or narrowed applies here too.** Before,
a grant could be revoked everywhere in the product and the
console stayed open, because the console was not asking. It
asks now.

Note also what level it asks for: the one that lets you
change an application, not merely see it. Behind one door
sit arbitrary queries, decrypted connection details and a
restore. A **viewer** grant does not open a console; an
**operator** grant does. The roles are the ones in
[Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/).

**A key's ceiling is checked before the row is loaded.** An
agent credential carries a ceiling — a limit on what it may
do, whoever holds it. That ceiling is now checked first, on
the way in, before Flui even looks the application up. It
used to be missing here, which meant a narrowly scoped key
held by an application's own owner could walk into an
arbitrary query prompt its scopes never mentioned. Asking
first is also why that refusal is safe: it can be specific
about the key's own limits without saying anything about
whether the id you named exists.

**Applications the platform installed answer to the
installation.** Flui's own workloads belong to nobody in
particular. Their consoles open only to a principal holding
authority over the whole installation — held globally, not
narrowed to one cluster or one set of applications.

### Refusals that say nothing

There is exactly one refusal that tells you what happened:
the application exists, and it is not yours to reach.

**Every other refusal answers as an absence, in the same
words.** A console that is fenced off, an id that does not
exist, an application with no recorded owner — all three
read identically, and none of them repeats the id back at
you. That is deliberate. A refusal that names its reason
teaches a stranger that this id runs something here, and a
refusal that differs from the one next to it can be told
apart by anyone willing to read it. Somebody guessing ids
learns nothing from any of it.

## Read-only by default, and it means it

Every console defaults to read-only. A write has to be asked
for explicitly; nothing about a console is write-first.

On the relational console this is not a checkbox that
watches for the word `DELETE`. It is enforced at the
database session. Each query opens a transaction, sets it
read-only, applies the limits, and then **rolls back**
rather than commits. A statement that tries to write fails
at the engine, and nothing it did survives, because the
transaction is discarded either way.

Two more guards ride along on every query:

- **A statement timeout of about 30 seconds.** A missing
  `WHERE` or an accidental cross join is cut off by the
  database rather than holding a connection open.
- **A row cap of about 1000 rows.** The grid shows the first
  slice and tells you it was truncated. This is a tool for
  inspection, not for bulk export.

The other consoles follow the same rule in their own terms.
Browsing is read by nature. A command runner passes through
a read-only gate: arbitrary commands are allowed while they
are reads, and a write or destructive one — a flush, a
delete, a topic removal — is refused unless the write path
was asked for.

The reason for all of this is blast radius. The console is
the everyday "let me just check something" tool, and the
everyday tool should be incapable of breaking the thing it
is inspecting.

## How it connects: the owner's own credentials

To run anything, the console has to authenticate to the
service. Today it does that with the service's **own owner
credentials** — the same user, password and database the
catalog generated when it installed the building block.

You never type them and they are never stored a second time.
Flui reads them, at the moment of the query, from the secret
the install already owns. Relational engines carry a user
and a database; caches authenticate with a password alone,
and are often installed with no authentication at all, in
which case the console connects anonymously.

Here is the honest version: **everyone who can open a
console connects as the owner of that service.** That is
survivable today, because the default is read-only, because
opening a console now requires a grant, and because every
query is recorded server-side, allowed and refused alike.
It is still a known limitation, not a destination.

### The forward path: a role per person

What makes the owner-credential model temporary is a
deliberate seam. The thing that turns "this application"
into "a live connection" is one narrow piece — a connection
resolver. The one in place resolves the owner credentials
and reports the role as `owner`. A later one will resolve a
dedicated role per Flui user and report the role as `user`,
and it slots in behind the same seam, with no change to the
query layer, the transport, or the helper above it.

## How the browser reaches a private database

Flui databases are not reachable from outside the cluster
network. So how does a console running in your browser reach
one?

**Through Flui's backend.** The browser talks only to the
Flui API. The backend opens a private link to the running
database, runs the query over it, and hands back the result.
The link is kept warm for about a minute so a burst of
queries reuses it, then it closes. The browser never holds a
connection to the database and never learns its address.

That is also why the connection-details panel is safe. It
returns what you need to reason about a connection — engine,
database name, user, port — and **never the password.** The
password does not travel over the API at all.

For a native client, `flui db tunnel` puts the same idea on
your own machine: a local port, bound to loopback, forwarded
through the control plane, with nothing opened to the
internet. That is a task page:
[Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/).

## Two things it will never open

Two databases under the product are closed to the web
console absolutely: Flui's own database, which holds every
user, key, encrypted provider token and application row, and
the identity provider's tables, which live in the same
place, so the same door opens every session and credential
on the installation.

That exclusion is declared in one place, with its reason
next to it, and it hangs on nothing that could go missing —
no label, no declared engine, no recorded owner. It is not a
side effect of anything; taking a database out of that fence
means deleting a line on purpose.

They are still reachable, from the CLI, by someone holding
authority over the whole installation. That is its own task
page, because the stakes are:
[Reach the platform's own database](/tasks/reach-the-platform-database/).

## The helper is data-blind

Most consoles offer a helper: describe what you want in
plain words, and it writes the query or the command, with an
explanation, for you to read and run yourself. It never runs
anything on your behalf — and it never sees your data.

This is the load-bearing safety property, so be precise
about it. What is sent to the model is structure and your
question. On the relational console that means table and
column names, types, primary keys and foreign keys, your
prompt, and Flui's own baked-in notes on that engine's
dialect and its traps. On the key-value console it is
narrower still: a key count and a breakdown by type, never
key names and never values. On the document and search
consoles it is names, field paths and inferred types, never
the contents of a record. On Kafka it is topic and group
names, never a message.

What is never sent is row data. The helper reads shape; it
does not read, sample or forward what is stored. That is
what makes it safe to point a hosted model at a production
database.

Whatever the helper writes then runs under exactly the rules
a hand-typed query runs under — read-only by default, the
timeout, the row cap. A suggestion that would change data is
flagged as such so the dashboard can put a confirmation in
front of it, but the flag is a hint; the read-only session
underneath is the real boundary.

The helper ships no model of its own. It uses the same
inference layer as the rest of Flui's assistant features, so
it inherits whatever you configured there — Flui's native
inference or your own provider. That has its own chapter:
[Inference and bring-your-own LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/).

## What it is, and what it is not

- It **is** a fast, safe way to look inside the data
  services you already run on Flui — query, browse, scan,
  read a value, get a draft — without exposing anything and
  without a second tool to host.
- It is **not** an administration suite, a migration runner
  or a bulk-export tool. The row cap and the read-only
  default are what make it the right thing to reach for
  first.

## Where to read next

- [Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/) —
  `flui db tunnel` and a native client.
- [Reach the platform's own database](/tasks/reach-the-platform-database/) —
  the two reserved names, and the rules around them.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/) —
  the roles and grants a console now asks about.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/) —
  databases are applications in Flui's model, with the same
  lifecycle, logs and metrics as anything else.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/) —
  where the building blocks these consoles operate on come
  from.
- [Inference and bring-your-own LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/) —
  the inference layer the data-blind helper draws on.

sections.title: The action cycle
sections.body:
An agent connected to Flui acts as the person who connected
it. It holds their credential, so it can do what they can do.
That is what makes it useful, and it is also the problem: the
same key that deploys an application also adds machines you
pay for, moves a database between clusters, or takes an
application away along with its storage.

Flui's answer is not to make the agent less capable. It is to
put a person between the model and the act. More than forty
write routes are declared **inside the action cycle**: when
the caller is an agent, the call does not run. It becomes a
question addressed to a person.

This chapter is the *why* behind that pause. It is written
for the person connecting an agent and for the agent itself —
both end up reading it.

## What the agent gets instead of an effect

The call is refused, and the refusal is not an error. It
carries:

- a **request id**;
- **one plain sentence** describing what was asked for —
  "add nodes to cluster *this one*", not "infrastructure";
- a **link to the page** where a person answers;
- when the action has a price, the fact that a price exists;
- when the route said so, what happens if the person allows
  it.

The person answers one of three ways:

- **once** — let this exact call through, remember nothing;
- **always** — let it through *and* write down a standing
  permission;
- **no** — refuse it.

The wording the agent receives says, in as many words, that
this is a wait and not a failure, that nothing was changed,
and that varying the arguments to get around it will only
raise a second question rather than answer the first.

## The answer arrives by retrying, not by waiting

Nothing holds a connection open while somebody thinks. The
agent finds out by making the identical call again: if the
person allowed it, it goes through.

That is a deliberate choice, and it buys two things. A
request can sit unanswered for an hour without a socket held
open somewhere. And it works for an agent with no special
client support at all — an agent driving Flui with plain
HTTP calls meets exactly the same pause and learns the answer
the same way.

## Who counts as an agent

Two things make a caller an agent, and the caller can claim
neither of them for itself:

- its credential carries agent scopes;
- the call arrives through an agentic surface — the
  assistant inside Flui.

A person filling in a dashboard form or typing a `flui`
command is untouched. On this side of the table they are the
approver, not the applicant, and pausing to ask them to
confirm what they just typed would be theatre.

The in-product assistant is gated all the same, even though
the same human being is at both ends of it. The question that
decides the pause is not *whose credential is this* but **who
wrote the arguments**. A form carries what a person typed. A
tool call carries what a model chose. Confirming the second
is not theatre, because what is confirmed is not what they
wrote.

## An agent cannot answer its own request

An agent key is issued *as* its person. Every permission
check on the page where requests are answered would therefore
pass, and the applicant would be holding the approver's pen.

So the refusal there is on what the caller **is**, not on
what it may do. An agent credential is turned away from the
decision routes even though its permissions are, by
construction, sufficient. The same rule keeps the in-product
assistant on the applicant's side: the chat cannot approve
its own request, while the person reading it in the dashboard
can.

A request also belongs to somebody. It is answered by the
person it was addressed to — running the whole installation
is not standing to answer a question asked of someone else,
and another person's request reads as not existing rather
than as forbidden.

## An hour is the life of a request

A request expires after one hour.

The reason is the price. A request carries an estimate of
what the action will cost, and a price agreed on Tuesday
against a quote taken on Monday is a lie told by a database.
Once the window closes, the request is no longer answerable;
the agent's next attempt refreshes it, with a fresh window
and a fresh price, keeping the same id so the number the
agent already reported still points at the thing the person
is looking at.

## "Always" is one action, one resource, one credential

"Always allow" sounds wide. It is not.

A standing permission is recorded against a specific action
**and** the specific resource that action names — "add nodes
to *this* cluster", not "add nodes". Pointed at another
cluster, it does not match, and the agent is back to asking.

It is also tied to **that one credential**. A different key,
even one the same person minted a minute later, starts from
requests again. A permission is given to an agent, not to a
person's whole future.

And a request that cannot name its own resource is only ever
offered **once**. If the action has no edge to write down,
there is nothing narrow to concede, so nothing standing is
offered at all.

## A standing permission grants nothing

This is the load-bearing rule, and it is worth stating
plainly: allowing an agent to stop asking can never let it do
something it could not already do.

The pause is the **last** check. By the time a call reaches
the action cycle, everything that decides whether the call is
allowed at all has already run and already said yes. All the
cycle can remove is the pause in front of it. A permission is
not negotiable; a pause is.

So "always" is not a grant. It is the removal of a question
about something the person's own access already permitted.

## Taking it back

A person can see what their agents may do without asking,
revoke any of it, and — before deciding — see **what is
still running** under that permission.

Revoking is immediate and total for anything that has not
started: the standing permission is read on every single
request, so from the moment it is taken back nothing else
departs under it.

It does **not** abort work already running. There is a
separate, explicit option to also *ask* running work to stop,
and even that is honoured at the next safe step, never
mid-step — because a ten-step provisioning run cut in half
leaves paid-for resources orphaned somewhere, which is worse
than the thing the person was trying to stop.

The revoke dialog asks for the running list first for exactly
that reason. Taking a permission back and having three
provisionings continue is the honest answer, and a dialog
that hid it would make the revoke feel like something it is
not.

## Small rules that follow from the same thinking

**Repeated attempts collapse.** An agent retrying the same
call with the same arguments finds the request it already
raised. One question, however many attempts.

**The arguments are never stored.** They are read once, to
recognise a repeat, and thrown away. Some of them are
secrets — the answers to a catalog install can include an
administrator password — and a table built to be read by a
person deciding whether to say yes is no place for them. What
is kept is the sentence.

**A dry run does not ask.** A route that can be told "check
this and change nothing" — validating a manifest, for
instance — skips the pause. Putting a person in front of a
question about a deploy that is not happening would describe
the wrong act, and that sentence is what gets stored.

**The price is withheld from the agent on purpose.** Where a
request has a cost, the agent is told that a price exists,
that it cannot see it, and that the person deciding can. It
is instructed to say exactly that rather than describe the
action as free or invent a figure.

**A settled "no" reads as settled.** Retrying something that
was already refused gets a distinct answer: the person
answered, stop, tell them what was refused and offer another
course of action. It is deliberately not phrased as an
access-control failure, because an agent that reads it as one
goes off asking for permissions the person just declined.

## Where a person answers

In the dashboard, on the **Agents** page, which is where
requests raised by your agents wait for you. The link in the
refusal points straight at the individual request. The API
serves the same thing directly.

There is **no CLI command** for this today. You cannot list
requests, approve one, or revoke a standing permission from
the terminal. If your only surface is the CLI, the pause is
still enforced — the answering happens elsewhere.

## The trade-off, said out loud

A pause an agent does not understand is a bad experience. The
agent stops, reports something confusing, and the person
wonders why nothing happened.

Flui works hard on the wording of that refusal for exactly
this reason: it says it is a wait, says what was asked for,
says who can allow it and where. But there is a real gap
today, and it is worth knowing about: **the onboarding
document Flui hands an agent when it connects does not
mention the action cycle at all.** The tool that serves it
claims the document teaches the pattern; version 1.2.0 of the
document does not contain it. An agent following it will meet
its first pause with no idea what one is.

Until that is fixed, the fix is manual and cheap: tell the
agent about the cycle, or point it at this page. An agent
that knows the rule reports "I asked, and someone needs to
allow it" instead of "it failed".

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The Flui Assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/) —
  the surfaces an agent reaches Flui through, and the scope
  model underneath them.
- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/) — where
  the credential an agent carries comes from, and whose it is.

sections.title: What a cluster may buy for itself
sections.body:
Most platforms make autoscaling a switch. You turn it on, and
from then on something you cannot see spends your money while
nobody is in the room. When the bill arrives, the only record
of why is a graph.

Flui does not have that switch. Nothing on an installation
scales itself until somebody writes down what a specific
cluster may buy, where it must stop, and whether it may act at
all. That written-down thing is a **scaling group**, and this
chapter is about why it is shaped the way it is.

## The group is the consent

A scaling group is a resource on a cluster. A cluster can have
more than one — one for the general work, one for the heavy
jobs — because those two fleets differ in every field below.

A group says:

- **Three bounds.** A **floor** (`min`), held now and always;
  a **target** (`desired`), where the fleet would like to sit;
  and a **ceiling** (`max`), as far as the urgent side may go
  right now. The target is deliberately not a promise: being
  under it buys nothing on its own. It is reached when the
  market allows, and it is the resting point a fleet returns
  to after a burst.
- **Where** it may buy — regions, plural. That plural is what
  makes "cheapest, anywhere" possible at all.
- **What** it may buy — machine shapes, in order of
  preference. The order *is* the preference.
- **A placement strategy** — `cheapest`, `closest`,
  `roomiest` or `uniform`.
- **A ceiling in money**, a monthly figure, optional.
- **A settle window** — how long work must have been stuck
  before this buys anything. Thirty seconds by default.
- **Whether it may act.** `provision: manual` means the group
  decides and tells you. `provision: automatic` means it may
  go and buy. This one field is the consent.

Nothing autoscales until one of these exists. There is no
installation-wide grant sitting above it, and that absence is
deliberate: a second ceiling outside the product would guard
one road out of your wallet while leaving the others open. The
group already carries its own ceilings, in money and in nodes,
where a reader can see them. What needs consent is acting
*without a person*, and that consent is one word on the group.

Removing a group takes no machine away. What it withdraws is
the permission — from then on the cluster decides nothing
about its own size.

## The settle window is not patience

Thirty seconds sounds like waiting for a better price. It is
not, and the difference matters.

The window exists to be sure the work is genuinely stuck
rather than caught mid-placement — another workload shutting
down, a node finishing a drain, the scheduler halfway round.
Once that window passes, nothing waits for anything. The
urgent side never holds out for a cheaper machine.

## Two forces on one fleet

Two very different pressures act on a fleet, and Flui keeps
them apart on purpose.

**Urgency.** Work cannot be placed. Its clock is seconds and
it never waits. It walks a ladder of fallbacks and takes the
first rung that would work:

1. the preferred shape, in the cluster's own region;
2. the preferred shape, in any region this group may buy in;
3. anything that holds the work, in the cluster's own region;
4. anything that holds it, anywhere the group may buy.

**Opportunity.** Patient growth toward the target when the
market allows. Its clock is hours, and **waiting is the
mechanism** rather than a delay in it. Nobody is held up if it
never fires. It is also what gives a machine back when the
fleet has overshot its target, and what quietly replaces a
stand-in that urgency bought in a hurry with the shape the
group actually wanted.

## The one rule where they meet

**Urgency always wins, and opportunity stands down entirely
while anything is waiting.**

Including when the cluster cannot be asked whether anything is
waiting. An unanswered cluster is not a quiet one: silence
does not rule a waiting workload out, so the patient side
stays down and nothing is decided.

There is exactly one thing that still holds while the cluster
is silent, and it is the floor. The floor is not a reading of
the cluster — it is a fact about the fleet's own records. Any
other design leaves an installation below its floor precisely
when its cluster is in trouble, which is the moment the floor
exists for.

## Why the ceiling is money

A limit of "at most six nodes" tells you almost nothing. Six
of one shape and six of another are different bills, and the
gap between them is the whole question.

So the ceiling a group carries is **an amount of money per
month**, weighed against what the fleet already commits. A
shape that would push the total past it loses, and the row
says so with both figures in it.

Two honest details follow from that:

- Flui refuses on **certainty only**. A machine carrying no
  published price adds nothing to the committed figure, so
  clearing the ceiling is never proof of being under it. Where
  the fleet is only partly priced, the decision says out loud
  that the figure is a floor and not the bill, and counts the
  machines it could not price.
- Where a group has named a ceiling, a machine with **no
  published price is not bought automatically**. A ceiling
  cannot be honoured against an unknown amount. The machine is
  named in an alarm for a person instead.

A group can also refuse shapes billed only by the month. They
make autoscaling cost-neutral at best: you cannot give the
machine back at the end of the hour.

## Why placement is never "it fits"

The four strategies choose among the shapes that **already
fit**. "It fits" is not one of them, and that is not a
cosmetic distinction.

A shape that cannot hold the waiting work is not a candidate
at all. Were fitting merely a preference, `cheapest` would
pick the shape that helps nobody: the money is spent, the
machine arrives, and the work is still waiting. So fitting is
a filter that runs first, and the strategy only breaks the tie
among the survivors:

- **cheapest** — lowest price first;
- **closest** — the cluster's own region first;
- **roomiest** — the largest machine first;
- **uniform** — keep the fleet one shape, which is what
  happens today without anybody choosing it.

Fitting is also measured honestly. Flui takes off what the
system itself needs on every machine before asking whether the
waiting work still fits. A machine that holds the request only
with nothing left over does not hold it.

## Every decision is a row, including the ones that did nothing

An autoscaler is only ever asked one question, and it is
always the same one: *why did you not scale?*

So a decline is written down in exactly the same shape as a
purchase — what it saw, what it did, why, and what it still
needs from a person — along with every rung it walked past and
the reason that rung lost. `flui scaling why` prints them, for
the whole cluster by default, naming the group each decision
came from. Filtering the declines out would remove the only
answer the command exists to give.

The rows are a resource, not a log: the same answer is
rewritten when it changes, and once an hour otherwise, so a
reader can see the loop is alive without the one interesting
row being buried under a thousand copies of "still nothing to
do".

`flui scaling preview` asks the same engine what it would do
if a machine were needed right now, spending nothing, and
shows the whole ladder.

### Why `refused-by-limit` has its own name

One reason a shape can lose is named apart from all the
others: **`refused-by-limit`** means the shape was available,
and affordable, and **this group's own rules excluded it
anyway**.

From the outside that is indistinguishable from the provider
having nothing to sell. Somebody stares at an empty result and
goes looking for an outage, when the answer was a line they
wrote themselves — a ceiling already reached, a region their
own cluster does not sit in, a shape marked deprecated, an
hourly-billing-only rule against a provider that bills by the
month. Named separately, it is one setting away from a
purchase. Left unnamed, it is a wild goose chase.

For the same reason, the reasons are ordered by how near the
rung came to buying, and the decision reports the nearest
miss — because that is the one a person can act on.

## What a provider can do is derived, never assumed

Flui never reads a provider's capabilities off its name. It
takes them from what that provider has declared, on three
separate questions:

- **Can Flui create a server here?**
- **Is there a catalogue** — a list of shapes with prices
  attached?
- **How is it billed** — by the hour, by the month, or not
  visibly at all?

Three flags and not one ladder, because a provider that
publishes a price list but has no create API is not a lesser
version of one that can buy. It is a different sentence
addressed to a person. There, deciding *is* the whole of what
happens: the group raises an alarm that names the shape, the
region and the price, and asks somebody to buy one and join it
with `flui node connect`. Where no catalogue exists at all,
the alarm instead says what a machine has to hold.

A provider Flui knows nothing about gets the closed answer: it
buys nothing, publishes nothing, and is billed for nothing
anyone can see.

This is also why `flui scaling list` shows the clusters that
look least interesting. A cluster with no scaling group at
all, and a cluster whose provider can only raise an alarm,
are both listed. A tidy filter would answer "all well" in
exactly the two cases where somebody is needed.

## `max: 0` is a fleet, not a switch

A ceiling of zero is allowed, and it is a statement rather
than a group turned off. It says: **this fleet should hold no
machines.**

What that states depends on who does the buying. Where the
group provisions manually, it says every machine on this
cluster is one somebody attached by hand. Where it provisions
automatically, it says urgency may buy nothing. Either way it
is a described state, not an absence of one — and since the
floor and the target can never sit above the ceiling, writing
it means writing all three bounds at zero deliberately.

If you want a group to stop acting, the field for that is
`provision: manual`.

## The group is a file

A scaling group can be written as a `kind: ScalingGroup`
document. `flui scaling export` writes one and
`flui scaling apply -f` reads it back. `--dry-run` says what
would be written without writing it. Several groups can live
in one file, separated by `---`.

The file is **the whole group**: a field left out is a field
reset to its default, not a field left alone. That is the
reading a reviewer gives the file, so it is the reading the
command gives it too, and the same file applied twice leaves
the same group.

Only what a person wrote is exported. What the provider can
do, and what the market is doing today, are read fresh every
time — they would be stale the moment the file was committed.

## When an agent asks for this

Writing a scaling group, or changing one, is one of the
actions that stops and asks a person when an agent is the
caller. What gets agreed to is not a machine; it is a standing
figure — how large this cluster may become and how much of
somebody's money it may spend with nobody in the room — so the
question a person answers carries that figure rather than the
word "scaling".

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/) —
  the machines a group is deciding about, and adding or
  resizing one by hand.
- [The cluster as a concept](/concepts/03-cluster-as-a-concept/) —
  what a cluster owns, and where its scaling groups sit.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/) —
  why buying, cataloguing and billing are three capabilities a
  provider can have or lack.

sections.title: Who can reach what
sections.body:
[Identity](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/) answers one
question — who is this. It does not answer the second one,
and the second one is the one that matters once more than
one person uses the installation: what may they touch.

This chapter is about the second question.

## Nothing is implied

The rule underneath everything else: **deny by default**.
An account that signs in perfectly and holds no grant
reaches nothing. The home screen and its own settings open;
no applications, no clusters, no sections. Signing in is not
access. It is only identity.

That is a deliberate trade. The alternative — a floor that
every authenticated person gets for free — is comfortable
right up to the day somebody asks what a new colleague can
see and nobody can answer. With deny by default the answer
is always the same shape: whatever somebody wrote down for
them, and nothing else.

The one exception is the installation's administrators,
who pass everything. The `owner` role below is the version
of that which can be written down, handed out, and taken
back.

## The ladder: viewer, operator, maintainer, owner

There are four roles, and they are a ladder rather than a
menu. Each rung carries everything the rung below it
carries, plus more.

**Viewer** — reads the applications in scope, and can open
the Clusters section so the machines those applications run
on are not a blank page.

**Operator** — the whole life of the applications in scope:
create, deploy, operate, scale, migrate and remove them.
No access management, no infrastructure.

Removing is in this rung, not higher up, and that is worth
a sentence because it looks generous. What protects an
application from a careless removal is not withholding the
verb from a whole role — it is the *scope* of the grant.
You can only remove what your grant already reaches, and
the removal says how much data goes with it before it asks.

**Maintainer** — an operator, plus the installation itself:
the clusters, who may reach what, the shared integrations,
the showcase, the demonstration.

**Owner** — everything, everywhere, including who else runs
this installation.

`flui iam roles` prints the four and exactly what each one
carries. `flui iam whoami` prints what the identity you are
using actually holds right now, which is the faster way to
answer "why can I not see this".

### An owner makes an owner

Conferring the `owner` role — or removing somebody else's
— needs user-management authority held over the **whole
installation**, not narrowed to one cluster or one set of
applications.

The reason is a door that would otherwise be open. A
maintainer can already hand out roles; that is most of the
job. Without this rule, a maintainer could hand themselves
the top rung through the access screen, and the ladder
would have no top. The same rule governs removal, because
stripping an installation of its owners one row at a time
is the same climb, descended.

## A grant is a principal, a role, and a reach

Access is not stored on people. It is stored as **grants**,
and a grant says three things:

- **who** — a person, a group, or a service account;
- **which role** — one of the four above;
- **how far it reaches** — the scope.

The scope is where the model earns its keep. It can be:

- **the whole installation** — everything, everywhere;
- **one cluster** — everything that lives on it;
- **one portal section** — the Clusters section, the Mail
  section, and so on;
- **a selector** — a standing description of applications.

A selector is not a list of applications. It is a rule
about them, and it can constrain the application kind, the
project, the provider, the cluster (by id or by name),
whether the application is a platform one or a user one, a
list of slugs, a set of tags, and the owner.

Every constraint you write must hold at once. Slugs are a
membership test — the application must be one of them.
Tags are an *all-of* test — the application must carry
every tag you name, not just one. An attribute the
application does not have never matches a selector that
constrains it.

The point of a rule rather than a list is what happens
later. An application deployed tomorrow that matches the
selector is covered tomorrow, with nothing to re-grant and
nobody to remember. That also means a selector is wider
than it looks when you write it, which is why the sentence
a person is asked to confirm says so out loud: *over every
application a standing rule matches, including ones
deployed later*.

From the terminal:

```bash
flui iam grant add \
  --principal alice@example.com \
  --role operator \
  --scope selector \
  --project shop --tag production
```

`--dry-run` says what the grant would open — and what the
same change closes — and creates nothing.

Groups exist so the same sentence does not have to be
written once per person: `flui iam group create`,
`add-member`, `remove-member`, `list`, `delete`. Members
are named by email address, and a grant addressed to the
group reaches all of them.

### Taking a grant back says what it costs

`flui iam grant remove <id>` reads out what the holder
stops being able to reach **before** it asks you to
confirm. `--dry-run` prints that and removes nothing.

The order is the whole feature. A warning shown after
somebody has already pressed yes is not a warning, it is a
receipt.

## Sections have three states, not two

A portal section used to be all or nothing: hold the
governing permission over the whole installation and see
the section, or do not see it at all.

That left no way to say the thing two different readers
need. A guest on a public demonstration should be able to
look around the product without changing it. A read-only
operator should be able to open the Backup section and read
what is there without being able to start anything.

So there is a third state: **read-only**. The section is
visible, its screens open, and its controls are drawn
disabled. Behind it, only safe reads get through — every
write is refused at the door, so the disabled buttons are
not the enforcement, they are the honest picture of it.

One honest limitation. Today the only role that opens
sections at this level is the one the platform writes for a
guest of the public demonstration; none of the four
assignable roles carries it yet. The reason is stated in
the product: two of these sections — Mail and Access —
answer with other people's personal data once the screen
actually loads, and there is no per-person filtering on
those screens yet. Until there is, opening them read-only
to a colleague would be a wider door than it looks.

## A refusal that tells you nothing

There are two kinds of "no", and confusing them leaks the
installation.

"You may not do this" is useful. It tells a person what to
ask for. But on some surfaces the *existence* of the thing
is itself the secret, and a refusal that differs from
"there is nothing here" hands a stranger a map: guess ids,
read the wording, and learn which ones run something worth
reaching.

So on those surfaces — the data consoles, a shell on a
machine, somebody's own model connection — **every refusal
that is not "this belongs to someone else" answers as an
absence**, in one wording, and does not repeat the id back
to you.

On the console the sentence is the same whether the
application does not exist, exists but records no owner,
belongs to the platform rather than to a person, or is one
of the two [platform databases](/concepts/25-the-database-console/)
that no console may ever open. Four different situations,
one answer. Probing ids teaches you nothing, which is the
only version of that promise worth making.

"It belongs to someone else" stays a distinct answer,
because that one *is* actionable: go and ask them.

The same instinct explains a quieter change. A route that
takes an id straight from the URL used to be protected by
a permission alone — and a permission check made without a
resource is satisfied by any grant that carries that
permission at all. So an operator scoped to their own
applications could reach somebody else's row by guessing a
uuid. Those routes now load the row and ask about *that
row*, so a row that records an owner is not reachable by
id by anyone else.

## A credential is a ceiling, never a grant

The last piece is the one people most often get backwards.

When a call arrives, two questions are asked, and they are
not the same question:

1. what may this **person** do — access control, the
   grants above;
2. what may this **key in their hand** do — its scopes.

Scopes can only take away. A key issued for "look at
applications" is worth exactly that even when the person
who minted it is an administrator — and it is worth that
everywhere, not only inside the agent toolbox: on plain
HTTP, and on a live-updates connection, held to the same
scopes. A key is issued *as* its person, so without this
rule a narrow key would quietly carry its owner's full
weight anywhere nothing was watching.

A credential that declares no scopes at all — an
interactive login, the CLI's own key, the platform's own
service identities — declares no ceiling and loses nothing.
This narrows; it never widens. No scope on any key can let
anybody do something their grants do not already allow.

A key can also be limited to named applications, named
projects, or both. Those two lists are alternatives rather
than requirements: an application is reachable the moment
either list covers it.

### Why the two refusals are worded differently

This is deliberate, and it is the part worth remembering.

A **scope** refusal says the credential's scopes do not
carry the permission this call needs. That is a *grant*
problem, and it is fixed by re-issuing the credential with
the right permission groups. No amount of IAM will help.

An **access-control** refusal says the caller is not
allowed on this resource. That is a *permission* problem,
and it is fixed with a grant.

Told the wrong one of those, a person goes to the wrong
screen, and an agent retries forever. So they never share a
sentence.

The application-list refusal is a third case, and says so:
that one is fixed by widening the **same** key's
application list. Nothing needs re-issuing, and whatever
holds the key keeps working against the new list.

One trap the refusal now names out loud. If agent scopes
are attached to a *person's* account in the identity
provider rather than to a machine account, they cap that
person's browser session too — correctly, because the key
is that account. What was missing was any way to find that
out, so the refusal now says where the scopes came from.
Agent scopes belong on a machine account, not on a person.

## Access as a file

Grants can be read and written as a document:

```bash
flui iam export > access-policy.yaml
flui iam apply -f access-policy.yaml
```

`export` writes a `kind: AccessPolicy` document — every
grant on the installation. `apply` reads one back and is
idempotent: it creates what is missing and leaves the rest
alone. `--prune` makes it a full sync, deleting grants the
file does not name.

**A naming caution.** The published `@flui-cloud/spec`
package still types the roles as `viewer`, `editor` and
`manager` — the names from before the rename. The
product's names are the current ones: **viewer, operator,
maintainer, owner**. Write those. If a tool built on the
spec package rejects `operator`, that is the package
lagging behind the product, not your file being wrong.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/) —
  who somebody is, which is the question this one starts
  from.
- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/)
  — the sharpest surface the rules above govern.

sections.title: How Flui protects data
sections.body:
Most backup documentation tells you which commands exist. This page tells you
something more useful and less comfortable: **which of your data is actually
being kept, and which is not.**

Flui protects four different subjects, with four different mechanisms, and they
do not substitute for one another. A cluster backup running nightly does not
mean your database is safe. That sentence is the reason this page exists.

## The four subjects

| Subject | Mechanism | Runs | Lives | Restores as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cluster state** | Velero snapshot | on a schedule | S3, outside the cluster | objects replayed into a cluster |
| **A Postgres database** | continuous WAL archiving (pgBackRest) | continuously + base backups | S3, outside the cluster | a **new** database, recovered to a moment you pick |
| **The control plane** | encrypted `pg_dumpall`, sealed to a key only you hold | on a schedule | S3, outside the cluster | offline, by an operator, from a runbook |
| **One volume** | a copy of the volume | on demand | S3 (durable), or a clone inside the cluster (fast) | a new volume, side by side |

### Cluster state

A Velero snapshot of the Kubernetes objects: Deployments, StatefulSets,
Services, Ingresses, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and anything else in scope —
including resources Flui did not create, such as a CRD you applied yourself.

It also captures volume data, but **only for volumes on the shared storage
class.** Volumes on the dedicated class cannot be read by Velero's file-system
backup, and the dedicated class is what databases use (see
[Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/)).
This is not a setting you can change: it is a property of how the two classes
provision volumes.

So a cluster backup that reports success may contain none of your database
data, and that is expected rather than broken. Every run records how many
volumes it captured and names the ones it skipped, so the gap is visible on the
job rather than discovered during a restore.

**What it does not cover:** container images, anything outside the cluster, and
volume data on dedicated storage.

### A Postgres database

For a database installed from the Flui catalog, continuous backup ships the
write-ahead log as it is produced and takes periodic base backups. That is what
makes it possible to recover the database *as of a moment you name* rather than
as of last night.

Recovery never touches the database you are looking at. It builds a **new**
install beside it, recovered to your chosen instant, with its own credentials,
and leaves you to decide what to do next.

**What it does not cover:** databases Flui did not provision. Continuous backup
is implemented with pgBackRest, which ships inside Flui's own Postgres image; a
plain `postgres` container running as one component of some other application
cannot be protected this way. For those, use a volume copy.

### The control plane

The database holding every user, API key, provider token and application record
Flui has. It is dumped, encrypted, and sealed to an **age** key pair you
generate on your own machine — the private half never touches the server,
because a key stored on the machine you are trying to recover is lost with it.

It is deliberately not restorable through the normal restore pipeline. Rebuilding
an installation from it is an operator procedure with a runbook, not a button.

**What it does not cover:** it is the platform's own records, not your
applications' data.

### One volume

Two shapes of the same thing, and the difference is where the copy lives:

- **A copy to object storage** sits outside the cluster. It survives the cluster
  being destroyed, and it survives the application being deleted. Slower to
  restore.
- **A clone inside the cluster** is faster and cheaper to make, but it lives on
  the same disk as the application and carries the application's own label — so
  deleting the application takes the clone with it. It is protection against a
  bad upgrade, not against a deletion.

Both restore side by side: a new volume is created next to the application,
which you can then promote.

## Which one do I want?

- *"I want to be able to go back to before that migration."* — continuous
  backup, for a Postgres database. For anything else, a volume copy taken first.
- *"Someone deleted a namespace."* — cluster state.
- *"I want to survive losing the whole cluster."* — cluster state for the
  objects, plus continuous backup or volume copies to object storage for the
  data. A clone inside the cluster does not survive this.
- *"I want to survive losing Flui itself."* — the control plane backup, and the
  age key kept somewhere else.

## The honest summary

If you set up exactly one thing, a nightly cluster backup, then today you have:
your configuration, your Kubernetes objects, and the data of applications on
shared storage. You do **not** have your databases. Protecting those is a
second, separate decision — and the product will not make it for you.
