# Flui CLI reference (generated)

> Generated from `oclif manifest` for flui CLI `0.13.0`. Do not edit by hand —
> regenerate with `pnpm kb:cli-ref`. This is the assistant's ground truth for commands.

CLI version: **0.13.0** · commands: **240**

## (root)

### `flui deploy`

Deploy an application from a flui.yaml manifest to a cluster. Supports both kind:CatalogApp (pre-built image) and kind:Application (source build via GitHub Actions). Author a manifest with `flui app init <framework>`; see every field with `flui app manifest`.

Arguments:
  - `file` — Path to flui.yaml manifest (default: ./flui.yaml)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Target cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-r, --repo` — GitHub repository full name owner/repo (default: auto-detect from git remote origin). Required for kind:Application.
  - `-b, --branch` — Git branch to deploy (default: auto-detect current branch). Used for kind:Application.
  - `-d, --domain` — Custom FQDN for the app (default: auto-assign from cluster DNS zone)
  - `--name` — Release name override (default: metadata.name from the manifest). Part of the app identity, so passing a new one installs the same repo and branch a second time instead of updating the first install. Pass it on every deploy that targets that install.
  - `--exposure` [public | internal] — Override deploy.exposure for this install: public (Ingress + TLS) or internal (private URL behind Flui authentication).
  - `-e, --env` — Environment variable override in KEY=VALUE format. Repeatable.
  - `--env-file` — Path to a KEY=VALUE file of env overrides (one per line, # comments and blank lines ignored). Values never appear in the process arguments, so this is the safe way to pass secrets. --env entries take precedence. Name a key with --secret to also mark it as one.
  - `--secret` — Mark a key from --env/--env-file as a secret (repeatable): stored encrypted and delivered as a Kubernetes Secret rather than a plain ConfigMap entry, and never printed by `app status -o json` or `app env list`. Without this, every --env/--env-file value is stored as plain text — including one that looks like a credential.
  - `--detach` — Return immediately after triggering the build/deploy without waiting for completion. Use `flui app status <name>` to track progress.
  - `--no-build` — Skip the GitHub Actions build and re-deploy the current image. Useful for fast iterations on flui.yaml config (env, ports, healthcheck, endpoint) without rebuilding. If the app was deleted, falls back to the GHCR latest tag for {owner}/{repoName}.
  - `--image` — Deploy a specific image reference (e.g. ghcr.io/owner/repo:sha). Skips the build pipeline. Useful for rollback to a known tag, or to deploy from GHCR when the app was deleted from Flui.
  - `--skip-endpoint` — Skip DNS and TLS provisioning for this install
  - `--no-tls` — Provision the endpoint with DNS only, without a per-app TLS certificate. Overrides the manifest domain.tls. Avoids Let's Encrypt rate limits; the app is served over HTTP.
  - `--cert-challenge` [http-01 | dns-01] — ACME challenge for the app endpoint. http-01 works without a DNS zone and forces a per-host cert; dns-01 needs a cluster DNS zone with a wildcard issuer. Default: derived from cluster config.
  - `--cert-provider` [lets-encrypt | lets-encrypt-staging] — Certificate issuer for the app endpoint. Default: cluster default.
  - `--hostname` [ip | domain] — How the app is exposed: ip (nip.io) or domain (cluster DNS zone). Default: derived from manifest/cluster.
  - `--no-wait` — Alias for --detach (kind:CatalogApp compat)
  - `--validate-only` — Validate the manifest locally against the flui.cloud/v1beta1 schema without deploying (no cluster or login needed). Combine with --json for machine-readable output.
  - `--json` — With --validate-only, emit the result as JSON: { valid, kind, errors[], warnings[] }.
  - `--skip-checks` — Bypass the framework post-checks (e.g. Next.js standalone output). Only use when you are certain the Dockerfile will succeed despite the warnings.
  - `--allow-master` — Allow dedicated (node-local) storage to be placed on the control-plane node when the cluster has no worker. Escape hatch for single-node clusters (kind:CatalogApp).
  - `--api-url` — Override the API base URL (e.g. http://localhost:3000/api/v1) for local-API testing against an unreleased backend. Default: active profile.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> ./apps/api/flui.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --repo acme/my-app --branch main
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --detach
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --env DATABASE_URL=postgres://... --env API_KEY=secret
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --env-file .env --secret DATABASE_URL --secret API_KEY
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --validate-only
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster my-cluster
```

### `flui reconcile`

Reconcile CLI state with API (DNS configuration)

Flags:
  - `-t, --type` [dns | all] (default: ["all"]) — Reconciliation type(s) to execute (default: all)
  - `--api-url` — Flui API URL (default: from config or http://localhost:3000/api/v1)
  - `--dry-run` — Show what would be reconciled without making changes

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --type dns
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --dry-run
```

### `flui search-assist-test`

THROWAWAY: drive the search copilot (assist + optional run) via CLI auth, for validation.

Arguments:
  - `appId` (required) — OpenSearch application id

Flags:
  - `--prompt` — Single NL prompt (omit to use --suite)
  - `--index` — Active index for the prompt
  - `--suite` — Run the built-in 12-prompt suite
  - `--run` — Also execute the generated query via /search/query
  - `--exec-os` — Run the generated body directly against this OpenSearch URL (e.g. http://localhost:9201) — proves runnability without touching the cluster
  - `--api-url` — API base URL override (e.g. http://localhost:3000/api/v1)
  - `--raw` — Dev Tools raw call: "METHOD /path" (e.g. "GET /_cat/indices")
  - `--body` — JSON body for --raw
  - `--body-file` — Read the JSON body from a file (overrides --body)
  - `--allow-writes` — Send readOnly:false with --raw/--assist-raw (lets mutations run)
  - `--assist-raw` — Use the Dev Tools copilot (/assist-raw) for --prompt; with --run, executes via /raw
  - `--db-assist` — Probe the SQL console copilot: POST /db/assist with this prompt, print raw result
  - `--get` — Generic GET /applications/:appId/<subpath>
  - `--post-path` — Generic POST /applications/:appId/<subpath> (body via --body)
  - `--del` — Generic DELETE /applications/:appId/<subpath>
  - `--abs-get` — Generic GET against an absolute API path (e.g. catalog/installs/:id)
  - `--abs-post` — Generic POST against an absolute API path (e.g. catalog/install-from-yaml), body via --body

### `flui ssh`

SSH into a cluster node

Arguments:
  - `node` (required) — Node to SSH into, as <cluster>/<node> (e.g. my-cluster/master, my-cluster/worker-1). A bare node name (master, worker-1) targets the control cluster.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> master
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> worker-1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> control-cluster/master
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> workload-cluster-1/master
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> workload-cluster-1/worker-1
```

### `flui update`

Update the flui CLI to the latest version

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui version`

Show the CLI version and the platform release it pins (component image tags + bootstrap ref). Useful for debugging an install.

Flags:
  - `--latest` — Show what `env create --latest` would resolve to (mobile tags: bootstrap master, :latest images) instead of the pinned release
  - `--json` — Output as JSON

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --latest
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --json
```

## app

### `flui app alerts`

Show alerts for an application — one row per episode, newest first

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `--firing` — Only alerts still firing
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 20) — How many to show
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --firing
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app backup create`

Archive an application volume to S3-compatible object storage. When --bucket is omitted the cluster provider auto-provisions one (Scaleway: full-auto using your compute key; Hetzner: requires Object Storage credentials connected). Otherwise pass an explicit endpoint + --bucket and S3 credentials via flags or FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY/FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-v, --volume` — Volume (PVC) name when the app has multiple volumes. Required if more than one PVC exists.
  - `-d, --description` — Optional human-friendly tag appended to the key prefix
  - `--pause` — Stop the workloads holding the volume, copy it at rest, then start them again. A deliberate outage for the length of the copy.
  - `--allow-inconsistent` — Copy even though the volume holds a database that is being written to. The copy may not restore cleanly.
  - `-D, --destination` — Registered backup destination id (see `flui backup destination list`). Preferred: the copy is recorded against it and shows up in `flui backup list`.
  - `-b, --bucket` — Destination S3 bucket name. Omit to auto-provision via the cluster provider.
  - `-e, --endpoint` — S3 endpoint URL (required when --bucket is set). Examples: https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud, https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
  - `-r, --region` (default: "auto") — S3 region
  - `--access-key` — S3 access key. Defaults to FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY env var.
  - `--secret-key` — S3 secret key. Defaults to FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env var.
  - `--key-prefix` — Override the destination key prefix (default: flui/<cluster>/<app>/<timestamp>/)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --description nightly
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app -b external-bucket -e https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com -r eu-central-1
```

### `flui app backup delete`

Delete an S3 backup of an application. Removes all objects under the export key prefix.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `exportId` (required) — Export id (S3 key prefix) returned by `flui app backup create`

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-b, --bucket` (required) — S3 bucket where the backup lives
  - `-e, --endpoint` (required) — S3 endpoint URL
  - `-r, --region` (default: "auto") — S3 region
  - `--access-key` — S3 access key id (defaults to FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY env)
  - `--secret-key` — S3 secret access key (defaults to FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env)
  - `-f, --force` — Skip confirmation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app flui/<cluster>/<app>/20260510170000-abc123 -b my-bucket -e https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud
```

### `flui app build`

Inspect or refresh the latest build for an application. Use --watch to follow the status until terminal.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text")
  - `--refresh` — Force the backend to re-poll GitHub Actions for the latest build now
  - `-w, --watch` — Poll until the latest build reaches a terminal status (COMPLETED / FAILED / CANCELLED)
  - `--interval` (default: 5) — Polling interval in seconds (with --watch)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --watch
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --refresh
```

### `flui app builds`

List recent builds for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table")
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 10)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --limit 5
```

### `flui app crash`

Show a single crash diagnosis. Use --dismiss to mark it resolved.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `id` (required) — Crash diagnosis ID

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `--dismiss` — Mark this crash diagnosis as resolved
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 5d3f...
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 5d3f... --dismiss
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 5d3f... --output json
```

### `flui app crashes`

Show recent crash diagnoses for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app delete`

Delete an application and remove all its resources from the cluster. Works for both catalog installs and source-deploy (flui.yaml) apps. System-protected apps require --force.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-f, --force` — Skip confirmation prompt
  - `--no-wait` — Return immediately after queuing the uninstall

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> uptime-kuma
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> uptime-kuma --force
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> uptime-kuma --no-wait
```

### `flui app env list`

List an application's variables — plain values, which sensitive keys are set, and which are still awaiting a value. Sensitive values are never shown.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
```

### `flui app env set`

Deliver the value of a sensitive variable. The value is prompted for (or read from standard input) and never appears in the command, its output, or any log.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `key` (required) — Variable name (the NAME, never the value)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `--stdin` — Read the value from standard input rather than prompting.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
pbpaste | <%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY --stdin
```

### `flui app image delete`

Delete a container image version from the registry (GHCR). Refuses to delete the currently deployed version. The latest-release guard can be overridden with --force.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `versionId` (required) — GitHub Packages numeric version id (from `flui app versions --output json`)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `--force` — Override the latest-release guard. The currently-deployed guard is never bypassable.
  - `-y, --yes` — Skip confirmation prompt

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 845914920
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api 845914920 --force
```

### `flui app init`

Copy Flui deploy files (Dockerfile + flui.yaml) from an official framework template into the current directory. Use this on an existing Git repository to make it deployable with `flui deploy`. Run `flui app init --list` to see the supported frameworks and versions.

Arguments:
  - `framework` — Framework template, optionally with a major version pin (e.g. `nextjs` or `nextjs@16`). Omit when using --list.

Flags:
  - `--list` — Print supported frameworks and versions, then exit
  - `--force` — Overwrite existing files without prompting
  - `--dry-run` — Print the actions that would be taken, no file writes
  - `--target` — Target directory (default: current working directory)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nextjs
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nextjs@16
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> fastapi --target ./api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --list
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nestjs --force
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nuxt --dry-run
```

### `flui app list`

List all applications in the cluster

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-x, --expanded` — Show the individual components of composed apps
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --expanded
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui app logs`

Fetch logs for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-l, --level` [error | warn | info | debug] — Filter by log level
  - `-n, --tail` (default: 100) — Number of lines to return
  - `-s, --search` — Full-text search query
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --level error
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --tail 500
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --search "connection refused"
```

### `flui app manifest`

Print the flui.yaml (kind: Application) schema & annotated example — for humans and LLMs.

Arguments:
  - `framework` — Framework for --example (e.g. nextjs, spring-boot, fastapi). Sets port + healthcheck.

Flags:
  - `--json` — Format output as json.
  - `--example` — Emit a fully-annotated example manifest instead of the field reference.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --json
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --example
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --example nextjs
```

### `flui app metrics`

Show instant Prometheus metrics (CPU/mem/network/replicas) for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app redeploy`

Redeploy an application from an existing image (tag or digest), without rebuilding

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `target` — Tag, short digest (12+ hex), or full sha256:<digest>

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `--build` — Deploy from an existing build id (alternative to tag/digest)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api a1cac27
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api sha256:812bdfd0a833...
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --build <buildId>
```

### `flui app releases`

List recent releases (deploy/rollback operations) for an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster`
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table")
  - `--current` — Only show the current (most recent) release
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 10)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --current
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --output json
```

### `flui app restart`

Trigger a rolling restart of an application

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api
```

### `flui app scale`

Scale an application to a desired replica count

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-r, --replicas` (required) — Desired replica count (0 = stop all pods)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --replicas 3
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-api --replicas 0
```

### `flui app schedule create`

Create a scheduled job (cron) on an application. The job runs the given command on the app's image + env, on the cron schedule. Overlapping runs are skipped by default (concurrency=Forbid).

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-n, --name` (required) — Schedule name (lowercase alphanumeric + dashes)
  - `-s, --schedule` (required) — Cron expression (5 fields), e.g. "0 3 * * *"
  - `-x, --command` (required) — Shell command to run (executed via /bin/sh -c)
  - `-t, --timezone` — IANA timezone (e.g. Europe/Rome). Default: cluster time
  - `--concurrency` [Allow | Forbid | Replace] (default: "Forbid") — Overlap policy
  - `--disabled` — Create the schedule suspended (not running)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --name nightly-cleanup --schedule "0 3 * * *" --command "node dist/cleanup.js"
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app -n report -s "*/15 * * * *" -x "php artisan report:run" --timezone Europe/Rome
```

### `flui app schedule delete`

Delete a scheduled job (cron) from an application.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug
  - `name` (required) — Schedule name

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule list`

List the scheduled jobs (cron) of an application. Each runs a command on the app's image + env on a cron schedule.

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app
```

### `flui env create`

Create control cluster infrastructure on K3s

Flags:
  - `-p, --provider` [hetzner | scaleway] — Cloud provider for the control cluster (default: the profile's configured provider)
  - `--node-size` — Server type for cluster nodes (run "flui server-types list --provider <provider>" to see available types). Defaults to the provider recommended size.
  - `-r, --region` — Region/location code. Defaults to the provider default region.
  - `--node-count` (default: 0) — Number of worker nodes (0 = master-only, default: 0)
  - `--disk-size` — Root disk size in GB. Required for network-storage instance types (Scaleway PRO2, ENT1). Optional for local-SSD types — defaults to the included size of the instance type.
  - `-d, --detached` — Detached mode: start cluster creation and exit immediately
  - `--wait` — Wait for cluster to be ready before returning (polls operation status)
  - `--configure-firewall` — Automatically configure firewall after cluster creation
  - `--firewall-ip` — Source IP/CIDR for firewall (comma-separated, default: auto-detect)
  - `--non-interactive` — Never prompt. Any missing answer becomes an error instead of a question — required when driving the CLI from a script or a managed runner, where a prompt would hang forever holding cloud resources.
  - `--ssh-mode` [ca | ephemeral-key] (default: "ca") — How the cluster is reached while it is built. "ca" (default) enrols this machine's SSH certificate authority on every node and leaves it there. "ephemeral-key" creates no CA at all and uses a throwaway key that is revoked on the nodes and deleted at the provider before the run ends — the cluster is then unreachable over SSH until its owner runs "flui env adopt". Use it when provisioning on someone else's behalf.
  - `--auth-mode` (default: "oidc") — Authentication mode (only oidc is supported)
  - `--acme-staging` — Use Let's Encrypt staging endpoint (untrusted cert, no rate limits) — useful while iterating to avoid burning prod quota
  - `--latest` — Install mobile dev tags instead of the pinned release: bootstrap scripts from `master` and `:latest` Docker images. Default: every component is pinned to the CLI release version.
  - `--no-shared-storage` — Disable Flui shared storage (NFS+fscache). Default: shared storage enabled — master gets a Volume hosting the NFS export, workers mount it. Disable to fall back to local-path on each node bundled disk.
  - `--shared-storage-size` (default: 20) — Size in GB of the master shared storage Volume (only when shared storage is enabled). Default: 20.
  - `--host` — BYOS: install onto an existing Linux host (IP or DNS) over SSH instead of provisioning via a cloud provider. Enables BYOS mode.
  - `--port` (default: 22) — BYOS: SSH port of --host (default: 22)
  - `--user` (default: "root") — BYOS: SSH user for --host (default: root)
  - `--ssh-key` — BYOS: SSH private key for --host. Optional — if omitted, Flui reuses an existing key that already works, otherwise it authorizes one (asking for the host password once) and never stores the password. A passphrase-protected key is supported only when loaded in your ssh-agent (run `ssh-add` first).
  - `--ssh-password` — BYOS: host password, for non-interactive key authorization (e.g. CI). Prefer the FLUI_SSH_PASSWORD env var to keep it out of shell history. Used only in-memory to install the key, then auth switches to the key.
  - `--master-public-ip` — BYOS: externally reachable IP of --host (defaults to --host); used for endpoints/TLS
  - `--skip-precheck` — BYOS: skip the host readiness precheck
  - `--best-effort` — BYOS: continue even if the precheck reports problems
  - `--local-stub` — BYOS (dev): stop after bootstrap + CA check; skip observability/kubeconfig/secret patch. Use with BOOTSTRAP_SCRIPTS_URL=file://… for local Podman testing.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --node-size cx32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -d
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --region fsn1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --wait
```

### `flui iam grant add`

Create an access grant: bind a principal to a role at a scope. Scope is one of everything (global), a cluster, a portal section, or a selector over app attributes (kind/project/provider/tags/slugs — AND-ed; tags match ALL).

Flags:
  - `-t, --type` [user | group | service_account] (default: "user") — Principal type
  - `-p, --principal` (required) — Principal reference (email, group name, or service-account id)
  - `-r, --role` [viewer | operator | maintainer | owner] (required) — Role to grant. `owner` is the top of the ladder and conferring it requires iam:manage-users at global scope — i.e. an owner makes an owner.
  - `-s, --scope` [global | cluster | section | selector] (default: "global") — Scope type
  - `--cluster` — Cluster id (scope=cluster)
  - `--section` — Portal section key (scope=section)
  - `--kind` — App kind, e.g. DATABASE (scope=selector)
  - `--project` — Project (scope=selector)
  - `--provider` — Provider (scope=selector)
  - `--cluster-id` — Cluster id (scope=selector)
  - `--cluster-name` — Cluster name (scope=selector)
  - `--app-type` [system | user] — App type (scope=selector)
  - `--app` — App slug — repeatable (scope=selector)
  - `--tag` — Tag — repeatable, app must carry ALL (scope=selector)
  - `--selector` — Raw selector JSON (overrides individual selector flags)
  - `--dry-run` — Say what this grant would open — and what the same change closes — and create nothing
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p alice@acme.com -r maintainer
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -t group -p platform -r viewer -s cluster --cluster c1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p bob@acme.com -r operator -s selector --kind DATABASE
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p ci-deployer -t service_account -r operator -s selector --app acme-api --app acme-web
```

  - `--headless` — Print URLs instead of opening a browser

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github --headless
```

### `flui integration setup-github-app`

Configure the GitHub App credentials in Flui (admin only). Interactively prompts for App ID, slug, client ID/secret, webhook secret and private key path. Secrets are hidden during input and encrypted at rest in the database.

Flags:
  - `--private-key-file` — Path to the GitHub App private key PEM file (skips the path prompt)
  - `--callback-url` — OAuth callback URL configured on the GitHub App. Defaults to <api-url>/repositories/github-app/user-callback

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --private-key-file ./flui-cloud.pem
```

### `flui integration status`

Show the current GitHub integration status: configured mode, live health check, and (in PAT mode) your own connection state.

Arguments:
  - `provider` (required) — Integration provider (currently only `github`)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> github
```

## mail

### `flui mail connect`

Connect a mail provider and set up everything that can be set up

Arguments:
  - `provider` (required) — One of: scaleway-tem, brevo, zeptomail, smtp

Flags:
  - `--scope` [transactional | bulk] (default: "transactional") — What this sender carries. Never the same account for both — a suspension caused by a mailing list would stop password resets too.
  - `--domain` — Sending domain. Flui registers it and publishes the records.
  - `--secret` — API key or relay password. Not needed for Scaleway, which reuses the compute key. Prefer leaving this out: the value is then prompted for and never enters your shell history or `ps` output.
  - `--stdin` — Read the credential from standard input rather than prompting.
  - `--label` — What you call it
  - `--region` — ZeptoMail only, and required: the regional API host.
  - `--host` — SMTP relay host
  - `--port` — SMTP relay port
  - `--username` — SMTP username
  - `--allow-bulk` — SMTP only: declare that this relay permits one-to-many mail. Never deduced.
  - `--activate` — Start sending through this one straight away. Without it a provider is stored and only takes the scope if nothing else holds it — switch later with `flui mail use`.
  - `--spf-include` — SMTP only: the include from the relay setup page
  - `--dkim-selector` — SMTP only: verbatim from the relay
  - `--dkim-value` — SMTP only: verbatim from the relay
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> brevo --scope bulk --domain news.example.com
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> scaleway-tem --domain mail.example.com
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> smtp --host smtp.example.com --port 587 --username postmaster --allow-bulk
```

### `flui mail disconnect`

Disconnect a mail provider

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Connection id, from `flui mail providers --json`

Flags:
  - `--yes` — Required. The stored credential is destroyed.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> <id> --yes
```

### `flui mail events`

Delivery outcomes reported by the mail provider

Flags:
  - `--since` — ISO timestamp. Exclusive.
  - `--message-id` — Show only this message
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --since 2026-08-11T00:00:00Z
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --message-id 4f2c…
```

### `flui mail overview`

The state of sending: what is broken, what it costs, and since when

Flags:
  - `--window` [24h | 7d | 14d | 30d] (default: "14d") — How far back to look
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --window 24h
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --json
```

### `flui mail providers`

Show which provider carries which kind of mail

Flags:
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui mail publish`

Register a sending domain with the provider and publish the records it needs

Arguments:
  - `domain` (required) — The sending domain

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> example.com
```

### `flui mail readiness`

Report what still stands between Flui and a sent message

Flags:
  - `--domain` — Sending domain to inspect. Omitted, only the credential is checked.
  - `--json` — Print the raw response

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --domain fluicloud.eu
```

### `flui mail remove`

Hand a sending domain back to the mail provider

Arguments:
  - `domain` (required) — Sending domain to remove

Flags:
  - `--yes` — Required. This cannot be undone, so it is not the default.
  - `--keep-dns` — Revoke at the provider and leave the zone entirely untouched.
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> old.example.com --yes
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> old.example.com --keep-dns --yes
```

### `flui mail send`

Send a message through the configured mail provider

Flags:
  - `--from` (required) — Sender address. Must be on a domain the provider has verified.
  - `--to` (required) — Recipient address
  - `--subject` (required)
  - `--text` — Plain-text body
  - `--html` — HTML body
  - `--scope` [transactional | bulk] (default: "transactional") — One-to-one triggered by a user action, or one-to-many. A provider whose terms forbid the stated scope refuses the message rather than suspending the account later.
  - `--reference` — Your own correlation id

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --from noreply@example.com --to someone@example.net --subject Hello --text "Hi there"
```

### `flui mail suppressions`

Addresses Flui has stopped writing to

Flags:
  - `--scope` [all | bulk] — Show only entries with this reach
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --scope bulk
```

### `flui mail test`

Prove a domain can actually deliver, or that a hard bounce is caught

Arguments:
  - `domain` — Verified sending domain. Omit it when using --connection.

Flags:
  - `--connection` — Probe one provider instead of a domain, from `flui mail providers`. The only way to prove a bulk sender, or one configured and not yet sending.
  - `--to` — Where to send it. Defaults to your own address — the one you can check.
  - `--bounce` — Send to a subdomain of this domain that deliberately does not exist, so a real refusal travels the whole path and you can watch it arrive.
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> example.com
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> example.com --to me@elsewhere.test
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> example.com --bounce
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --connection 7f3c1b0e-...
```

### `flui mail unsuppress`

Start writing to a suppressed address again

Arguments:
  - `address` (required) — The address to release

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> someone@example.com
```

### `flui mail use`

Switch a scope onto a provider that is already configured

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Connection id, from `flui mail providers`

Flags:
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> 7f3c1b0e-...
```

## migrate

### `flui migrate app abort`

Abort an app migration before cutover (destination torn down, source untouched)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate app create`

Move an application workload to another cluster

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application to move (name or id)

Flags:
  - `-t, --to` (required) — Target cluster name or id
  - `-f, --from` — Source cluster name or id (default: auto-detect)
  - `--cutover` [auto | manual] (default: "auto") — Cutover mode

### `flui migrate app cutover`

Fire the cutover for a parked (manual) app migration

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

### `flui migrate app destroy-source`

Destroy the drained source workload after cutover (irreversible)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate app list`

List app-workload migrations

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate app show`

Show an app-workload migration by id

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate db abort`

Abort a DB migration before cutover (replication link + destination torn down, source untouched)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate db create`

Move a managed-Postgres app to another cluster

Arguments:
  - `dbapp` (required) — Managed-Postgres app to move

Flags:
  - `-t, --to` (required) — Target cluster name or id
  - `-f, --from` — Source cluster name or id (default: auto-detect)
  - `--mode` [live | restore] (default: "live") — Migration mode
  - `--cutover` [auto | manual] (default: "auto") — Cutover mode
  - `--at` — restore mode only: ISO-8601 instant to recover to
  - `--name` — display name for the new install
  - `--verify` — exact per-table count(*) comparison at cutover

### `flui migrate db cutover`

Fire the cutover for a parked (manual) DB migration

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

### `flui migrate db list`

List managed-Postgres migrations

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate db show`

Show a managed-Postgres migration by id

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate full abort`

Abort a full migration before cutover (both legs torn down, source untouched)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate full create`

Move a consumer app together with its managed-Postgres data

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Consumer application to move

Flags:
  - `--db` (required) — Managed-Postgres app (name or id) whose data migrates with the app
  - `-t, --to` (required) — Target cluster name or id
  - `-f, --from` — Source cluster name or id (default: auto-detect)
  - `--cutover` [auto | manual] (default: "auto") — Cutover mode
  - `--staging` [scaled-down | live-fenced] (default: "scaled-down") — Staging mode for the destination app before cutover

### `flui migrate full cutover`

Fire the cutover for a parked (manual) full migration

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

### `flui migrate full destroy-source`

Destroy the drained source app workload after cutover (irreversible)

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `-y, --yes`

### `flui migrate full list`

List full-app migrations

Flags:
  - `--json`

### `flui migrate full show`

Show a full-app migration by id

Arguments:
  - `id` (required) — Migration id

Flags:
  - `--json`

## node

### `flui node add`

Add worker node(s) to the cluster. Provisions new servers and joins them to K3s.

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-n, --count` (default: 1) — Number of workers to add (1-5)
  - `--no-wait` — Return immediately after queuing the operation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --count 2
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --count 3 --no-wait
```

### `flui node connect`

BYOS: join an existing Linux host to the cluster as a worker node (over SSH, no provisioning).

Flags:
  - `--host` (required) — IP or DNS of the existing host to join as a worker
  - `--port` (default: 22) — SSH port of --host
  - `--user` (default: "root") — SSH user for --host
  - `--ssh-key` — Path to the SSH private key that already authenticates to --host (default: ~/.ssh/id_rsa)
  - `--master-ip` — Address the new node uses to reach the master k3s API (https://<addr>:6443). Defaults to the cluster master IP.
  - `--node-network` — CIDR of the private network the nodes share (host firewall must allow it for node-to-node k3s traffic). Defaults to the /24 of the detected private IP.
  - `--skip-precheck` — Skip the host readiness precheck
  - `--best-effort` — Continue even if the precheck reports problems

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --host 203.0.113.10
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --host 10.0.0.12 --master-ip 10.0.0.11 --node-network 10.0.0.0/24
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --host localhost --port 2223 --ssh-key ~/.flui/byos-local/operator_key --master-ip 10.89.0.2
```

### `flui node list`

List all nodes in the cluster (master + workers)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui node remove`

Cordon, drain and remove a worker node from the cluster. Cannot remove the master.

Arguments:
  - `nodeId` (required) — Node ID to remove (from `flui node list`)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect when only one cluster exists)
  - `--no-wait` — Return immediately after queuing the operation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> <node-id>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> <node-id> --no-wait
```

## operating-context

### `flui operating-context list`

The operating-context notes that reach you, each with its verdict on itself

Flags:
  - `--app` — Only the notes that apply to this application slug
  - `--cluster` — Only the notes that apply to this cluster id
  - `--archived` — The notes that were retired, with the day and the hand that withdrew each
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --archived
```

### `flui operating-context probes`

The live facts a note can be made to lean on, and what each one is asked for

Flags:
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui operating-context write`

Write a note about how this installation is run, at a level you cover

Flags:
  - `--level` [global | cluster | selector] — Where the note applies
  - `--cluster` — The cluster, for a cluster note
  - `--selector` — The selector, as JSON, for a selector note — passed to the API unchanged
  - `--nature` [practice | rationale]
  - `--topic` — The subject two notes could disagree about
  - `--title`
  - `--body` — The note itself
  - `--check` [none | attestation | probe] — How the premise is checked
  - `--valid-for-days` — How long a signature is worth, for an attested note
  - `--probe` — The live fact the note leans on
  - `--param` — name=value for the fact, repeatable
  - `--op` [equals | notEquals | atLeast | atMost | exists]
  - `--expected` — What the fact is expected to be
  - `--yes` — Do not ask to confirm
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --level cluster --cluster prod-eu --nature practice
```

## repo

### `flui repo connect`

Connect (import) a GitHub repository into your Flui account so it can be deployed with `flui deploy`. Pass the full name `owner/repo`, or omit it for an interactive picker over the repositories accessible via your GitHub integration.

```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

Disconnect a repository from your Flui account. Requires admin privileges. Does not delete the repository on GitHub.

```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme/my-app --yes
```

### `flui repo list`

List repositories connected to your Flui account.

Flags:
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:

```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

## sandbox

### `flui sandbox expire`

End one guest area now, through the reaper

Arguments:

Flags:
  - `-f, --force` — Skip the confirmation
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> user-guest-e182d08a
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> user-guest-e182d08a --force
```

### `flui sandbox list`

Guest areas this instance is holding

## scaling

### `flui scaling apply`

Write a scaling group from a file — what a cluster may buy for itself, and where it must stop.
The file is the whole group: a field left out is a field reset to its default, and the same file applied twice leaves the same group. Several groups may live in one file, separated by `---`.
`bounds.max: 0` is a fleet that should hold no nodes, not a group switched off: where the group provisions manually it says every machine present is one somebody attached, and where it provisions automatically it says urgency may buy nothing.

Flags:
  - `-f, --file` (required) — Path to the ScalingGroup YAML/JSON file
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID, for a file that names none. Refused when the file names a different one.
  - `--dry-run` — Read and check the file, say what would be written, and write nothing.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f scaling.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f scaling.yaml --dry-run
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f scaling.yaml --cluster prod-eu
```

### `flui scaling export`

Export a scaling group as a `kind: ScalingGroup` document — the file `flui scaling apply` reads back.
Only what somebody wrote is exported. What the provider can do, and what the market is doing, are read fresh every time and would be stale in a committed file.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `--all` — Every group of the cluster, as one file of `---` separated documents
  - `-o, --output` [yaml | json] (default: "yaml") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> > scaling.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --all --cluster prod-eu > scaling.yaml
```

### `flui scaling get`

Show a scaling group: its three bounds, where and what it may buy, and what it may spend.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json | yaml] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output yaml
```

### `flui scaling list`

One line per cluster: what it may buy, what it is spending, and what is waiting.
Clusters with no scaling group are listed too, and so are the ones that can only raise an alarm — the two cases a filter would hide precisely when somebody is needed.

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Show the scaling groups of one cluster instead
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui scaling preview`

What a scaling group would do if a node were needed right now — the same engine the reconciler runs, on demand, buying nothing.
Every rung of the ladder is shown with the reason it lost. `refused-by-limit` is this group’s own rules and not the market, which from the outside looks exactly like an outage.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui scaling why`

The last scaling decision and its reason — including the times it decided to do nothing, which are the interesting ones.
Answers about the whole cluster by default, naming the group each decision came from. Name a group to narrow it to that one.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: every group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 1) — How many decisions back to show, newest first
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --limit 10
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

## server-types

### `flui server-types list`

List available server types for a provider

Flags:
  - `-p, --provider` [hetzner | scaleway] (required) — Cloud provider
  - `-r, --region` — Filter by region/location
  - `-m, --memory` — Filter by RAM in GB: exact "16", range "8-32", min "8-", or max "-32"
  - `-s, --sort` [price | memory | cores | disk | name] (default: "price") — Sort by field
  - `--desc` — Sort in descending order
  - `--json` — Output as JSON
  - `--force-refresh` — Force refresh cache from API

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --region fsn1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory 16
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory 8-32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory -32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --sort memory
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --sort price --desc
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --json
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --force-refresh
```

## showcase

### `flui showcase add`

Publish one application to the showcase

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application slug, name or id

Flags:
  - `--note` — The line shown next to it, stored as the application's description
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> umami-29491d --note "Measures flui.cloud. Real visitors."
```

### `flui showcase list`

Applications published to the showcase

Flags:
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui showcase remove`

Take one application out of the showcase (it keeps running)

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application slug, name or id

Flags:
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> umami-29491d
```

## template

### `flui template use`

Create a new GitHub repository from a Flui framework template and connect it to your account.

Arguments:
  - `framework` (required) — Framework template to use (e.g. astro, nextjs, nestjs)
  - `name` (required) — Name for the new GitHub repository

Flags:
  - `--org` — GitHub organisation or user to create the repo under (default: your account)
  - `-d, --description` — Repository description
  - `--public` — Create as a public repository (default: private)
  - `--no-import` — Skip auto-importing the repository into Flui

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> astro my-astro-site
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nextjs my-app --public
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nestjs my-api --org my-org
```

## vault

### `flui vault init`

Create the vault that protects stored credentials on this machine. Run this before configuring anything else.

Flags:
  - `--stdin` — Read the passphrase from standard input rather than prompting. For scripted setup; the value never appears in the process list.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
printf "my passphrase" | <%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --stdin
```

### `flui vault lock`

Close the vault now, without waiting for it to time out.

### `flui vault status`

Show whether the vault exists, whether it is unlocked, and how long it has left.

Flags:
  - `--format` [text | json] (default: "text")

### `flui vault unlock`

Unlock the vault for this session so commands can open stored credentials.

Flags:
  - `--stdin` — Read the passphrase from standard input rather than prompting.
  - `--idle-minutes` — How long the vault may sit unused before it locks itself again (default 30). Same effect as setting FLUI_VAULT_IDLE_MINUTES, offered here because that variable has no way to announce itself.
  - `--max-minutes` — Absolute lifetime of the unlock, regardless of activity (default 480) — the backstop against a long-running session holding the key open all day just by staying busy. Same effect as FLUI_VAULT_MAX_MINUTES.

sections.body:
The `app` topic groups every command that acts on an application
running in a cluster — both catalog installs (`kind: CatalogApp`)
and source-built apps (`kind: Application`). The behaviour is the
same on both sides: the application is the unit of operation,
whatever put its image in the registry.

Almost every verb under `app` takes an application name or slug as
its first positional argument, and accepts `-c, --cluster
<name|id>` to pick the cluster (auto-detected when the active
profile has only one). The output flags follow the rest of the
CLI: `-o, --output table|json` (or `text|json` on the streaming
commands), `-f, --force` to skip confirmations, `--no-wait` to
queue and exit.

Two verbs are the exception, because they run locally and do not
target a running application: `flui app init` and `flui app
manifest`. Both are under [Project setup](#project-setup).

This page is the reference — the verbs and their flags. For the
*how*, the task pages walk the same ground in order:
[Watch and operate a running
application](/tasks/watch-and-operate-an-application/),
[Set an application's configuration and
secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/), and
[Remove an application and its
data](/tasks/remove-an-application/).

## Read this before you delete anything

`flui app delete` now deletes the application's **persistent
volumes** as well. The data goes; Flui cannot bring it back.

Because that is the most destructive thing you can do to an
application, the command reads the cluster first and prints what
will be lost before it asks. And when it cannot read the cluster,
it says **unknown** — never "none". Full detail in
[Deletion](#deletion).

## Project setup

### `flui app init [<framework>]`

Copies Flui's deploy files — a `Dockerfile` and a `flui.yaml` —
from an official framework template into the current directory,
turning an existing Git repository into something `flui deploy`
can build.

```bash
flui app init --list           # list supported frameworks
flui app init nextjs           # latest supported Next.js
flui app init nextjs@16        # pin a major version
flui app init fastapi --target ./api
flui app init nestjs --force   # overwrite existing files
flui app init nuxt --dry-run   # print the actions, write nothing
```

| Flag / Arg | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<framework>` | Framework template, optionally with a major-version pin (`nextjs`, `nextjs@16`). Omit when using `--list`. |
| `--list` | Print the supported frameworks and versions, then exit. |
| `--force` | Overwrite existing files without prompting. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the actions that would be taken; write nothing. |
| `--target <dir>` | Target directory. Default: the current working directory. |

`app init` adds Flui files to a repository you already have. To
create a *new* repository from a template instead, use `flui
template use` — see [Templates](/cli/templates/).

### `flui app manifest`

Prints the authoring reference for `flui.yaml` (`kind:
Application`): every field, what it does, and which fields the
spec accepts but does not yet apply on source deploys. It runs
fully offline — no cluster, no login — and the field list comes
from the published spec schema, so it cannot drift from what
`flui deploy` validates.

```bash
flui app manifest                    # the field reference
flui app manifest --json             # the raw JSON Schema
flui app manifest --example          # an annotated example
flui app manifest --example nextjs   # port + healthcheck for a framework
```

This prints the *shape* of a manifest, not the manifest of any
particular application. It is the command to point an assistant
at when it needs to write a `flui.yaml` that is actually valid.

## Inspection

### `flui app list`

Lists the applications in the cluster with their high-level
state. Catalog installs made of several parts show as one row;
`-x, --expanded` breaks them out into their components.

```bash
flui app list
flui app list --expanded
flui app list --output json
```

### `flui app status <name>`

Shows the live runtime status of one application: how many
replicas are ready against desired, the current release, and any
condition that needs attention.

```bash
flui app status my-api
flui app status my-api --output json
```

### `flui app logs <name>`

Streams application logs from the cluster. By default returns the
last 100 lines; filter by level, search the text, or widen the
window.

```bash
flui app logs my-api
flui app logs my-api --level error
flui app logs my-api --tail 500
flui app logs my-api --search "connection refused"
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-l, --level` | — | Filter by `error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug`. |
| `-n, --tail <n>` | `100` | Number of lines to return. |
| `-s, --search <q>` | — | Full-text search. |
| `-o, --output text\|json` | `text` | Output format. |

### `flui app metrics <name>`

Instant resource metrics for one application: CPU, memory,
network I/O, replica count. Useful to spot-check a workload's
footprint or to line a spike up against a deploy.

```bash
flui app metrics my-api
flui app metrics my-api --output json
```

## Configuration

The values an application runs with come from three places — the
manifest, what you pass at deploy time, and what is stored
against the app. Which one wins, and why the rule changed, is
[Set an application's configuration and
secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/). These two verbs read
and write the stored set.

### `flui app env list <app>`

Lists the application's variables in three states: plain values,
sensitive keys that are **set** (the fact, never the value), and
keys that are still **awaiting a value** — declared by the
manifest but never supplied by anybody.

```bash
flui app env list my-api
```

"Awaiting a value" is a state, not an error: the command exits 0
either way. No sensitive value is printed, because none is
available to print — the API answers with a mask.

### `flui app env set <app> <KEY>`

Delivers the value of a sensitive variable. There is no `--value`
flag and that is deliberate: a value passed as an argument lands
in your shell history, is visible to every other process on the
machine while the command runs, and — when an agent composed the
command — is copied into a model's context on the way.

So the value is prompted for, or read from standard input.

```bash
flui app env set my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
pbpaste | flui app env set my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY --stdin
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--stdin` | Read the value from standard input rather than prompting. |
| `-c, --cluster` | Cluster name or ID. |

The command prints the key and whether it is now configured; the
value is never echoed back and cannot be read back later. It
takes effect on the next rollout — `flui app redeploy <app>`.

Two cases are refused rather than written: a key linked to a
building block's own secret, and the display mask sent back as if
it were a value. In a non-interactive shell the command refuses
to prompt and tells you to use `--stdin`.

## Runtime diagnostics

### `flui app crashes <name>`

Lists recent **crash diagnoses** for the application — automatic
reports produced when a workload restarted unexpectedly,
summarising the exit code, the signals the runtime saw, and the
probable cause.

```bash
flui app crashes my-api
flui app crashes my-api --output json
```

### `flui app crash <name> <id>`

Shows one crash diagnosis in full, including the reasoning chain
the platform used to classify it. `--dismiss` marks it resolved
so it stops appearing as an active issue on the dashboard.

```bash
flui app crash my-api 5d3f...                # show one diagnosis
flui app crash my-api 5d3f... --dismiss      # mark it resolved
```

Get `<id>` from `flui app crashes`.

### `flui app traffic <name>`

HTTP traffic for one application, measured at the ingress rather
than inside your code: request rate, the split by status class,
error percentages, latency, and a breakdown by method and by
status code.

```bash
flui app traffic my-api
flui app traffic my-api --window 1h
flui app traffic my-api --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-w, --window <d>` | `5m` | Rate window. Longer is smoother on low traffic. |
| `-o, --output` | `table` | `table` or `json`. |

An application that is not exposed through the ingress has no
edge traffic, and the command says so rather than printing
zeroes.

Latency percentiles come from a histogram with fixed buckets. When
those buckets are too coarse to separate this application's
responses, the command prints the boundaries it had and labels the
percentiles as estimates. The mean is measured, not estimated.

### `flui app alerts <name>`

Alerts for the application, one row per episode, newest first.
Each row carries the alert name, its severity, a one-line summary
and its timing.

```bash
flui app alerts my-api
flui app alerts my-api --firing     # only what is still firing
flui app alerts my-api --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--firing` | off | Only alerts still firing. |
| `-n, --limit <n>` | `20` | How many to show. |
| `-o, --output` | `table` | `table` or `json`. |

A resolved alert marked with `*` stopped reporting rather than
sending a resolution, so its end time is approximate. The
distinction is printed instead of hidden, because "it went quiet"
and "it recovered" are not the same event.

### `flui app build <name>`

Status of the **latest** build of a source-built application
(`kind: Application`). With `--watch` the command stays in the
foreground polling until the build reaches a terminal status.

```bash
flui app build my-api
flui app build my-api --watch
flui app build my-api --refresh     # force the backend to re-poll the CI
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--refresh` | — | Force a fresh poll of the upstream CI. |
| `-w, --watch` | — | Poll until the build reaches a terminal status. |
| `--interval <s>` | `5` | Polling interval in seconds. |

### `flui app builds <name>`

Recent build history (default: last 10).

```bash
flui app builds my-api
flui app builds my-api --limit 50
```

## Release management

A "release" is one rollout of an image into the cluster — a
deploy or a rollback. A given image can be released more than
once; not every image gets released.

### `flui app releases <name>`

Release history.

```bash
flui app releases my-api
flui app releases my-api --current        # only the running release
flui app releases my-api --limit 50
```

### `flui app versions <name>`

Image versions present in the container registry for this
application, annotated with whether each one is the current
deployment, a previous release, or unreleased.

```bash
flui app versions my-api
flui app versions my-api --limit 50
flui app versions my-api --output json
```

### `flui app redeploy <name> [<target>]`

Re-deploys an existing image, **without rebuilding**. The target
is a tag, a short digest (12+ hex chars), or a full
`sha256:<digest>`. Alternatively `--build <id>` deploys the image
produced by a specific prior build.

```bash
flui app redeploy my-api a1cac27
flui app redeploy my-api sha256:812bdfd0a833...
flui app redeploy my-api --build <build-id>
```

This is the rollback path: pick a known-good `app versions` entry
and redeploy it. It is also how a newly delivered variable
reaches a running application.

## Lifecycle

### `flui app start` / `flui app stop` / `flui app restart`

The everyday lifecycle verbs. `stop` scales to 0 replicas
(workloads disappear but their configuration and volumes are
preserved); `start` restores the previous replica count;
`restart` performs a rolling restart — one replica replaced at a
time, the running count never drops.

```bash
flui app start my-api
flui app stop my-api
flui app restart my-api
```

`flui app stop` is equivalent to `flui app scale my-api
--replicas 0`.

### `flui app scale <name> --replicas <n>`

Sets the desired replica count.

```bash
flui app scale my-api --replicas 3
flui app scale my-api --replicas 0       # same as `app stop`
```

What `scale` actually achieves depends on the application's
storage class (see [Storage classes and dedicated
placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/)
for the conceptual model):

- **Shared storage** — every replica reads and writes the same
  network filesystem, so the platform can run as many replicas as
  you ask for, on any node. This is the case for stateless apps
  and for anything using the default storage class.
- **Dedicated storage** — the application is pinned to the node
  that holds its local disk, and there is only one such disk.
  Raising replicas above `1` would mean several copies competing
  for the same on-disk state, which is unsafe. For these apps,
  horizontal scaling at the platform level is **not supported**:
  give the workload more capacity by resizing its host node (see
  [`flui env
  scale-master`/`scale-node`](/cli/environments/#flui-env-scale-master-flui-env-scale-node)).
  Application-level scaling for stateful workloads that *can* run
  as a cluster (read replicas, primary/replica databases, sharded
  queues) is a separate, planned direction — handled
  per-application rather than through `flui app scale`.

## Scheduled jobs

A scheduled job runs a command on the application's **own image
and configuration**, on a cron schedule. It is the same
environment your app runs in, so a job can reuse the app's code,
its database connection and its variables without a second
deployment to maintain.

### `flui app schedule create <app>`

```bash
flui app schedule create my-app \
  --name nightly-cleanup \
  --schedule "0 3 * * *" \
  --command "node dist/cleanup.js"

flui app schedule create my-app \
  -n report -s "*/15 * * * *" \
  -x "php artisan report:run" --timezone Europe/Rome
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-n, --name <s>` | required | Schedule name (lowercase alphanumeric and dashes). |
| `-s, --schedule <s>` | required | Cron expression, five fields. |
| `-x, --command <s>` | required | Shell command, run through `/bin/sh -c`. |
| `-t, --timezone <tz>` | cluster time | IANA timezone, e.g. `Europe/Rome`. |
| `--concurrency` | `Forbid` | Overlap policy: `Allow`, `Forbid` or `Replace`. |
| `--disabled` | off | Create it suspended, not running. |

The default overlap policy is `Forbid`: if a run is still going
when the next one is due, the next one is skipped. That is the
safe default for jobs that touch shared state. `Replace` stops
the running one and starts the new one; `Allow` lets them
overlap.

### `flui app schedule list <app>`

Lists the application's schedules with their cron expression,
whether they are enabled or suspended, the last time each one
was scheduled, and the command.

```bash
flui app schedule list my-app
flui app schedule list my-app --output json
```

### `flui app schedule runs <app> <name>`

Recent runs of one schedule with their status — `Succeeded`,
`Failed`, `Running` — and whether each was started by the
schedule or by hand. How far back the history goes is bounded by
what the cluster keeps.

```bash
flui app schedule runs my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule logs <app> <name>`

Logs of one run. Defaults to the most recent run; `-r, --run`
targets a specific one, named as it appears in `schedule runs`.

```bash
flui app schedule logs my-app nightly-cleanup
flui app schedule logs my-app nightly-cleanup \
  --run my-app-nightly-cleanup-28912345
```

An old run whose workload has already been cleaned up has no logs
left to show, and the command says so rather than failing.

### `flui app schedule trigger <app> <name>`

Runs the schedule now, whatever its cron timing says. Useful to
prove a job works without waiting until 3am.

```bash
flui app schedule trigger my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule delete <app> <name>`

Removes the schedule.

```bash
flui app schedule delete my-app nightly-cleanup
```

## Data management

Two complementary surfaces operate on an application's persistent
volumes:

- **Snapshots** live inside the cluster — a full clone of a
  volume, stored as another volume on the same cluster's local
  storage. The clone copies the actual file contents (not a
  pre-allocated declared size), so a snapshot occupies roughly
  the space the source data currently uses. Restore is a local
  volume-to-volume copy: faster than fetching from object
  storage, but not instant. The cost adds up with retention —
  each snapshot doubles the on-node disk that workload uses, so
  keeping many around pulls the cluster's free capacity down
  quickly.
- **Backups** archive the volume's contents to S3-compatible
  object storage outside the cluster — much cheaper, slower to
  restore, and durable across a cluster destroy.

The two sets are independent; neither implies the other.

The difference matters when you remove an application. A backup
sits outside the cluster and a removal does not reach it. A
snapshot is a volume on the same cluster, carrying the same
application's label — so it is part of what a removal takes away.
A snapshot is protection against a bad upgrade, not against
deleting the app.

### `flui app snapshot create <name>`

Creates a snapshot of an application's volume. If the application
has more than one volume, pass `--volume <name>`.

```bash
flui app snapshot create my-app
flui app snapshot create my-app --description before-upgrade
flui app snapshot create my-app --volume data
```

### `flui app snapshot list`

Lists snapshots. Without filters, lists every snapshot in the
cluster; filter by application with `--app`.

```bash
flui app snapshot list
flui app snapshot list --app my-app
flui app snapshot list --app my-app --output json
```

### `flui app snapshot restore <name> <snapshot-id>`

Restores a snapshot into a **new side-by-side volume**. The
application is left untouched — the new volume is created
alongside it and can be promoted later with `snapshot swap`. Pass
`--swap` to restore and promote in one step.

```bash
flui app snapshot restore my-app <snapshot-id>
flui app snapshot restore my-app <snapshot-id> --swap
flui app snapshot restore my-app <snapshot-id> --swap --volume <name>
```

With `--swap` the CLI also needs to know which application volume
to retarget. Without `--volume` it assumes the volume is named
`data` — the conventional default. Pass `--volume <name>`
explicitly whenever your app's primary volume is named something
else, or whenever it has more than one.

### `flui app snapshot swap <name> <new-pvc-name>`

Swaps the application's live volume for a different one —
typically the one `snapshot restore` just created. Triggers a
rolling restart; the previous volume is kept until you delete it
explicitly. The CLI asks to confirm before applying; `--force`
skips the prompt.

```bash
flui app snapshot swap my-app my-app-data-restored-20260511
flui app snapshot swap my-app new-pvc --volume <name>
flui app snapshot swap my-app new-pvc --volume <name> --force
```

Same rule as `restore --swap` for `--volume`: without it the CLI
assumes `data`.

### `flui app snapshot delete <name> <snapshot-id>`

Deletes a snapshot. Asks to confirm; skip with `--force`.

```bash
flui app snapshot delete my-app <snapshot-id>
flui app snapshot delete my-app <snapshot-id> --force
```

### `flui app backup create <name>`

Archives an application's volume to S3-compatible object storage.
If `--bucket` is omitted, the cluster's provider auto-provisions
one; otherwise pass `--endpoint` plus `--bucket` and S3
credentials (by flag, or through `FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY` /
`FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY`).

```bash
flui app backup create my-app                            # auto-provisioned bucket
flui app backup create my-app --description nightly
flui app backup create my-app --bucket my-archive \
                              --endpoint https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud \
                              --access-key <key> --secret-key <secret>
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-b, --bucket <name>` | Destination S3 bucket. Auto-provisioned when omitted. |
| `-e, --endpoint <url>` | S3 endpoint URL. Required when `--bucket` is set. |
| `-r, --region <code>` | S3 region (default: `auto`). |
| `-v, --volume <name>` | Volume name when the app has more than one. |
| `-d, --description <s>` | Human-friendly tag appended to the key prefix. |
| `--access-key <k>` | S3 access key. Required when `--bucket` is set; otherwise read from `FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY`. |
| `--secret-key <s>` | S3 secret key. Required when `--bucket` is set; otherwise read from `FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY`. |
| `--key-prefix <s>` | Override the destination key prefix. Default: `flui/<cluster>/<app>/<timestamp>/`. |

When `--bucket` is set, **all three** of `--endpoint`,
`--access-key` and `--secret-key` are mandatory (the last two can
come from the matching environment variables). Pass them together
or none at all — passing the bucket without credentials fails up
front.

Auto-provisioning works fully on Scaleway (it reuses the same
compute key); on Hetzner it needs Object Storage credentials to
be connected. There is also a top-level [`flui
backup`](/cli/backups/) topic for scheduled, policy-driven
backups with their own destinations and jobs — `app backup` is
the ad-hoc, single-app variant.

### `flui app backup delete <name>`

Deletes an S3 backup. Removes every object under the export key
prefix.

```bash
flui app backup delete my-app <backup-id>
```

## Deletion

### `flui app delete <name>`

Permanently removes the application and everything it was using
in the cluster — **including its persistent volumes**. The data
is deleted, not moved to a bin. Flui cannot bring it back.

Before it asks, the command reads the cluster, works out which
storage belongs to this application, and prints it: one sentence
with the total, then each volume by name and size.

```
This also deletes 10 GiB of data in 1 volume.
It cannot be undone.
```

That sentence is written once by the platform, so the CLI, the
dashboard and an agent all quote the same number. Three surfaces
quoting three different numbers is how a warning stops being read.

**Unknown is never "none".** If the cluster cannot be reached, or
its credentials cannot be read, the command says so and tells you
to assume data will be lost. An empty list means "none found"
only when the reading actually succeeded.

```
The volumes this would delete could not be read from the cluster.
Assume data will be lost — it is not known to be none.
```

The confirmation is not a yes/no. You type the application's name
exactly — the one moment designed to make you read the list above
it. `--force` skips that question. It does not skip the listing:
the preview is printed either way.

```bash
flui app delete my-app
flui app delete my-app --force            # skip confirmation
flui app delete my-app --no-wait          # queue and exit
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster` | Cluster name or ID. |
| `-f, --force` | Skip the typed confirmation. Also the acknowledgement a system-protected app requires. |
| `--no-wait` | Return as soon as the removal is queued. |

If the application you name is one part of a catalog install, the
preview lists every part and the removal takes all of them —
there is no half-removed bundle.

Some applications are **system-protected** (typically the
components Flui itself depends on inside the control cluster).
For those, `--force` is required as an explicit acknowledgement.

For a catalog install the CLI waits for the uninstall to finish,
up to five minutes, unless you pass `--no-wait`. For a
source-built application it queues the delete and returns; check
with `flui app list`.

The whole story, including how to take a backup first, is
[Remove an application and its
data](/tasks/remove-an-application/).

### Storage older removals left behind

Deleting the volumes repairs the future only. Every installation
that has been running for a while still holds storage from
removals that happened before this changed — unattached,
unlisted, and still on the bill.

```bash
flui cluster volumes
flui cluster volumes --output json
flui cluster volumes --remove user-a1b2c3/data-uptime-kuma-0
```

A volume is only reported when nothing mounts it and no existing
application owns it. The scan errs by omission on purpose: a
volume it cannot attribute to a departed application is left out
rather than offered for deletion. Removing one is permanent.

### `flui app image delete <name> <version-id>`

Removes an image version from the container registry. Two guards
protect your ability to roll back:

- The version that is **currently deployed** can never be deleted
  — that guard cannot be bypassed.
- The version of the **most recent release** is also refused;
  `--force` overrides this second guard only.

```bash
flui app image delete my-api 845914920
flui app image delete my-api 845914920 --force
flui app image delete my-api 845914920 --yes     # skip the prompt
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--force` | Override the latest-release guard only. |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip the confirmation prompt. |
| `-c, --cluster` | Cluster name or ID. |

`--force` and `--yes` are different things: `--force` lifts a
guard, `--yes` skips the question.

Get `<version-id>` from `flui app versions <name> --output json`
— it is the numeric registry id, not the tag.

sections.title: Authentication
sections.body:
The CLI never holds your password. It holds an **API key**,
stored in the active profile, and every command that talks
to the Flui API sends it.

That one sentence is why this page has four commands and
not one. Your own terminal wants a key that can do
everything you can do. A build pipeline, or an agent, wants
a key that can do far less — and you want to be able to see
what you have handed out, and take it back.

A key is always a **ceiling, never a grant**. It can only
narrow what its issuer could already do. Nobody mints a key
worth more than themselves.

## `flui auth login`

The everyday path, for your own machine. The CLI opens a
browser, runs an OIDC sign-in against the identity provider
inside your installation, then uses the resulting token to
mint an API key and saves it in the active profile.

```bash
flui auth login              # opens a browser
flui auth login --headless   # prints the authorization URL instead
flui auth login --key-name my-laptop
```

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
