| `--headless` | Print the authorization URL instead of opening a browser. Useful over SSH. |
| `--key-name <name>` | Name attached to the generated key, shown later in listings. Default: `cli`. |
| `--prompt <mode>` | How the identity provider greets you. `select_account` (the default) shows the account picker, so you confirm or switch user before a key is minted; `login` forces re-authentication; an empty value reuses the current session silently. |
| `--profile <name>` | Profile to save the key into. Default: the active profile. |

After login every command uses the saved key with no
further prompts. The key is long-lived; rotating it means
running `flui auth login` again.

**The key `login` mints is unscoped.** It carries your full
weight, because it is you, at your own terminal. It is not
the kind of key you hand to anything else — for that, read
on.

### About the OAuth callback

The CLI listens for the redirect on `http://localhost:8899`,
with fallbacks through `8900`, `8901`, `8902` and `8910`.
There is a 120-second window between opening the URL and
receiving the callback.

## `flui auth generate-api-key`

For a key that is not you at a terminal: a build pipeline,
a script, an agent.

```bash
flui auth generate-api-key --name agent \
  --scope mcp:app:read --scope mcp:obs:read

flui auth generate-api-key --name ci-pipeline \
  --expires 365 --unscoped
```

### It refuses to guess

A request naming neither `--scope` nor `--unscoped` is
refused before anything else happens — before the network,
before the profile, before you go and find a token:

```
Say what this key may do.
  --scope <mcp:...>   a limited key; repeat the flag for more than one
  --unscoped          a key carrying your full weight
Omitting both used to mean --unscoped, silently.
```

That last line is the reason for the refusal. Saying
nothing used to mint the widest credential the installation
can issue. The widest credential should have to be asked
for out loud.

### It needs a session token

This command mints a key from a browser session token, not
from an existing key. Pass it with `--token`, or set
`FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN`.

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--token <jwt>` | `FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN` | Session bearer token to mint with. |
| `--name <name>` | `cli` | Human-readable name for the key. |
| `--expires <days>` | no expiry | Expiry in days from now. |
| `--scope <scope>` | — | A scope for the key. Repeat for more than one. Cannot be combined with `--unscoped`. |
| `--unscoped` | `false` | Issue a key with no scope ceiling, carrying your full weight. |
| `--profile <name>` | active profile | Profile to save the key into. |

### The key is shown once, and never again

The plaintext key is written straight into the profile. The
command prints the key's id, name, expiry and scopes — and
then this:

```
⚠  The plaintext key is not shown and cannot be retrieved again.
```

That is not a formality. The installation stores a digest
of the key, not the key, so there is nothing to hand back
later — not to you, not to anyone.

From the CLI you never see the value at all. It goes
straight into the profile, encrypted, and every later
command reads it from there. So if what you need is the
literal string, to paste into a CI secret or an agent's
configuration, mint the key in the dashboard instead: the
API returns the plaintext once, to whoever asked for it,
and the dashboard is the surface that shows it to you.

One consequence to plan for either way: a key minted here
**replaces the key already in that profile**. Pass
`--profile` to write it somewhere else if you do not want
to log out of the profile you are working in.

### Scopes

A scope is one line of what a key may do, shaped
`mcp:<area>:<depth>`. The full set:

```
mcp:onboarding:read      mcp:catalog:read
mcp:app:read             mcp:app:write             mcp:app:destructive
mcp:obs:read             mcp:spec:validate
mcp:backup:read          mcp:backup:write
mcp:migration:read       mcp:migration:write       mcp:migration:destructive
mcp:mail:read
mcp:iam:read             mcp:iam:write
mcp:infra:read           mcp:infra:write           mcp:infra:destructive
```

Two rules worth knowing before you type them.

**A scope you do not hold yourself is refused, not
trimmed.** The whole request fails and says which scope
caused it. A key that quietly came back smaller than you
asked for would be a key nobody could reason about.

**Every scoped key also gets `mcp:onboarding:read`,** whether
you ask for it or not. That is the scope that lets an agent
read the "how this installation is operated" document
before it does anything. An unscoped key already reaches
everything, so nothing is added to it.

### There is no `--groups` flag

The API and the dashboard offer a friendlier unit than raw
scopes: **permission groups** — fifteen of them, on two
axes, each with one sentence written for a person, granted
whole or refused whole.

The CLI does not have them. From the terminal you mint by
raw scope, or `--unscoped`. Groups are an API and dashboard
concept today.

If you are deciding what an agent should be allowed to do,
read [Choose what your agent may
do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/) first, then come
back and name the scopes by hand — or mint the key from the
dashboard instead.

## `flui auth api-keys`

Lists the keys issued for the identity you are signed in
as. Not everybody's keys — yours.

```bash
flui auth api-keys
flui auth api-keys --output json
```

Each row is a name, a state, the scopes it carries, and its
id. The state is one of three:

- **active** — usable now;
- **expired** — past the expiry it was minted with;
- **revoked** — switched off, and still listed, so a key
  that once existed does not vanish from the record.

A key with no scopes prints as *unscoped — the full weight
of the issuer*.

## `flui auth revoke-api-key <id>`

Takes a key back. It stops working immediately.

```bash
flui auth revoke-api-key 6f1c2d34-...
```

The id is the one printed by `flui auth api-keys`; it is
not the key itself, which you no longer have. You can only
revoke keys you minted — an id belonging to somebody else,
or to nothing, answers as not found.

Revoking does not remove the row. It marks it revoked, so
the listing keeps saying that this key existed and was
turned off.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_API_KEY` | Overrides the key stored in the profile for this invocation. The API URL still comes from the profile. |
| `FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN` | Session bearer token used by `generate-api-key`, instead of `--token`. |
| `FLUI_PROFILE` | Active profile selector — see [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/). |

The full inventory of `FLUI_*` variables is in
[Environment variables](/cli/environment-variables/).

sections.title: Backups
sections.body:
The `backup` topic groups every command for **policy-driven, scheduled backups** managed through the API. A backup [policy](#flui-backup-policy) defines *what* to capture (cluster-wide, specific namespaces, or specific applications) and *when* (a cron schedule), the API runs it as a [job](#flui-backup-job), and the resulting artifacts land in one or more S3-compatible [destinations](#flui-backup-destination). A captured artifact can later be replayed into a cluster with [restore](#flui-backup-restore). A **platform**-class policy is the exception — it protects Flui's own control plane instead, and is configured separately with [`flui backup platform`](#flui-backup-platform). > **`flui backup …` is not `flui app backup …`.** This topic is the > scheduled, policy-driven surface that operates at the > cluster/namespace/application level and is configured against the > API. `flui app backup create` — documented on > [Applications](/cli/applications/#flui-app-backup-create-name) — is a > separate, one-off command that archives a **single application's > volume** to S3. Reach for `app backup` for an ad-hoc snapshot of one > app's data; reach for `backup` when you want recurring, retained, > multi-destination coverage of a whole cluster or set of workloads. Unlike most of the CLI, the `backup` commands target the API directly rather than a single active cluster, so they do **not** take the usual `-c, --cluster ` flag. Where a command needs a cluster it takes an explicit `--cluster ` (cluster **ID**, not name), and the commands that read data accept `--json` for machine-readable output. The sections below group the commands by intent: destinations, policies, jobs, restores, and — separately — platform configuration, which protects the installation's own control plane rather than an application or a cluster. ## `flui backup destination` A destination is an S3-compatible storage target where backup artifacts are written. Supported providers are `hetzner_object_storage`, `scaleway_object_storage`, `minio`, and `generic_s3`. ### `flui backup destination create` Registers a new destination. All connection details are required: provider, endpoint, region, bucket, and access/secret keys. Encryption defaults to `flui_managed`; pass `--encryption-mode byo_passphrase` with `--encryption-passphrase` to supply your own. ```bash flui backup destination create \ --name my-s3 --provider hetzner_object_storage \ --endpoint https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com \ --region fsn1 --bucket flui-backups \ --access-key AK --secret-key SK flui backup destination create \ --name scw --provider scaleway_object_storage \ --endpoint https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud \ --region fr-par --bucket flui-bkp \ --access-key AK --secret-key SK ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--name ` | — | Display name (≤120 chars). Required. | | `--provider

` | — | Storage backend: `hetzner_object_storage`, `scaleway_object_storage`, `minio`, `generic_s3`. Required. | | `--endpoint ` | — | S3 endpoint URL (e.g. `https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud`). Required. | | `--region ` | — | S3 region. Required. | | `--bucket ` | — | Target bucket. Required. | | `--access-key ` | — | S3 access key. Required. | | `--secret-key ` | — | S3 secret key. Required. | | `--prefix ` | — | Optional path prefix inside the bucket. | | `--encryption-mode ` | `flui_managed` | `flui_managed`, `byo_passphrase`, or `none`. | | `--encryption-passphrase ` | — | Passphrase to use; required when `--encryption-mode=byo_passphrase`. | | `--force-path-style` | — | Force path-style S3 URLs (needed for MinIO / some providers). | | `--use-sse` | — | Use server-side encryption (SSE-S3) at the provider. | | `--cost-per-gb-month-cents ` | — | Provider cost in cents per GB·month, used for the billing estimate. | ### `flui backup destination list` Lists the destinations configured in the API, with provider, region/bucket, usage, and health when available. ```bash flui backup destination list flui backup destination list --json ``` ### `flui backup destination show ` Shows one destination in full, including endpoint, prefix, encryption mode, health, and reported usage. ```bash flui backup destination show flui backup destination show --json ``` ### `flui backup destination test ` Verifies connectivity to a destination by performing a real S3 PUT/GET/DELETE round-trip against the bucket. Use it right after `create` to confirm the credentials and endpoint work. ```bash flui backup destination test ``` ### `flui backup destination delete ` Removes a destination from the API. **Existing artifacts already in the bucket are NOT removed** — only the registration is deleted. Asks to confirm; skip with `-y, --yes`. ```bash flui backup destination delete flui backup destination delete --yes ``` ## `flui backup policy` A policy ties a **scope** (what to back up) to a **schedule** and one or more **destinations**. The API runs the policy on its cron schedule (and on demand via [`backup job run`](#flui-backup-job-run)), producing artifacts subject to the policy's retention. ### `flui backup policy create` Creates a policy. `--name`, `--cluster` (cluster ID), `--scope`, and at least one `--destination` are required. The scope decides what gets captured: `cluster_all` for the whole cluster, `namespaces` (narrow it with `--scope-namespaces ns1,ns2`), `applications` (narrow it with `--scope-apps ,`), or `label_selector`. The `--destination` flag is repeatable and takes a spec of the form `[:primary|replica[:priority]]` — pass it once per target to mirror a backup across several destinations. ```bash flui backup policy create \ --name daily-all --cluster \ --scope cluster_all --schedule "0 2 * * *" \ --retention-days 14 --destination flui backup policy create \ --name app-snap --cluster \ --scope applications --scope-apps , \ --destination :primary --destination :replica:1 ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--name ` | — | Policy name. Required. | | `--cluster ` | — | Cluster ID the policy applies to. Required. | | `--scope ` | — | `cluster_all` or `namespaces` for a volume-class policy; `applications` (exactly one id) for a database-class one. The Velero engine only narrows by namespace, so `applications` and `label_selector` are refused for volume policies rather than silently capturing the whole cluster. Required. | | `--scope-namespaces ` | — | Comma-separated namespaces (for `scope=namespaces`). | | `--scope-apps ` | — | Comma-separated application IDs (for `scope=applications`). | | `--profile

` | `single` | Destination profile: `single`, `mirrored`, or `custom`. | | `--schedule ` | — | Cron schedule, e.g. `"0 2 * * *"` for daily 02:00 UTC. | | `--retention-days ` | `30` | Days to keep each artifact (minimum 1). | | `--retention-max-copies ` | — | Cap on the number of retained copies (minimum 1). | | `--include-pvcs` | — | Also capture volume data — but only for volumes on the **shared** storage class. Volumes on the dedicated class, which is what databases use, cannot be read by Velero's file-system backup and are skipped; each run records which ones. Protect those with a database-class policy or a volume copy. | | `--[no-]enabled` | enabled | Create the policy disabled with `--no-enabled`. | | `--destination ` | — | `[:primary\|replica[:priority]]`. Required, repeatable. | ### `flui backup policy list` Lists policies, optionally filtered to one cluster. Each row shows the profile/scope, cluster, cron schedule, and whether it is disabled. ```bash flui backup policy list flui backup policy list --cluster flui backup policy list --json ``` ### `flui backup policy show ` Shows one policy: cluster, profile, scope, schedule, retention, and its destination list (each with role and priority). ```bash flui backup policy show flui backup policy show --json ``` ### `flui backup policy delete ` Deletes a policy. **Existing backups are kept** — only the policy and its schedule are removed. Asks to confirm; skip with `-y, --yes`. ```bash flui backup policy delete flui backup policy delete --yes ``` ### `flui backup policy pause ` Turns a policy's schedule off. Everything about the policy — scope, schedule, retention, destinations — stays exactly as configured; the API just stops enqueueing new runs from it until someone resumes it. `flui backup job run` still works on a paused policy, so an on-demand backup stays possible; only the cron schedule stops firing. One exception: a **database**-class policy ships WAL continuously, and pausing it does not stop that stream — it would tear a hole in the recovery window. Deleting the policy is the only way to stop it. ```bash flui backup policy pause ``` ### `flui backup policy resume ` Turns a paused policy's schedule back on. ```bash flui backup policy resume ``` ## `flui backup job` A job is one execution of a policy — either a scheduled run or an on-demand trigger. Jobs are where you see a backup's status, timing, bytes transferred, and any error. ### `flui backup job run` Triggers an on-demand backup for a given policy, outside its normal schedule. Returns the queued job's ID so you can track it with `backup job show`. ```bash flui backup job run --policy ``` ### `flui backup job list` Lists the backup jobs for a cluster. `--cluster` (cluster ID) is required. ```bash flui backup job list --cluster flui backup job list --cluster --json ``` ### `flui backup job show ` Shows one job: its policy, status, start/completion times, bytes transferred, and error message if it failed. ```bash flui backup job show flui backup job show --json ``` ## `flui backup restore` A restore replays a captured artifact back into a cluster. You can restore a whole cluster, a single namespace, one application, or the observability stack. Preview first to see exactly what a restore would touch. ### `flui backup restore preview` Dry-run that reports the resources a restore would create or replace, without changing anything. Takes the artifact ID and the destination it lives in. Output is JSON. ```bash flui backup restore preview \ --artifact --source-destination ``` ### `flui backup restore create` Creates a restore job. Required: the `--artifact` to restore, the `--source-destination` it lives in, the `--target-cluster` to restore into, and the `--target-kind`. For namespace and application targets, also pass the matching selector flag. ```bash flui backup restore create \ --artifact --source-destination \ --target-cluster --target-kind cluster flui backup restore create \ --artifact --source-destination \ --target-cluster --target-kind application \ --target-app --strategy velero_rebuild ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--artifact ` | Backup artifact ID to restore. Required. | | `--source-destination ` | Destination where the artifact lives. Required. | | `--target-cluster ` | Cluster to restore into. Required. | | `--target-kind ` | `cluster`, `namespace`, `application`, or `observability`. Required. | | `--target-namespace ` | Target namespace; required when `--target-kind=namespace`. | | `--target-app ` | Target application ID; required when `--target-kind=application`. | | `--strategy ` | Restore strategy: `velero_rebuild` or `os_snapshot`. | ### `flui backup restore list` Lists restore jobs, with status, target kind, and target cluster. ```bash flui backup restore list flui backup restore list --json ``` ### `flui backup restore show ` Shows one restore job: status, source artifact and destination, target, strategy, timing, and error message if it failed. ```bash flui backup restore show flui backup restore show --json ``` ## `flui backup platform` Everything above protects an application or a cluster. A **platform**-class policy protects something else: this installation's own control plane — the database holding every user, API key, provider token and application record Flui has. That backup can't be sealed with a key the control plane holds itself — if the master is what's lost, a key stored on the master is lost with it. So a platform backup is encrypted to an **age** key pair you generate on your own laptop. Only the public half — the recipient — is registered on the policy. The private identity never touches the master. ### `flui backup platform init` Generates that identity, entirely on your machine, and writes it to a passphrase-protected recovery file (default `./flui-master-recovery.age`). Prints the public recipient. Pass `--policy ` to register the recipient on an existing platform-class policy in the same step; without it, `init` just prints the recipient and the command to run once you have a policy ID. **Keep the recovery file and its passphrase somewhere off the master, and keep both.** They are the only way to decrypt a platform backup. Flui does not hold a copy — lose either one and every platform backup becomes permanently unrecoverable. ```bash flui backup platform init \ --policy \ --out ./flui-master-recovery.age ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--policy ` | — | Platform backup policy to register the recipient on. | | `--heartbeat-url ` | — | Dead-man's-switch URL the master pings while its last platform backup stays fresh. Only takes effect together with `--policy`. | | `--out ` | `./flui-master-recovery.age` | Where to write the recovery file. | | `--passphrase ` | — | Passphrase for the recovery file. Prompted (and confirmed) if omitted. | | `--force` | — | Overwrite an existing file at `--out`. | | `--json` | — | Print `{recipient, out}` as JSON and exit. Does **not** register `--policy`, even if it's passed — do the two steps separately when scripting. Requires `--passphrase`, since it can't prompt. | `flui backup policy create --engine-class platform` creates the policy; this command then registers the recipient on it. Pass `--policy` to do the second step here, or run it later once you have the policy ID. ### `flui backup platform status` Lists every platform-class policy: whether a recipient is registered, whether a dead-man's-switch URL is set, its schedule, and whether its last run is still fresh — inside a 45-minute window — or stale. A paused platform policy is marked `[disabled]`. ```bash flui backup platform status flui backup platform status --json ```

sections.title: Clusters and nodes
sections.body:
This page covers the commands that act on a cluster as a
whole, or on the machines inside it: `cluster`, `node`,
`server-types` and `ssh`.

## Which cluster a command is talking to

An installation has one **control cluster** — the one that
runs Flui itself — and any number of **workload clusters**,
which run only your applications.

Those two are stored in different places, and that is the
one thing to know before reading the rest of this page. The
CLI keeps its own local record of the cluster it created on
this machine, which is the control cluster. Workload
clusters are created from the dashboard or by an agent, and
they live only in the installation's database, so the CLI
has to ask the API for them.

Some commands read both, and some read only the local
record:

- `flui cluster list`, `flui cluster volumes` and
  `flui ssh` read both, so they see every cluster.
- `flui node list`, `flui node add`, `flui node remove` and
  `flui cluster destroy` read the local record only. Point
  them at a cluster created from the dashboard and they
  answer that it does not exist.

The commands that take `-c, --cluster <name|id>` auto-detect
the target when there is only one cluster to choose from,
and refuse to guess when there is more than one.

For the control cluster's own lifecycle — create, status,
resize, destroy — use the [`env`](/cli/environments/) topic.
It is the only surface that always targets the control
cluster and exposes the operations specific to it.

## `flui cluster list`

Lists every cluster of the installation: name, type
(`control` or `workload`), provider, region, node count,
status and id. The control cluster is printed first, since
it is the one a bare `flui ssh master` addresses.

```bash
flui cluster list
flui cluster list --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-o, --output table\|json` | `table` | Output format. |

If the API cannot be reached — you are not logged in, or the
installation is down — the command still prints the clusters
it holds locally and says plainly that the workload clusters
could not be listed. It does not report an empty list as if
there were nothing there.

The JSON form deliberately prints an allow-list of fields.
The local record also holds cluster credentials, and those
have no business on standard output, where they can be
redirected into a file or pasted into a chat.

## `flui cluster destroy`

Permanently destroys a workload cluster and all its nodes.
The command asks you to retype the cluster name before it
proceeds.

```bash
flui cluster destroy <cluster-name-or-id>
flui cluster destroy <cluster> --force                # skip confirmation
flui cluster destroy <cluster> --force --no-wait      # queue and exit
```

| Argument / Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<cluster>` | Cluster name or ID (required). |
| `-f, --force` | Skip the typed confirmation prompt. |
| `--no-wait` | Queue the destroy operation and return immediately. |

> The control cluster is **not** in scope here, and the
> command refuses it by name. For that one, use
> [`flui env destroy`](/cli/environments/#flui-env-destroy).

## `flui cluster volumes`

Removing an application now takes its storage with it. That
was not always true. Every removal made before it changed
left its disk behind, and nothing listed those disks — so a
cluster can be carrying storage that belongs to applications
which no longer exist, and you have been paying for it
without a way to see it.

This command is the way to see it.

```bash
flui cluster volumes
flui cluster volumes --output json
flui cluster volumes --remove user-a1b2c3/data-uptime-kuma-0
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | auto-detect | Target cluster. |
| `--remove <ref>` | — | Delete one abandoned volume, given exactly as the listing printed it. Permanent. |
| `-f, --force` | off | Skip the typed confirmation of `--remove`. |
| `-o, --output table\|json` | `table` | Output format. |

The listing is deliberately cautious, because a false
positive here is somebody's data. A volume is only called
abandoned when it sits in a place Flui made for
applications, nothing is using it, nothing that could
re-create it still exists, no living application is
attributed to it, and it has been sitting there for at least
fifteen minutes. Each entry prints the reason it qualified.

Read that the right way round: a volume the listing does not
show is not proof that nothing is left. The command errs on
the side of leaving things alone. And when the cluster's
credentials cannot be read at all, it says so instead of
printing an empty list.

`--remove` takes one entry, exactly as the listing printed
it, and asks you to type the volume's name to confirm. The
platform then re-runs the whole check on its side before it
deletes anything, so a volume that has come back into use in
the meantime is refused rather than removed. What it deletes
is gone for good.

Listing is read-only and needs access to the infrastructure
area. Removing needs authority over the cluster's machines,
which is a level above reading them — so somebody who can
see the list cannot necessarily act on it.

## Nodes

The `node` topic operates on the machines of a cluster. The
master is listed by `node list` but cannot be added or
removed here: it is created with the cluster and goes away
only with `cluster destroy` or `env destroy`.

### `flui node list`

Lists every node in the target cluster — master and workers
— with its role, status, address and name. When the master
of the control cluster is reserved for the control plane,
the listing says so on the master's row.

```bash
flui node list
flui node list --cluster my-cluster
flui node list --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | auto-detect | Target cluster. |
| `-o, --output table\|json` | `table` | Output format. |

### `flui node add`

Buys one or more new servers from the cluster's provider and
joins them as workers. They are created in the same
provider, region and size as the cluster already uses —
`node add` has no flag to choose a different size.

```bash
flui node add                            # add one worker
flui node add --cluster my-cluster       # target a specific cluster
flui node add --no-wait                  # queue and exit
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | auto-detect | Target cluster. |
| `-n, --count <n>` | `1` | Number of workers to add. Range: 1–5. |
| `--no-wait` | `false` | Queue the operation and return immediately. |

### `flui node remove`

Removes a worker from the cluster. The order matters and the
platform holds to it: stop giving the node new work, move
the work already on it to the other nodes, then delete the
server at the provider. The master cannot be removed this
way — `node remove` refuses it, and destroying the whole
cluster is the operation you want instead.

```bash
flui node remove <node-id>
flui node remove <node-id> --cluster my-cluster
flui node remove <node-id> --no-wait
```

Take `<node-id>` from `flui node list`. The CLI checks the
id against the cluster's current nodes **before** queuing
anything, so an unknown id fails immediately with a pointer
back to `node list` rather than becoming a queued operation
that was never going to work.

The CLI waits five minutes. If the removal takes longer —
a slow move of the work, an application in no hurry to
release its node — it hands control back and tells you the
operation is still running; `flui node list` shows the final
state. `--no-wait` skips the wait entirely.

| Argument / Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<node-id>` | Node ID to remove (required, the master is rejected). |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | Target cluster (auto-detect when only one). |
| `--no-wait` | Queue and return immediately. |

### `flui node connect`

`flui node add` buys a machine. When the machine is already
yours, there is nothing to buy — and that is what this
command is for. It joins a Linux host you already have to
the cluster as a worker, over SSH, provisioning nothing.

It applies to an installation running on your own servers.
The command joins the **control cluster**, and if that
cluster was created at a cloud provider instead it stops and
points you at `flui node add`.

```bash
flui node connect --host 203.0.113.10
flui node connect --host 10.0.0.12 --master-ip 10.0.0.11 --node-network 10.0.0.0/24
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--host <addr>` | required | Address or DNS name of the host to join. |
| `--port <n>` | `22` | SSH port of the host. |
| `--user <name>` | `root` | SSH user on the host. |
| `--ssh-key <path>` | `~/.ssh/id_rsa` | Private key that already authenticates to the host. |
| `--master-ip <addr>` | the cluster's master address | The address the new machine uses to reach the master. |
| `--node-network <cidr>` | the `/24` of the detected private address | The private network the nodes share. |
| `--skip-precheck` | off | Do not inspect the host first. |
| `--best-effort` | off | Continue even when the inspection reports problems. |

Three things have to be true of the host before this works,
and the command tells you all three before it starts: you
can reach it over SSH with the key you named, it can reach
the cluster's master on the shared private network, and it
is a clean machine with no cluster software on it already.

It then inspects the host and reports what it found —
operating system, architecture, memory, processors. An
unsupported architecture, less than about 2 GB of memory, or
a cluster runtime already installed each count as a problem,
and the command stops rather than joining a host that will
misbehave later. `--best-effort` proceeds anyway;
`--skip-precheck` does not look at all. Neither is the
normal path.

When it finishes it prints the new node's name and private
address. `flui node list` is the confirmation.

## Server types

### `flui server-types list`

Lists the machines a provider sells, with CPU, memory, disk
and monthly price. Read it before you pick a size — for a
new installation, or before resizing an existing node — so
that the size you ask for is one that exists.

```bash
flui server-types list --provider hetzner
flui server-types list --provider hetzner --region fsn1
flui server-types list --provider scaleway --memory 8-32
flui server-types list --provider scaleway --sort memory
flui server-types list --provider hetzner --json
flui server-types list --provider hetzner --force-refresh
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-p, --provider hetzner\|scaleway` | required | Which provider's catalogue to read. |
| `-r, --region <code>` | — | Filter by region or location code. |
| `-m, --memory <expr>` | — | Filter by memory in GB: `16` exactly, `8-32` a range, `8-` a minimum, `-32` a maximum. |
| `-s, --sort price\|memory\|cores\|disk\|name` | `price` | Sort key. |
| `--desc` | off | Sort descending. |
| `--json` | off | Machine-readable output. |
| `--force-refresh` | off | Skip the local cache and re-read from the provider. |

Results are cached locally and the command says when the
cache expires. `--force-refresh` goes back to the provider.

## SSH access

### `flui ssh <cluster>/<node>`

Opens a shell on a node. You do not set up a key: for each
connection the CLI makes a throwaway key pair, has it signed
for five minutes by the certificate authority the active
profile manages, uses it, and cleans up afterwards. Nothing
long-lived is left on the machine you connected from.

The argument names a node, and it takes two forms:

```bash
flui ssh master                      # the control cluster
flui ssh worker-1                    # the control cluster
flui ssh workload-cluster-1/master   # any cluster, by name
flui ssh workload-cluster-1/worker-2
```

A bare node name means the **control cluster**. Put a
cluster name in front of it, separated by a slash, and you
can reach any cluster of the installation — including the
workload clusters that only exist in the installation's
database.

| Argument | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<cluster>/<node>` | Node of a named cluster. |
| `<node>` | Node of the control cluster. |

The node part accepts `master`, `worker-N`, or a node's own
server name as shown by `flui node list`. Get any of it
wrong and the error prints the clusters available and the
nodes inside them, so the next attempt is a correction
rather than a guess.

On an installation running on your own server, the address,
port and user recorded when it was installed are used;
otherwise the connection is `root` on port 22.

SSH is the lowest-level surface Flui exposes. It is there
for direct shell work — debugging, looking at system
processes, one-off inspection. For everyday operations —
metrics, logs, restarts, deploys — the higher-level
commands are the right entry point, and you should not need
a shell at all.

## Where to go from here

- [Add a cluster and give it capacity](/tasks/add-a-cluster/)
  — the same ground as a task, with the dashboard and agent
  paths alongside the CLI.
- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/)
  — what a node is, and what stays constant when a cluster
  changes shape.
- [Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/)
  — the removal that now takes the storage with it.
- [CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/) — the control
  cluster's own lifecycle.

sections.title: Databases
sections.body:
The `db` topic is the path for working with a Flui database
building block from your own machine — with `psql` or pgAdmin
for Postgres, `mariadb` or DBeaver for MariaDB, `redis-cli`
for Valkey/Redis, or your application's ORM. A Flui database
is just an application running in the cluster, so it is
identified the same way as any other.

Flui databases are **not exposed outside the cluster
network** — there is no public endpoint to point a client at.
That is the right default, and everything on this page exists
because of it. The commands fall into three jobs:

- **Connect.** [`flui db credentials`](#flui-db-credentials-app)
  prints the in-cluster address and credentials — what another
  app *running on Flui* uses.
  [`flui db tunnel`](#flui-db-tunnel-app) opens a temporary
  local tunnel so a client *on your machine* can connect.
- **Copy the data out, and back.**
  [`flui db dump`](#flui-db-dump-app) streams a dump to a file
  or to a backup destination;
  [`flui db restore`](#flui-db-restore-app-file) runs one back
  into the live database.
- **Check it is still healthy.**
  [`flui db disk`](#flui-db-disk-app) is how full the storage
  is, [`flui db backup-status`](#flui-db-backup-status-app) is
  how far back you can recover, and
  [`flui db pitr-restore`](#flui-db-pitr-restore-app) rebuilds
  a Postgres database as of a moment in time.

If you would rather not install a local client, the dashboard
ships an in-browser console for the same databases — see
[The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/).
These CLI commands are the native-client path; the console is
the in-browser one. For the *how* rather than the flags, read
[Open a database from your
machine](/tasks/open-a-database/).

## Two shapes of command

The `db` commands are not all addressed the same way, and it
saves a confusing error to know which is which.

`credentials` and `tunnel` resolve the database **by name,
slug or id**, and take `-c, --cluster <name|id>` to say where
to look (auto-detected when the active profile has only one
cluster). Both read the password straight from the cluster
over SSH — never from the API.

`dump`, `restore`, `disk`, `backup-status` and `pitr-restore`
go straight to the API with the application's **id**, which
`flui app list` prints. They have no `-c, --cluster` flag,
because the id already says which cluster the database is on.

Every one of them asks the same access question first. Owning
the database is not by itself enough — you need a grant that
reaches it, and an agent key is held to its own limits before
the database is even looked up. That story is
[Who is allowed to open
one](/tasks/open-a-database/#who-is-allowed-to-open-one).

## `flui db credentials <app>`

Shows how to connect to a Flui database: the in-cluster
service address and its credentials, plus a ready-to-copy
`DATABASE_URL`. This is the connection information for
**another app running on Flui in the same cluster** — the host
is the in-cluster address, not a public one.

The password is read from the cluster over SSH and is
**hidden by default**. Pass `--show` to print it in plaintext.

```bash
flui db credentials postgresql-051f58
flui db credentials postgresql-051f58 --show
flui db credentials postgresql-051f58 --show --hide-after 30
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | auto-detect | Cluster to resolve the database in. |
| `--show` | off | Print the password in plaintext (hidden otherwise). |
| `--hide-after <seconds>` | `0` | Opt-in optical wipe: hold the terminal for N seconds with a countdown, then erase the password from the screen. Only takes effect together with `--show` on a TTY; `0` returns immediately. |

To connect a native client from your own machine, use `flui
db tunnel` instead — the in-cluster host shown here is not
reachable from outside the cluster.

## `flui db tunnel <app>`

Opens a **local tunnel** to a Flui database so you can connect
a native client. Because Flui databases are not exposed
outside the cluster, the command forwards the connection
through the control plane over SSH — **no public endpoint is
opened**. It stays in the foreground; press CTRL-C to close
the tunnel.

Once the tunnel is up, the command prints the loopback
host/port, the credentials, a connection string, and a
one-line client invocation for the engine (for example a
`psql` or `mariadb` command).

```bash
flui db tunnel postgresql-051f58
flui db tunnel postgresql-051f58 --local-port 5544
flui db tunnel postgresql-051f58 --no-retry
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | auto-detect | Cluster to resolve the database in. |
| `--local-port <n>` | engine default | Local port to bind on `127.0.0.1`. Defaults are engine-specific: `55432` for Postgres, `53306` for MariaDB, `56379` for Valkey/Redis, `57017` for FerretDB. |
| `--[no-]retry` | on | Reconnect automatically if the SSH session drops. Disable with `--no-retry`. |

With the tunnel running, point any client at `127.0.0.1` on
the local port — for example:

```bash
flui db tunnel postgresql-051f58        # leaves the tunnel open in this terminal

# in another terminal
psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 55432 -U <user> -d <database>
```

### The two reserved names

Two names are not applications. `platform-postgres` and
`identity-provider` are answered by `flui db tunnel` itself,
and they open Flui's own database and the identity provider's
tables. They are the only names on this page that are typed
verbatim rather than looked up, they are closed to the browser
console absolutely, and they need authority over the whole
installation.

The rules are different enough that they have their own page:
[Reach the platform's own
database](/tasks/reach-the-platform-database/).

## `flui db dump <app>`

Takes a dump of the database and streams it to your machine.
Nothing is exported by hand: the dump is produced **inside the
cluster by the engine's own tool**, so the tool and its
version always match the database.

What you get depends on the engine:

- **Postgres and MariaDB** — a plain SQL dump.
- **Redis and Valkey** — a snapshot file (`.rdb`).
- Anything else answers that a logical dump is not supported
  for it, and says to use a volume snapshot instead. Nothing
  is written.

By default the dump lands in the current directory under a
name Flui suggests — the database name and the date, with the
right extension. `-o` picks your own.

`--s3-destination` sends the dump to a backup destination
instead of downloading it, which is what you want for
anything large or scheduled. The ids come from `flui backup
destination list`; see [Backups](/cli/backups/).

```bash
flui db dump 4f0b2c1e-…
flui db dump 4f0b2c1e-… -o backup.sql
flui db dump 4f0b2c1e-… --s3-destination 9a71…
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-o, --output <file>` | `<database>-<date>.<ext>` | Write the dump to this file. Note this is a **filename**, not the `-o table\|json` of the rest of the CLI. |
| `--s3-destination <id>` | off | Store the dump in this backup destination instead of downloading it. Prints the bucket and key it wrote. |

## `flui db restore <app> <file>`

Runs a dump file back into the **live** database. This is the
destructive half of the pair: the statements in the file are
executed against the database as it stands, so existing data
is overwritten. Flui cannot undo it.

Because of that, the command asks before it starts, and the
default answer is no. `--yes` skips the prompt for scripts.

Restore is available for **Postgres and MariaDB**. A Redis or
Valkey snapshot cannot be replayed into a running instance
this way; that recovery goes through a volume snapshot, and
the command says so rather than half-doing it.

```bash
flui db restore 4f0b2c1e-… backup.sql
flui db restore 4f0b2c1e-… backup.sql --yes
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--yes` | off | Skip the confirmation prompt. |

## `flui db disk <app>`

How full the storage under a database is. A database that
runs out of room stops writing, and that failure looks like
an application bug for the first ten minutes, so this is
worth checking before you go hunting.

The number reported is the fullness of the **filesystem
hosting the database's storage**, because that is the
boundary where writing actually stops. It prints used, total,
free, where it is mounted, and a status of `none`, `warning`
or `critical`, with a line telling you to free space or grow
the disk when it is not `none`.

Where the reading is not available — the database is not
running, or its storage cannot be read — it says so plainly
rather than reporting zero.

```bash
flui db disk 4f0b2c1e-…
```

The command takes no flags.

## `flui db backup-status <app>`

Answers one question for a Postgres database: **how far back
can I go?** It prints whether continuous backup is on, the
schedule of its base backups, the recoverable window from
oldest to newest, how many base backups exist, and when the
last one was taken.

The newest end of the window is roughly *now*, because the
database keeps shipping its write log continuously between
base backups. That is what makes a restore to an arbitrary
moment possible at all.

If the database cannot be reached, the window is reported as
unavailable rather than as empty. The two are not the same
thing and the command does not pretend they are.

Continuous backup is not switched on from here. It comes from
a backup policy of the database kind covering that
application:
`flui backup policy create --engine-class database --scope applications
--scope-apps <app-id> --destination <dest-id>`, or the same choice in
the dashboard. See [Backups](/cli/backups/).

It also needs a database Flui itself provisioned: continuous backup
is implemented with pgBackRest, which ships in Flui's own Postgres
image. A plain `postgres` container running as part of some other
application cannot be protected this way.

```bash
flui db backup-status 4f0b2c1e-…
flui db backup-status 4f0b2c1e-… --json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--json` | off | Machine-readable output. |

## `flui db pitr-restore <app>`

Rebuilds a Postgres database **as of a moment in time**.

The important part is what it does not do: it never touches
the source. Instead of rewinding the database you are looking
at, Flui creates a **new install** and recovers it from the
continuous backup up to the instant you name. You end up with
two databases — the live one, untouched, and yesterday's,
running beside it — and you decide what to do next.

That is the difference between this and `flui db restore`.
`restore` overwrites; `pitr-restore` copies.

`--name` is required, because the result is a real
application that needs a name of its own. Leave `--at` out to
recover to the latest recoverable point; give it an ISO-8601
instant to pick a moment. `--cluster` here means the **target**
cluster for the new install, and defaults to the cluster the
source is on — which makes this a way to bring a database up
somewhere else, as well as a way to go back in time.

The command returns as soon as the restore job is created.
The new install boots in recovery mode; watch for it with
`flui app list`. It comes up with its own Flui-managed
credentials, not the source's.

```bash
flui db pitr-restore 4f0b2c1e-… --name pg-restored
flui db pitr-restore 4f0b2c1e-… --name pg-asof --at "2026-07-03T12:00:00Z"
flui db pitr-restore 4f0b2c1e-… --name pg-dr --cluster <cluster-id>
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--name <name>` | *required* | Display name for the restored install. |
| `--at <instant>` | latest | ISO-8601 instant to recover to, for example `2026-07-03T12:00:00Z`. |
| `--cluster <id>` | source's cluster | Cluster to build the restored install on. |
| `--yes` | off | Skip the confirmation prompt. |

There is nothing to recover from until continuous backup has
been running: with no backup for the application, the command
says so and stops.

## How it relates to the dashboard console

These commands are the **native-client** path: they put a
real database endpoint on your loopback interface so any
local tool or ORM can talk to it, and they move dumps in and
out. The dashboard's
[database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/) is the
**in-browser** path — run a query or browse keys without
installing anything, with a helper that never sees your data.
The console also has panels for the backup, disk and
point-in-time work above.

Both operate on the same Flui database building blocks; pick
whichever fits the task.

sections.title: Deploy
sections.body:
`flui deploy` takes a `flui.yaml` manifest and rolls the
application onto a cluster. The same command handles both
manifest kinds:

- **`kind: CatalogApp`** — the image already exists in a
  registry; Flui pulls and deploys it.
- **`kind: Application`** — the image is built from source by
  the CI of the platform that hosts the repo, then the
  resulting image is deployed.

The user-visible flow is the same in both cases: read the
manifest, target a cluster, run; the difference is whether
there is a build step in front. See the concept chapters
[Catalog vs Application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/)
and
[Build pipeline, today and tomorrow](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/)
for the model.

Three things on this page surprise people, so they come
first:

- `--name` is part of an application's identity. A new one
  installs the repository a second time.
- A value passed with `--env` is stored and displayed in
  plain text unless you name the key with `--secret`.
- `--validate-only` no longer only reads the file. It also
  asks this installation whether the manifest would land.

## `flui deploy [<file>]`

```bash
flui deploy                                # ./flui.yaml, auto-detect repo/branch/cluster
flui deploy ./apps/api/flui.yaml           # explicit manifest path
flui deploy --repo acme/my-app --branch main
flui deploy --env-file .env --secret DATABASE_URL --secret API_KEY
flui deploy --detach                       # queue and exit
flui deploy --validate-only                # check the manifest, don't deploy
flui deploy --cluster my-cluster           # pin a target cluster
```

| Argument / Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<file>` | Path to the manifest. Default: `./flui.yaml`. |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | Target cluster. Auto-detected when the active profile has only one. |
| `-r, --repo <owner/repo>` | Source repo. For `kind: Application`, auto-detected from `git remote origin`. |
| `-b, --branch <name>` | Branch to build. For `kind: Application`, auto-detected from the current branch. |
| `--name <name>` | Release name. Part of the application's identity — see below. |
| `--exposure <public\|internal>` | Override how the app is reached. `public` gets an address and a certificate; `internal` gets no public address at all. |
| `-d, --domain <fqdn>` | Custom hostname for the app. Auto-assigned from the cluster's DNS zone otherwise. |
| `--hostname <ip\|domain>` | Whether the address is derived from the cluster IP (a `nip.io` address) or sits under the cluster's DNS zone. |
| `--no-tls` | Publish the address without a certificate for this app. The app is served over plain HTTP. |
| `--cert-challenge <http-01\|dns-01>` | How the certificate is validated. `http-01` issues a dedicated per-host certificate and works on any reachable domain; `dns-01` uses the cluster's wildcard certificate and needs a DNS zone. |
| `--cert-provider <lets-encrypt\|lets-encrypt-staging>` | Which issuer signs the certificate. `lets-encrypt-staging` issues untrusted test certificates and avoids rate limits while you iterate. |
| `--skip-endpoint` | Skip the public address and its certificate entirely. |
| `-e, --env KEY=VALUE` | Per-deploy variable override. Repeatable. Plain text unless marked. |
| `--env-file <path>` | Read `KEY=VALUE` overrides from a file, one per line. `#` comments and blank lines are ignored. `--env` wins on the same key. |
| `--secret KEY` | Mark a key from `--env` / `--env-file` as sensitive. Repeatable. |
| `--detach` | Return as soon as the build/deploy is queued. Track with `flui app status`. |
| `--no-wait` | Alias of `--detach`, kept for symmetry with other commands. |
| `--no-build` | Skip the build step and redeploy the current image. Useful when you only changed `flui.yaml` settings. |
| `--image <ref>` | Deploy a specific image reference (e.g. `registry/owner/repo:sha`). Skips the build pipeline; useful for rollbacks. |
| `--allow-master` | Let an app that needs a real disk land on the master when the cluster has no worker. `kind: CatalogApp`. |
| `--validate-only` | Check the manifest and exit, without deploying. |
| `--json` | With `--validate-only`, print the result as JSON. |
| `--skip-checks` | Bypass the framework pre-flight checks (e.g. the Next.js standalone-output check). `kind: Application` only. |
| `--api-url <url>` | Talk to a different API address than the active profile's. |

### Auto-detect rules

`flui deploy` with no arguments behaves as follows:

- The manifest is `./flui.yaml`.
- For `kind: Application`: the repo is whatever `git remote
  origin` points at, the branch is the current one (from
  `git branch --show-current`).
- The cluster is the only one in the active profile; with
  more than one cluster, pass `-c, --cluster`.

Any of these can be overridden with the corresponding flag.

If there is no `flui.yaml` in the current directory but there
are manifests below it, the command lists them and stops.
Each `flui.yaml` is one deployable application, so it asks
you which one you meant instead of guessing.

## `--name` names an install, not a label

This is the flag most likely to cost you something, so read
it before you use it.

For `kind: Application`, Flui identifies an application by
four things together: the cluster, the repository, the
branch, and the name. That is what lets one repository hold
several applications — a monorepo with one `flui.yaml` per
deployable — and what lets you install the same repository
twice on purpose, once for production and once for a demo.

`--name` sets the fourth part. It is not a display label
over the top of an existing install. It is the install.

Two consequences follow, and both bite in the same way:

- **A new `--name` creates a new application.** It does not
  rename the old one. The first install stays where it is,
  still running, still costing you the same.
- **You must pass it every time.** Flui looks the
  application up before it can read anything stored about
  it, and it looks it up by name. Deploy once with
  `--name api-staging` and then deploy again without it, and
  the lookup misses — so a second application is created
  from the same repository and branch.

When you pass `--name`, the deploy prints it in the header
before anything is submitted. If it is not the one you
expect, stop there.

`--exposure` and `--domain` are the other two install-time
overrides. Those two *are* stored on the application and
re-applied on later deploys, which is what stops somebody
else's `flui deploy` from quietly reverting your install to
whatever the manifest says. Only `--name` has to be repeated.

On a `kind: CatalogApp` install, `--name` is only the
display name. The warning above does not apply there.

## What you type on the command line stays plain text

`--env` is an override, not a vault. Every value you pass
with `--env` or `--env-file` is stored as an ordinary
setting: it is kept as text, and it is shown back to anyone
who can read the application's configuration. A password
passed this way stays a plain value for as long as the
application exists.

`--secret` is how you say otherwise:

```bash
flui deploy --env-file .env --secret DATABASE_URL --secret API_KEY
```

A key named with `--secret` is marked sensitive. Flui hands
it to the application as a secret rather than as plain
configuration, and stops showing it: `flui app env list`
tells you the key is set and never what it holds.

Two details worth knowing:

- `--secret` only accepts a key that this deploy is actually
  passing. Naming a key that `--env` and `--env-file` do not
  declare is an error, not a silent no-op — a typo there
  would otherwise deploy the credential in plain text.
- The deploy prints a warning when a key *looks* like a
  credential (its name contains `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`,
  `TOKEN`, `_KEY` or `PRIVATE`) and is not marked. It is a
  nudge, never a gate; the deploy continues.

`--secret` is carried on `kind: Application` deploys. A
`kind: CatalogApp` install does not send it today, so a
value passed there with `--env` stays a plain value.

### Prefer `--env-file` for anything sensitive

A value written into the command itself goes into your shell
history, and is visible to every other process on the machine
for as long as the command runs. `--env-file` keeps the value
out of the command entirely — the file is read by the CLI and
nothing else sees the arguments.

For a single value on an application that already exists, use
`flui app env set <app> <KEY>` instead. It has no `--value`
flag on purpose: it prompts, or reads standard input, and the
value never appears in the command.

The manifest itself is the other place a variable can be
declared, and it is usually the better one. See
[Environment variables](/cli/environment-variables/).

## `--validate-only` asks two questions now

It used to answer one: *does this file parse and match the
spec*. It still answers that, and it still answers it with
no cluster, no login and no network — that half is the whole
reason it is fast.

But a file can be perfectly well-formed and still have
nowhere to go. So when there is an installation to ask, it
is asked as well:

```bash
flui deploy --validate-only
flui deploy --validate-only --cluster my-cluster
```

The second half reports, in plain rows:

- **Target cluster** — does it exist, is it ready.
- **Source repository** — is that repository connected to
  Flui.
- **Build and registry** — are the credentials the build
  needs in place.
- **Room on the cluster** — measured against the CPU and
  memory this manifest asks for.
- **Where it lands** — whether this deploys onto a workload
  cluster, or onto the control cluster alongside the API and
  the dashboard.
- **What this deploy does** — whether it creates a new
  application or updates an existing one.
- **How it is reached** — the address, and whether the
  pieces behind it are there.

A row can also come back as `unknown`, which means this
installation could not answer that question. An unknown row
never blocks a deploy. A failure to look is not a refusal,
and a check that pretended otherwise would send you
rewriting a manifest that was correct all along.

The second half is skipped, with the reason printed, when
you are not signed in, when no cluster can be resolved, or
when the installation cannot be reached. The output always
says which halves ran — silence would read as "everything
was checked", which is the one thing it must never imply.

Two limits to know: the installation half runs for
`kind: Application` manifests, and it needs the schema to
pass first.

`--json` prints the whole answer — validity, kind, errors,
warnings and the installation half — as one JSON object. The
command exits non-zero when the manifest is invalid or when
the checks say it would not deploy, which makes it usable as
a gate in a script.

`--api-url` points the command at a different API address
than the one in the active profile. It is for testing
against an installation you are running yourself; leave it
alone otherwise.

## Fast iteration

When you change only configuration in `flui.yaml` (variables,
ports, healthcheck, endpoint) and don't need a new image:

```bash
flui deploy --no-build                              # re-deploy the current image
flui deploy --image registry/owner/repo:abc123      # deploy a known-good image
```

`--no-build` skips the build entirely; `--image` lets you pin
a specific image you already trust (rollback, hand-picked
tag).

## How the app is reached

Left alone, Flui reads the cluster setup and gives the app an
address with a certificate:

- with a DNS zone and a wildcard certificate, the app reuses
  the shared wildcard (`dns-01`, no per-app validation);
- otherwise it issues a dedicated per-host certificate
  validated over HTTP (`http-01`).

Override that when you need to:

```bash
flui deploy --cert-challenge http-01              # force a dedicated per-host certificate
flui deploy --cert-provider lets-encrypt-staging  # untrusted test certs, no rate limits
flui deploy --hostname ip                         # a nip.io address instead of a domain
flui deploy --no-tls                              # an address, no certificate
flui deploy --exposure internal                   # no public address at all
```

`--cert-challenge http-01` is the one to reach for when you
want an app to hold its own certificate even though the
cluster has a wildcard available. `--no-tls` is for staying
out of the way of certificate rate limits while you iterate;
the app is served over plain HTTP, so it is not a state to
leave an app in. `--skip-endpoint` skips the address and the
certificate altogether — you can set them later from the app.

`--exposure internal` is a different thing from all of them:
the app gets no public address, other applications on the
cluster can reach it, and you reach it through the dashboard.

These flags work on both manifest kinds. On a `kind:
Application` deploy the same settings also live in your
`flui.yaml` under `domain:` — `hostnameMode`,
`certChallenge`, `certificateProvider` — and the flag wins
over the file:

```yaml
domain:
  auto: true
  tls: true
  certChallenge: http-01      # dedicated per-host certificate
```

When an override contradicts the manifest, the deploy prints
both values rather than quietly winning.

## Single-node clusters and `--allow-master`

An application that asks for a real disk of its own is placed
on a worker, not on the master. On a cluster with no worker
at all, that deploy fails rather than falling back silently.

`--allow-master` is the escape hatch: it lets such an app
land on the master anyway. It is there for the genuinely
small case — a single-node cluster, or a deliberate decision
to keep one app on the control plane. The default is the
safe one.

The flag is carried on a `kind: CatalogApp` install. See
[Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/).

## Deploys made by an agent

Typing `flui deploy` yourself is never paused. A deploy asked
for by an agent is: the call stops and becomes a question for
a person to answer. Checking a manifest does not ask, because
nothing is happening. See
[The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

## `flui catalog validate <file>...`

Validates one or more `flui.yaml` manifests against the Flui
spec. Read-only, and entirely local: nothing is deployed,
nothing on a cluster is touched, no login is needed.

```bash
flui catalog validate ./flui.yaml
flui catalog validate ./catalog/vaultwarden.flui.yaml ./catalog/memos.flui.yaml
```

`<file>...` is repeatable: pass several manifests in one
shot. The validator covers both `kind: CatalogApp` (full
schema check) and `kind: Application` (lighter checks — some
fields are populated by the build pipeline so they are not
required at validation time). It exits non-zero if any file
fails.

This is the file half on its own, for several files at once.
`flui deploy --validate-only` is the one to use when you want
the installation half too.

sections.title: Dev tools
sections.body:
The `dev` topic groups two helpers aimed at Flui contributors who run
the `flui.api` repo on their workstation against a real, remote
cluster. They write to local files in the source repos and open
network tunnels back to cluster services — they do not deploy or
operate applications.

If you are not a Flui contributor and you only want to deploy and
manage applications, you do not need this topic. The everyday surface
is [`flui deploy`](/cli/deploy/) plus [`flui app *`](/cli/applications/).

## `flui dev creds`

Writes the cluster's secrets (database password, queue password, JWT
signing key, encryption key, SSH CA) into `<apiPath>/.env.local` so a
locally-running API process can read them. `.env.local` is meant to
be git-ignored by the source repo.

```bash
flui dev creds
flui dev creds --dry-run                       # show what would be written
flui dev creds --api-path ../flui.api          # one-off override
flui dev creds --no-backup                     # don't back up the existing file
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--api-path <path>` | Override the `apiPath` preference for this run. |
| `--[no-]backup` | Back up the existing `.env.local` before overwriting keys. Default: on. |
| `--dry-run` | Print which keys would be written without touching the file. |
| `--save` | Persist any prompted preference into the active profile. |

Pair with `flui dev tunnel` to expose the matching services on
localhost; without that, the secrets are there but nothing on
`localhost:5432` etc. answers.

## `flui dev tunnel`

Opens SSH tunnels from your workstation to the in-cluster services
the local API needs to talk to. The command stays in the foreground —
CTRL-C closes every forward at once.

```bash
flui dev tunnel                                # default set of forwards
flui dev tunnel --ports postgres,redis         # narrower set
flui dev tunnel --ports postgres,redis,kube-api,grafana
flui dev tunnel --no-retry                     # exit on disconnect
flui dev tunnel --no-kill-local                # don't reclaim local ports
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--ports <list>` | `postgres,redis,kube-api,vmsingle,loki` | Comma-separated forwards. Available: `postgres`, `redis`, `kube-api`, `grafana`, `vmsingle`, `loki`. |
| `--[no-]retry` | on | Auto-reconnect if the SSH session drops. |
| `--[no-]kill-local` | on | Kill any local process bound to the requested ports before opening the tunnel. |

## Typical local-dev flow

```bash
flui env export-config --api-path ../flui.api      # 1. endpoints into .env
flui dev creds --api-path ../flui.api              # 2. secrets into .env.local
flui dev tunnel --ports postgres,redis,kube-api    # 3. open the tunnels

# in another terminal
cd ../flui.api && pnpm run start:dev               # 4. run the API locally
```

The four steps map roughly to "tell the API where the cluster is",
"give it the credentials to talk to it", "open the network paths",
and "start it". Once the loop is set up, only `dev tunnel` typically
needs to run continuously; the other two are run on cluster changes.

sections.title: Environment variables
sections.body:
Nearly everything the CLI needs, it already has: the active
profile knows the API to talk to, the vault holds the
credentials, the config holds your preferences. The
`FLUI_*` variables exist for the moments when that is not
true — a script, a pipeline, a one-off run against a
different installation — and for the values you would
rather not type where your shell will remember them.

All of them are **optional**. The CLI works without any.

For most values the cascade is:

```
explicit CLI flag
  >  env var
  >  ./flui.config.json in this directory
  >  active profile value
  >  schema default
```

`flui config show` prints each preference next to the layer
it came from, which is the fastest way to answer "why is
this value what it is".

Two variables do **not** follow that order, and both are
called out below.

## Profile and API targeting

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_PROFILE` | Which profile this one command talks to. Order: `FLUI_PROFILE` → the `~/.flui/context` file → `default`. |
| `FLUI_API_KEY` | The API key to send. Checked **before** the profile, so it wins over the stored one. |
| `FLUI_API_URL` | The API to talk to **when the profile has none**. See the caution below. |

`FLUI_API_URL` is a fallback, not an override. If the
active profile has an API URL saved, that URL is used and
the variable is ignored. To point an existing profile
somewhere else, change the profile
(`flui config set api-url …`) or use a different one with
`FLUI_PROFILE`.

`FLUI_API_KEY` is the opposite: it is read first, and it is
read as plain text. That means a command using it does not
need the [vault](/cli/profiles-and-config/) open, which is
what makes it the variable pipelines actually use.

## Preferences

These four mirror the preferences in the layered config, so
you can override a stored value without running
`flui config set`. See
[Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) for the
full resolution model.

| Variable | Preference | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLUI_EMAIL` | `email` | Contact email for Let's Encrypt and operational notifications. Required — there is no default. |
| `FLUI_CERTIFICATE_MODE` | `certificateMode` | One of `production` (the default), `staging`, `preflight` — see [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/). |
| `FLUI_API_PATH` | `apiPath` | Path to the local `flui-core` repo. Only relevant to contributors using `env export-config` / `dev creds`. |
| `FLUI_DASHBOARD_PATH` | `dashboardPath` | Path to the local `flui-dashboard` repo. Same scope as `apiPath`. |

Preferences are not secrets. They are stored in plain text,
and reading or writing one never asks for the vault.

## The vault

The vault seals every stored credential behind a passphrase
you type once per session. Three variables touch it, and
none of them is a passphrase — the passphrase is only ever
prompted for, or piped in with `--stdin`.

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_PROFILE_KEY` | Hands the CLI a profile key directly: 32 bytes, base64. No vault is consulted. |
| `FLUI_VAULT_IDLE_MINUTES` | How long an unlocked vault stays open with nothing happening. Default `30`. |
| `FLUI_VAULT_MAX_MINUTES` | How long it stays open at all, however busy you were. Default `480`. |

`FLUI_PROFILE_KEY` is the escape hatch for a caller with no
terminal *and* no home directory that outlives the run — a
provisioning worker, for example. Generate one with
`openssl rand -base64 32`. The key then lives only in
whatever started the CLI: when that caller forgets it,
anything the run sealed stops being openable. A value that
is present but malformed is an error, never a quiet
fallback to the vault.

The two timers are read in whole minutes. Anything that is
not a positive whole number falls back to the default, so a
typo can neither make a session permanent nor make it
useless.

## Installing on a machine you own

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_SSH_PASSWORD` | The host password for `flui env create --host`, so an unattended run can authorize its key. |

When you install onto a machine you already have, Flui
needs to get an SSH key onto it. If a key that already
works is found, nothing else happens and this variable is
never used. If none is, Flui authorizes one — and that
takes the host password once.

Interactively you are asked for it. In a pipeline nobody is
there to answer, so `flui env create` also accepts
`--ssh-password`. Prefer the variable: a flag lands in your
shell history and in the process list, where anyone on the
machine can read it.

The password is used in memory to append the public key to
the host, and nothing else. It is never written down, and
every step after that uses the key.

```bash
FLUI_SSH_PASSWORD='…' flui env create \
  --host 203.0.113.10 --non-interactive
```

See
[installing on a machine you already own](/cli/environments/#installing-on-a-machine-you-already-own)
for the rest of that flow.

## S3 credentials

Read by `flui app backup create` and
`flui app backup delete` when `--access-key` /
`--secret-key` are not passed inline.

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY` | Default S3 access key for app-level backups. |
| `FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY` | Default S3 secret key for app-level backups. |

Same reasoning as the host password: passing a secret as a
flag leaves it in your history.

## Identity provider session token

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN` | Bearer token used by `flui auth generate-api-key` to mint a key. |

For automation that already obtained a session token out of
band, instead of running `flui auth login` with a browser.

## Running with nobody watching

A command that stops to ask a question is fine at your
terminal and fatal in a pipeline: with no answer coming, it
does not fail, it *hangs* — holding whatever it had already
created.

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_NON_INTERACTIVE` | Set to exactly `1`. Every would-be prompt becomes an immediate error naming the flag that would have answered it. |
| `FLUI_EVENTS_FD` | A file descriptor number (above 2) to receive progress from `flui env create` as one JSON object per line. |

`FLUI_NON_INTERACTIVE=1` is the variable form of the
`--non-interactive` flag that `flui env create` and
`flui env scrub` carry. It also reaches the prompts in
`flui app env set`, `flui vault init` and
`flui vault unlock`.

`FLUI_EVENTS_FD` is for a program wrapping the CLI rather
than a person reading it. Milestones go to that descriptor,
so the spinner, the colours and the streamed install log on
your terminal stay exactly as they are.

## Working on Flui itself

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_RELEASE_FILE` | Path to a JSON file overriding which build gets installed. Without it, the CLI looks for `flui.release.json` in the current directory. |

An install pins every component to the release the CLI
shipped with. This file overrides any part of that pin —
how a development or staging build gets installed. Fields
you leave out stay pinned.

## Examples

```bash
# Run one command against another profile, without
# switching the active one
FLUI_PROFILE=staging flui app list

# Talk to an installation with a key from the environment,
# vault untouched
FLUI_API_KEY=… flui app list

# Override the certificate mode for one run
FLUI_CERTIFICATE_MODE=staging flui env export-config --dry-run

# Back an app up to S3 with credentials from the environment
FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY=… FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY=… \
  flui app backup create my-app \
  --bucket archive --endpoint https://s3.example.com
```

sections.title: Environments
sections.body:
The `env` topic owns the lifecycle of the **control
cluster** — the Flui cluster that runs the platform itself:
API, dashboard, identity provider, and observability
backend. Workload clusters (the ones that host user
applications) are managed via
[Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/).

> `env destroy` permanently deletes the control cluster
> and all its data. To delete a workload cluster, use
> `flui cluster destroy` — never `env destroy`.

For the walkthrough — the first install, and the ways back
when a run does not finish — see
[Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/). This page is
the reference.

## Provisioning

### `flui env create`

The single command that brings the control cluster up.
Interactive when provider credentials or admin email are
missing (see [Getting started](/cli/getting-started/) for
the first-run experience).

```bash
flui env create                       # all defaults, streams provisioning live
flui env create --node-size cx32      # pick a specific server size
flui env create --node-count 2        # add two worker nodes
flui env create --region fsn1         # pin a region
flui env create --acme-staging        # use Let's Encrypt staging
flui env create -d                    # detached: queue and exit
flui env create --wait                # block with a single spinner instead of streaming logs
```

The available **node sizes and region codes are
provider-specific** — a code that exists on one provider
means nothing on another. To see what each provider offers,
use `flui server-types list`:

```bash
flui server-types list --provider <name>                # all sizes for a provider
flui server-types list --provider <name> --region <r>   # filter by region
flui server-types list --provider <name> --json         # machine-readable
```

If you omit `--node-size` or `--region`, `env create` picks
the provider's recommended default for each, so most users
never need to specify them explicitly.

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-p, --provider` | the profile's configured provider | Cloud provider — see [Getting started](/cli/getting-started/) for the providers supported today. |
| `-r, --region` | provider default | Region code, provider-specific (`flui server-types list --provider <name>` to list). |
| `--node-size` | provider recommended | Server type, provider-specific (`flui server-types list --provider <name>` to list). |
| `--node-count` | `0` | Number of worker nodes (`0` = master-only). |
| `--disk-size` | included with the size | Root disk size in GB. Required for network-storage instance types; optional for types that bundle a local SSD. |
| `--configure-firewall` | `true` | Configure the firewall after creation. |
| `--firewall-ip` | auto-detect | Source IPs / CIDRs allowed by the firewall (comma-separated). |
| `--acme-staging` | `false` | Use Let's Encrypt staging — non-trusted cert, no practical rate limits. |
| `--no-shared-storage` | `false` | Disable Flui shared storage (NFS+fscache). Falls back to dedicated local-disk placement on each node. See [Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/). |
| `--shared-storage-size` | `20` | Size in GB of the master shared-storage volume (only when shared storage is enabled). Minimum: 10. |
| `--ssh-mode` | `ca` | How the cluster is reached while it is built. `ca` enrols this machine's SSH certificate authority on every node and leaves it there. `ephemeral-key` creates no authority at all and uses a throwaway key that is revoked and deleted before the run ends — the cluster is then sealed until its owner runs `flui env adopt`. |
| `--non-interactive` | `false` | Never prompt. A missing answer becomes an error instead of a question — what you want from a script or a runner, where a prompt would hang holding paid resources. |
| `-d, --detached` | `false` | Queue the operation and exit immediately. |
| `--wait` | `false` | Block with a single spinner instead of streaming logs. |
| `--latest` | `false` | Install the rolling development component tags (bootstrap `master`, `:latest` images) instead of the versions pinned to this CLI release. See [`flui version`](/cli/utilities/#flui-version) and [Creating a cluster](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/). |

Default mode streams the cloud-init log of the master live
over SSH — this is the recommended path for interactive use.
`-d` and `--wait` are for scripts/CI and degraded modes
respectively; see [Getting started](/cli/getting-started/)
for the full rationale.

#### Installing on a machine you already own

Pass `--host` and Flui installs over SSH onto a Linux
machine you already have, instead of asking a provider for
one. Nothing else about the command changes.

```bash
flui env create --host 203.0.113.10
flui env create --host box.example.com --user ubuntu --port 2222
```

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--host` | — | Address to install onto. Passing it is what turns this mode on. |
| `--user` | `root` | SSH user on that host. |
| `--port` | `22` | SSH port. |
| `--ssh-key` | reuse, else authorize one | Private key for the host. If omitted, Flui reuses a key that already works, otherwise it authorizes one — asking for the host password once and never storing it. A passphrase-protected key works only when it is loaded in your `ssh-agent`. |
| `--ssh-password` | — | Host password for unattended runs. Prefer the `FLUI_SSH_PASSWORD` variable, so it stays out of your shell history. |
| `--master-public-ip` | `--host` | The address the world should use, when it differs from the one you install over. |
| `--skip-precheck` | `false` | Skip the host readiness check. |
| `--best-effort` | `false` | Continue even when the readiness check reports problems. |

## Status and credentials

### `flui env status`

One-shot status of the control cluster: state (creating /
ready / error / stopped), node count, and any in-flight
operation.

```bash
flui env status
```

### `flui env credentials`

Shows how to sign in: the public addresses of the dashboard
and the API, the bootstrap admin login, and the identity
provider's own console. Secrets are hidden unless you ask
for them. The bootstrap password is meant to be changed the
first time you log in.

```bash
flui env credentials                  # endpoints, secrets hidden
flui env credentials --format json    # machine-readable output
flui env credentials --show-secrets   # include secret values
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--format text\|json` | Output format. Default: `text`. |
| `--show-secrets` | Print secret values in plain text. Prefer `flui dev creds` for local development — it writes them to a file instead of your terminal. |

## Power state

### `flui env stop` / `flui env restart`

Power off the control-cluster servers without deleting their
