volumes, then power them back on. Useful for cutting costs
on idle development installations.

```bash
flui env stop
flui env restart
```

### `flui env destroy`

**Permanently destroys** the control cluster. On a provider,
that means the servers, their attached volumes and the
shared storage are deleted at the provider, and the
environment's private network with them. Data survives only
if an active backup policy already covered it.

It asks you to type the cluster's name back before it
starts, and backs up your local profile first. `--force`
skips the question.

```bash
flui env destroy
flui env destroy --force              # skip the confirmation prompt
```

#### On a machine you own, destroy also cleans the machine

There is nothing to delete at a provider, so the leftovers
would be on the host itself — and a host left dirty cannot
be installed onto again. So on a bring-your-own-server
installation, **destroy tears the host down by default**:
Flui, the cluster runtime and all their data are removed
over SSH, leaving a machine you can install onto again. SSH
trust is kept, precisely so `flui env create --host` can run
a second time.

```bash
flui env destroy                      # de-register and tear the host down
flui env destroy --keep-host          # de-register only, leave the host as it is
flui env destroy --remove-access      # also stop the host trusting Flui at all
flui env destroy --dry-run            # print the teardown script, run nothing
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-f, --force` | Skip the typed confirmation. |
| `--keep-host` | Skip the host teardown. The host stays dirty — a later install on it fails until it is cleaned. |
| `--purge-host` | Ask for the teardown explicitly. It is already the default on your own machine; on a provider-created cluster it is ignored, because the servers are deleted at the provider anyway. |
| `--remove-access` | Full decommission: also removes Flui's SSH certificate trust and its managed key, and re-enables password login, so the host no longer trusts Flui. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the host teardown script without running it or deleting anything. |
| `--host`, `--user`, `--port`, `--ssh-key` | Clean a host when no local record of it survives — an install that half-failed, or a profile that is gone. |

If the host teardown fails, the local records are still
removed and the command says so; clean the machine by hand.

### `flui env reinstall`

Sometimes the server is fine and the installation on top of
it is not. `flui env reinstall` wipes Flui off the existing
server and runs the install again from the start —
**without** deleting the server, its firewall, its network
attachment or its attached shared-storage volume.

Everything *inside* the cluster is lost: your applications,
the database, the dashboard's state. It is the same data
loss as `env destroy`, without losing the machine.

```bash
flui env reinstall
flui env reinstall --dry-run          # print the teardown, run nothing
flui env reinstall --force            # skip the typed confirmation
flui env reinstall --detached         # start it and exit
```

Two limits apply today: it is for clusters Flui provisioned
on a provider, and only single-node ones. On your own
machine the equivalent is `flui env destroy --purge-host`
followed by `flui env create --host` again.

## Capacity and scaling

### `flui env capacity`

Reports the **control cluster's master node** capacity
(allocatable / used / free CPU and memory) and a sorted list
of server-type **upgrade/downgrade candidates with monthly
cost delta**. Use it to plan a `flui env scale-master`
operation — especially when a dedicated workload that has to
run on the master (because the control cluster has no worker
free to take it) doesn't fit on the current size. See
[Storage classes and dedicated
placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/)
for how dedicated apps choose a node.

```bash
flui env capacity
flui env capacity --top 5                # show 5 candidates instead of 10
flui env capacity --direction upgrade    # only larger sizes
flui env capacity --direction downgrade  # only smaller sizes
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--top <n>` | `10` | Maximum number of candidates listed. |
| `--direction` | `all` | Filter candidates: `all`, `upgrade`, or `downgrade`. |

### `flui env scale-master` / `flui env scale-node`

Vertically scale the control cluster's master or a worker
node to a different server type. Planned-maintenance
operations: the cluster stops the node accepting new work,
powers it down, asks the provider to change the type, powers
it back up, re-opens it, and waits for the cluster to report
healthy. Expected downtime ~3–5 minutes — applications
pinned to the node (a dedicated database, for instance) are
unavailable for that window; snapshot them first. See
[Storage classes and dedicated
placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/)
for the conceptual model.

```bash
flui env scale-master                            # auto-pick next upgrade candidate
flui env scale-master --type cpx41               # pick a specific type
flui env scale-node worker-1 --type cpx31        # NAME is positional
flui env scale-node worker-1 --type cx32 --confirm
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-t, --type <name>` | Target server type. If omitted, auto-picks the next-bigger candidate (smallest positive cost delta). |
| `--upgradeDisk` | (Hetzner) Also grow the local OS disk. **One-way**: cannot be reversed by a later downgrade. |
| `--confirm` | Skip the typed confirmation prompt. |

`scale-node` requires the worker name as a positional
argument (`worker-1`, `worker-2`, …); `scale-master` does
not (the master is unambiguous).

### `flui env set-master-protection <on|off|show>`

On a multi-node control cluster, Flui reserves the master
for the control plane so newly scheduled workloads land on
the workers, keeping the node that runs the platform free.
The protection is applied automatically when the cluster
grows past a single node and lifted when it shrinks back;
this command lets you set it explicitly or inspect the
current state. It is best-effort — a failed change never
fails the scaling that triggered it. See [Nodes and cluster
topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/) for the
model.

```bash
flui env set-master-protection show   # report current state
flui env set-master-protection on     # reserve the master (new workloads go to workers)
flui env set-master-protection off    # lift the reservation
```

### `flui env storage`

Shows the status of the cluster's shared storage: the
underlying provider volume, the NFS export, and a summary of
the storage claimed by applications.

```bash
flui env storage
```

### `flui env storage-expand`

Grows the cluster's shared-storage volume on the provider
and extends the filesystem on top over SSH. It runs online
— no downtime, no application restarts — but it is
**one-way**: the providers Flui integrates with let volumes
grow, not shrink.

```bash
flui env storage-expand --size 50              # new size in GB
flui env storage-expand --size 100 --confirm   # skip the typed confirmation
flui env storage-expand                        # defaults to current + 10 GB
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-s, --size <gb>` | New volume size in GB (must be greater than current). Default: current size + 10 GB. |
| `--confirm` | Skip the typed confirmation prompt. |

## Firewall

### `flui env update-firewall`

This command has one job: **manage the list of addresses
allowed to reach SSH**. Its everyday use is the boring one —
your workstation's public IP changed, or another operator
needs in.

```bash
flui env update-firewall                                # replace the list with your current IP
flui env update-firewall --ip 203.0.113.42
flui env update-firewall --ip "203.0.113.0/24,198.51.100.5/32"
flui env update-firewall --add                          # add your current IP, keep the rest
flui env update-firewall --add --ip 203.0.113.42
flui env update-firewall --remove --ip 198.51.100.5/32
flui env update-firewall --list                         # print the list, change nothing
```

Two things about it are worth knowing, because they are what
make it safe to run:

- **It touches only the SSH rule.** Every other rule on the
  firewall is read and written back exactly as it was. A rule
  you added yourself — an extra allowed address, a
  non-standard port — is not affected.
- **It talks to your provider directly**, not through the
  cluster. So it still works when the address it is fixing is
  the one currently locked out, which is the situation you are
  usually in when you run it.

Without `--add` or `--remove`, the list is **replaced** by
what you pass — or by your auto-detected public address when
you pass no `--ip` at all. `--add` and `--remove` edit the
existing list instead, and both accept `--ip` the same way.
`--list` only reads.

The command refuses a change that would leave the list
empty, because that locks everyone out of SSH, and tells you
so instead of doing it. It also declines quietly when there
is nothing to do — an address you are adding that is already
there, one you are removing that was never there.

One case behaves differently: if the cluster has **no
firewall yet**, a plain run creates one from the default
rules — SSH from the addresses you named, ports 80 and 443
open to the world. `--add`, `--remove` and `--list` need a
firewall to exist first.

On a machine you own, there is no provider firewall to
change. The command says so rather than failing, and points
you at the two commands below. SSH is deliberately left
reachable there — see [Firewall as a
policy](/concepts/12-firewalls/) for why.

### `flui env firewall apply` / `flui env firewall status`

The firewall as a whole, rather than just its SSH list.

```bash
flui env firewall apply
flui env firewall status
```

`apply` makes sure a firewall exists — seeding the default
rules if there is none — and then applies it. Everything
inbound is denied except the rules Flui declares. It is
idempotent: re-running it is safe, and re-running it is the
fix for most of what goes wrong here.

`status` reads it back: whether a firewall is configured at
all, the reconciliation state, when it was last applied,
whether it has drifted from the rules Flui wants, and the
rules actually in force. If there is none, it says so
plainly — nothing is filtering inbound traffic — and tells
you to apply one.

Which mechanism enforces the rules is decided by the
provider: a firewall the provider runs in front of the
machine, or a ruleset on the machine itself. The command and
its rules are the same either way.

## Handing an installation over

### `flui env adoption-token`

Issues a one-time token that lets someone take ownership of
this installation from a machine that has never touched it.
It exists for the handoff at the end of a provisioning run
someone did on your behalf, and as the recovery path when
the original token is lost.

```bash
flui env adoption-token
flui env adoption-token --format json
```

Single use, valid for one hour, tied to that one
installation. Anyone holding it can register a certificate
authority there, so treat it like a password.

### `flui env adopt <token>`

Run on the new owner's machine. It asks the installation to
describe itself, writes a local profile pointing at it, and
creates the SSH certificate authority **on this machine** —
so the key that opens those servers is born where it will
live, and whoever built the installation never holds it. The
public half is registered with the installation.

```bash
flui env adopt flui_adopt_eyJlbmRwb2ludCI...
flui env adopt <token> --endpoint https://your-install.example.com
flui env adopt <token> --skip-ca
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--endpoint` | The installation's address. Only needed when the token does not carry one. |
| `--profile` | Profile to write the adopted cluster into. Default: the active profile. |
| `--skip-ca` | Rebuild the local profile only, and leave SSH dormant. The right choice if you only ever use the dashboard. |

> Enrolling the registered key on each node is not
> automatic yet. The command says so when it gets there,
> and points at `flui env repair-ssh-ca`, run from a
> machine that already has SSH access to the nodes.

## Cleaning up after a failed run

### `flui env scrub`

Provisioning creates real, billable things before it
finishes: a server, a firewall, an SSH key. A run that dies
part-way cannot always clean up after itself, and what is
left is a small pile of resources in your provider account
with nothing pointing at them.

`flui env scrub` removes them, working from the JSON
resource list that run reported.

```bash
flui env scrub --ledger ./flui-run.json
cat flui-run.json | flui env scrub --stdin
flui env scrub --ledger ./flui-run.json --delete
```

Without `--delete` it touches nothing: it asks the provider
what actually exists, matches that against the list, and
prints what it would remove. The list decides what to look
for and the provider decides what is really there — anything
not in both is left alone. And if part of the account could
not be listed, it refuses to delete at all, because a blind
spot is not an empty account.

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--ledger <file>` | The resource list the run reported. |
| `--stdin` | Read that list from standard input instead. |
| `-p, --provider` | Look at one provider only. Default: every provider configured in this profile. |
| `--delete` | Actually remove what the plan resolved. |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip the confirmation prompt. |
| `--non-interactive` | Never prompt; fail instead of asking. |

### `flui env orphan-volumes`

The other kind of leftover: Flui-managed provider volumes
left behind by a previous failed `env destroy`. Useful to
recover quota after an incident; safe to run anytime.

```bash
flui env orphan-volumes                       # list orphans (all configured providers)
flui env orphan-volumes --provider hetzner    # scan a single provider
flui env orphan-volumes --cleanup             # detach and delete the listed orphans
flui env orphan-volumes --cleanup --yes       # skip the confirmation prompt
```

## Diagnostics and maintenance

### `flui env logs`

Tails the local log files that the Flui orchestration writes
while it drives an infrastructure operation — cluster
create, node scale, storage expand, destroy, firewall
update, and so on. Each operation produces one file at
`~/.flui/logs/<operationId>.log` on the workstation that ran
the command; this view simply reads from there.

```bash
flui env logs                         # most recent operation
flui env logs --tail 50
flui env logs --list                  # list operations that have logs
flui env logs --operation <id>        # logs for one specific operation
```

This is **not** where to look for runtime cluster logs
(use `flui env inspect`) or application logs
(use `flui app logs`). It is the diagnostic trail of *the
operation the CLI just ran*: what step it was on, what the
provider answered, where it failed.

### `flui env inspect`

Connects to a node over SSH and tails one of its system
logs. Useful when the high-level diagnostics aren't enough
and you need to see what the machine itself is doing.

The default invocation — `flui env inspect` with no flags —
is exactly the same view that `flui env create` streams live
during provisioning (the master's `cloud-init-output` log).
Run it after the fact, or against a different node, when you
need to re-watch what happened or see what is happening now.

```bash
flui env inspect                                  # master, cloud-init-output, last 100 lines
flui env inspect --node worker-1 --log cloud-init
flui env inspect -f --log k3s                     # follow live
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-n, --node` | `master` | Node name (`master`, `worker-1`, …). |
| `-l, --log` | `cloud-init-output` | One of `cloud-init`, `cloud-init-output`, `k3s` (the cluster runtime), `syslog`. |
| `-t, --tail` | `100` | Number of lines to show. |
| `-f, --follow` | — | Follow the log in real time. |

### `flui env cordon` / `flui env uncordon`

`cordon` stops a node accepting new work. What is already
running on it keeps running. Use it before planned
maintenance on a node you are about to touch by hand.

```bash
flui env cordon master
flui env cordon worker-1
flui env uncordon worker-1
```

`uncordon` re-opens the node. It is also the recovery helper
paired with `scale-master` / `scale-node`: those close the
node before resizing it and re-open it afterwards, so an
operation interrupted in the middle — crash, timeout,
network blip — leaves the node closed. This command flips it
back. On a healthy cluster you should never need it; a
successful scale leaves nothing to recover.

Both take the node as a positional argument: `master`, or a
worker's name.

### `flui env force-ready`

Forces the cluster status to `ready` when it is actually
operational but the platform left it stuck in `error` or
`creating` after a transient failure during an async
operation. Recovery helper — use it only after confirming
the cluster really is healthy.

```bash
flui env force-ready
flui env force-ready --skip-health-checks   # bypass health validation
```

### `flui env diag-ca`

Diagnoses the cluster's certificate authority configuration.
The first thing to run when you see TLS or self-signed
certificate errors from the dashboard or the API.

```bash
flui env diag-ca
```

### `flui env refresh-kubeconfig`

Re-fetches the cluster's authentication material from the
master over SSH and refreshes the locally cached copy. Use
it after a manual intervention on the master that may have
rotated the credentials.

```bash
flui env refresh-kubeconfig
```

### `flui env repair-ssh-ca`

Backfills the SSH certificate authority's private key into
the cluster's own secret bundle. Run it on clusters
provisioned before the authority seeding flow was complete —
the symptom is the dashboard's SSH terminal failing with
*"CA private key not available."* The key is read from the
active profile and written into the cluster over SSH; the
Flui API is restarted afterwards unless `--no-restart` is
set.

```bash
flui env repair-ssh-ca
flui env repair-ssh-ca --no-restart        # skip the API restart
flui env repair-ssh-ca --profile <name>    # read the key from another profile
```

### `flui env repair-storage`

Backfills the shared-storage volume id into the cluster's
records, for clusters whose storage entry was left
incomplete by an older install. The symptom is
`flui env storage-expand` reporting no Flui-managed shared
storage volume. After patching, it restarts the Flui API
unless `--no-restart` is passed.

```bash
flui env repair-storage
flui env repair-storage --no-restart
```

## Contributor-only commands

The commands below are not part of the normal operator
workflow. They exist for Flui contributors running the API
and dashboard repos locally against a remote cluster, or for
one-off recovery scenarios that require platform-internal
knowledge. End users can skip this section.

### `flui env sync`

Reads the live endpoint URLs (API, identity provider,
observability) from the cluster and writes them into the API
repo's `.env` and the dashboard's `config.json`, so a local
dev API/dashboard talks to the right remote endpoints.
Read-only on the cluster side; never touches database or
secret material.

```bash
flui env sync
flui env sync --dry-run               # show the diff without writing
flui env sync --debug                 # print the raw cluster discovery output
```

### `flui env export-config`

Writes the control cluster's endpoints (and non-sensitive
defaults) into the `.env` of the API repo, so you can run
the API locally against a remote cluster. Does not write
secrets — use `flui dev creds` for those.

```bash
flui env export-config
flui env export-config --dry-run
flui env export-config --no-backup
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--dry-run` | Show the diff without writing. |
| `--[no-]backup` | Back up an existing `.env`. |
| `--force` | Skip confirmation. |
| `--no-dashboard` | Do not update the dashboard's `config.json`. |
| `--api-path <path>` | One-off override of the `apiPath` preference. |
| `--dashboard-path <path>` | Override `dashboardPath`. |
| `--certificate-mode <mode>` | Override `certificateMode` (`production` / `staging` / `preflight`). |
| `--email <email>` | Override `email`. |
| `--save` | Persist any value entered at the prompt into the active profile. |

sections.title: Getting started with the CLI
sections.body:
This page used to be a walkthrough. It installed the CLI,
provisioned a control cluster, connected GitHub and
deployed an application, all in one sitting. That job now
has a page of its own — [Get Flui
running](/tasks/get-flui-running/) — and keeping a second
copy of it here only guaranteed that one of the two would
go stale.

So this page is about the tool rather than the job: how to
install it, where it keeps your credentials, how you sign
in, and how to read what it says before it says anything
else.

## Install

The CLI is published on npm as `@flui-cloud/cli`. The
command it puts on your path is `flui`.

```bash
npm install -g @flui-cloud/cli   # or pnpm add -g, yarn global add
flui --version
```

`flui update` replaces the global install with the latest
published version. It asks npm what the latest is, tells
you what it found, and asks before installing anything.

Two version numbers matter here, and they are not the same
number. `flui --version` is the CLI's own version. `flui
version` also prints the **platform release** this CLI
pins — the component versions a new installation would be
built from. When an install behaves strangely, the second
number is usually the one worth reading.

`flui --help` lists the topics. There are more than two
hundred commands, grouped into topics — `app`, `env`,
`iam`, `scaling`, `backup`, and so on — and every one of
them answers `--help` with its own flags and examples.
[The topic map](/cli/) is the shortest way in.

## The vault comes first

The CLI stores things you would not want read: provider
tokens, and the API key that *is* your account. Those were
always encrypted. The problem was where the key lived — in
the same directory as the data it protected. That is a
label, not a lock.

So the key now comes from a passphrase you know and the
machine does not keep. That is the **vault**, and it is
the first thing to set up, before you store a single
credential.

```bash
flui vault init      # once per machine
flui vault unlock    # once per session
flui vault status    # open? and for how long?
flui vault lock      # close it now
```

`flui vault init` asks for a passphrase and suggests a
five-word one you can accept with enter. It suggests words
for a reason: the passphrase is not stored anywhere and
cannot be reset, so it has to be one you can write down
and reproduce. Losing it means losing every credential
this machine has sealed. `init` refuses to overwrite a
vault that already exists, for exactly the same reason.

There is **one vault per machine** — the header lives at
`~/.flui/vault.json` — but not one key. Each profile gets
its own key, derived from your passphrase and that
profile's name. A command working in one profile cannot
open another profile's stored credentials, even though
both were sealed under the same passphrase.

After `unlock`, a small background helper holds the key
for the session and hands it to commands that ask for it.
Nothing is written to disk. It closes after thirty minutes
of inactivity, and after eight hours no matter how busy
you were. The first limit makes the vault comfortable; the
second stops that comfort becoming permanent.

A locked vault is not an error on its own. Most commands
read a preference or an API address, which are plain text,
and never ask for anything. Only a command that actually
opens a stored credential stops — and when it stops it
says the vault is closed and names `flui vault unlock`,
rather than reporting a decryption failure that would send
you looking for corrupt data.

If you are upgrading from a CLI that predates the vault,
nothing is lost. A profile still holding the old key file
is read exactly as before, and the first `flui vault
unlock` re-seals it under the vault and removes the old
file.

For scripted setup, both `flui vault init` and `flui
config set` take `--stdin` and read the value from
standard input:

```bash
printf 'my passphrase' | flui vault init --stdin
flui config set hetzner --stdin
```

That is not decoration. A value passed as a command
argument is visible to every process on the machine
through the process list, which is not acceptable for a
credential on a shared host.

## Signing in

Flui authenticates against the identity provider that runs
**inside your own installation**. There is no Flui account
anywhere else. That has one practical consequence: `flui
auth login` works only once there is an installation to
sign in to, and the active profile knows its address.

```bash
flui auth login                     # opens a browser
flui auth login --headless          # prints the URL instead
flui auth login --key-name my-laptop
```

The CLI opens your browser, runs a standard
code-with-PKCE sign-in against that identity provider,
and uses the result to mint a long-lived API key which it
saves in the active profile. Every later command uses that
key without asking again. The CLI never sees a password.

By default the sign-in shows the account picker, so you
confirm which user you are about to mint a key for.
`--prompt login` forces a fresh authentication; `--prompt
''` reuses the browser session silently.

**The key `login` mints is unscoped.** It carries your
full weight, because that is what signing in means.
Narrower keys are minted deliberately, and that is the
next section.

### When the browser is somewhere else

The CLI waits for the redirect on `http://localhost:8899`,
falling back through 8900, 8901, 8902 and 8910, and gives
up after two minutes. It listens on the loopback address
only.

On a machine with no browser, `--headless` prints the URL
so you can open it elsewhere — but printing it is not
enough on its own. The redirect still has to reach the
listener on the machine running the CLI, so forward the
port from wherever the browser is:

```bash
ssh -L 8899:localhost:8899 your-server
```

## A key has to say what it is for

`flui auth generate-api-key` mints a key without a
browser — for CI, for a script, for an agent. It used to
accept no scopes at all, and saying nothing quietly meant
*everything*. The widest credential the installation can
issue should never be what you get by not finishing a
sentence, so it is now refused:

```bash
flui auth generate-api-key --name ci --unscoped
flui auth generate-api-key --name agent \
  --scope mcp:app:read --scope mcp:obs:read
```

Naming neither `--scope` nor `--unscoped` stops the
command before anything else happens — before it needs a
token, a profile or a network — with a message naming the
two choices. `--unscoped` gives the key your full weight.
`--scope` gives it a ceiling; repeat the flag for more
than one.

A scope you do not hold yourself is refused whole, never
trimmed down to what happens to be allowed. A credential
that quietly comes back smaller than you asked for is one
nobody can reason about afterwards.

The command needs a session token from the identity
provider, passed as `--token <jwt>` or in
`FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN`. `--expires <days>` sets an expiry;
leave it out for a key that does not expire.

**There is no `--groups` flag.** The readable permission
groups — "deploy and operate applications", "operate the
infrastructure" — are a dashboard and API idea today. From
the terminal you name raw scopes. If you are minting a key
for an agent, [Choose what your agent may
do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/) explains what
each group covers and where to mint it.

A key is stored as a digest. The full value is printed
once, when it is created, and nothing on the installation
can hand it back afterwards. What you can do later is see
what exists and take one away:

```bash
flui auth api-keys              # name, state, scopes
flui auth api-keys -o json
flui auth revoke-api-key <id>   # stops working immediately
```

## The context banner

One workstation can drive several installations. The worst
mistake that arrangement allows is a command that worked
perfectly — on the wrong one.

So the commands that act on an installation as a whole
print a line before their output, naming where they are
about to act:

```
┌─ context production · api https://api.example.com
```

`context` is the active profile. `api` is the installation
that profile points at — or a yellow `(not set)`, which is
the normal state of a profile you have just created and
not yet pointed at anything. Some commands add the target
cluster's provider and region on the same line.

Not every command prints it. Today it is on the families
whose reach is the installation itself — `env`, `backup`,
`migrate`, `dns`, `catalog` and a few more. Elsewhere,
`flui context show` names the active profile.

## Profiles on disk

A **profile** is one installation as this machine sees it:
its API address, its credentials, its local view of what
that installation holds. Everything the CLI keeps lives
under `~/.flui`:

```
~/.flui/
├── context              # the name of the active profile
├── vault.json           # the vault header, one per machine
└── profiles/
    ├── default/
    └── production/
```

Each profile directory holds:

- `config.json` — your preferences in plain text, plus the
  sealed values: the provider credentials you stored and
  the API key `auth login` saved.
- `ca/` — the trust material this profile uses to reach
  cluster nodes.
- `clusters.json`, `nodes.json`, `firewalls.json`,
  `vnets.json`, `operations.json` — a local copy of what
  the installation last told the CLI. Safe to delete; the
  next command that needs them fetches them again.

The directories and files are created readable by their
owner only.

Moving between profiles is local and instant. Nothing in
any cluster notices; the CLI simply reads a different
directory from then on.

```bash
flui context list                    # every profile, active marked *
flui context show                    # just the active name
flui context create staging --switch # create it and switch
flui context use default             # switch back
flui context delete staging          # asks first; -f skips
```

`default` is created on first run and cannot be deleted.
Names accept letters, digits, hyphens and underscores.
`FLUI_PROFILE` overrides the active profile for one
command without switching.

Nothing operational crosses between profiles. The provider
token you saved in one is not visible from another, and
the keys that seal them are different keys. A command
typed in the wrong profile cannot reach into another
installation, because it simply does not hold the
credentials to.

If you only ever run one installation from this machine,
the auto-created `default` profile is enough and none of
this needs your attention.

## Where to go next

- [Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/) — the first
  installation, step by step, including the case where you
  are taking over one somebody else provisioned.
- [Deploy an application](/tasks/deploy-an-application/) —
  including the one-off GitHub and registry connections
  the first source-built deploy needs.
- [Multi-context](/concepts/07-multi-context-cli/) — why
  one workstation driving several installations is a
  different problem from one installation driving several
  clusters.
- [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) — the
  layered configuration, provider credentials, and the
  full profile reference.
- [Authentication](/cli/authentication/) — the login flags
  and the environment variables that override the active
  key.
- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/) — what to
  do with a scoped key once you have minted one.

sections.title: CLI Reference
sections.body:
A Flui installation has three surfaces: this CLI, the
dashboard, and the API both of them call. The CLI is the one
that exists first. When you create the control cluster there
is no dashboard yet — the dashboard runs *on* the control
cluster — so the first command is always typed here.

After that the three surfaces mostly do the same work. Which
one you reach for is a matter of taste, not capability. But
the overlap is not total, in both directions:

- **Only the CLI** creates and destroys the control cluster
  (`flui env create`, `flui env destroy`), holds the vault
  that protects credentials on your own machine
  (`flui vault`), takes over an installation somebody else
  provisioned (`flui env adopt`), and clears the provider
  resources an abandoned provisioning run left behind
  (`flui env scrub`). Those last three all work from what is
  stored on your own machine — the vault, the profile, the
  provider credentials — which is not somewhere a browser can
  reach. `flui env scrub` does not even call the API: it goes
  straight to the provider, because the installation it would
  have asked was never finished.
- **Only the dashboard and the API** answer an agent's paused
  write. When an agent asks for something that stops to ask a
  person, the person answers in the dashboard or against the
  API; there is no `flui` command for it. Minting an agent key
  by permission group is the same story —
  `flui auth generate-api-key` takes raw scopes or
  `--unscoped`, and has no group flag.

This page is a map of what exists. For *how* to do a
particular job — deploy an app, open a database, connect an
agent — see the [task pages](/tasks/), which show the same
job on each surface that can do it.

## How the CLI is organised

Commands are grouped into **topics** — `app`, `env`,
`backup`, `iam`, and so on. Each topic owns a set of verbs
that act on the same kind of thing: `flui app logs`,
`flui env create`, `flui iam grant add`.

Some topics group their verbs one level deeper, when the
topic covers more than one kind of object:
`flui backup policy list`, `flui migrate db create`,
`flui gateway routes add`.

Every command has `--help`, which prints its usage, its
flags and its examples. `flui <topic> --help` lists the verbs
in that topic, and `flui --help` lists every topic. That
built-in help is generated from the CLI itself, so it is
never out of date — when this page and `--help` disagree,
`--help` is right.

## Topics

| Topic | What it does | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app` | Everything about a running application: status, logs, metrics, HTTP traffic, alerts and crash reports; scale, restart, stop and start; releases, image versions and redeploys; volume snapshots and backups; scheduled jobs; variables; delete. | [Applications](/cli/applications/) |
| `auth` | Sign in through the browser, mint and revoke API keys, and list the keys you hold. | [Authentication](/cli/authentication/) |
| `backup` | Backup destinations, scheduled policies, on-demand jobs and restores, plus the platform's own backup setup. | [Backups](/cli/backups/) |
| `catalog` | List what this installation can install, install it, check how an install is going, and validate a manifest. | [Deploy](/cli/deploy/) |
| `cluster` | List every cluster, destroy a workload cluster, and list storage left behind by applications that no longer exist. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `config` | Layered configuration: preferences, and the provider credentials the CLI keeps encrypted. | [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) |
| `context` | Profiles — create, list, switch and delete the installations this workstation talks to. | [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) |
| `db` | Reach a Flui database from your machine: credentials, a local tunnel, dumps and restores, disk usage, continuous-backup state, point-in-time restore. | [Databases](/cli/databases/) |
| `demo` | The self-running cross-provider migration demonstration an installation can perform on itself. | `flui demo --help` |
| `dev` | Helpers for people working on Flui itself, not for operating an installation. | [Dev tools](/cli/dev-tools/) |
| `dns` | The zones a cluster publishes under, the single wildcard record that covers all of its applications, and second-provider replicas. | `flui dns --help` |
| `env` | The control cluster's whole life: create, status, capacity, storage, scale, firewall, stop and restart, reinstall, adopt, scrub, destroy. | [Environments](/cli/environments/) |
| `gateway` | Named routes at the edge of an application, and the policies on them: sign-in, rate limits, IP allowlists. | `flui gateway --help` |
| `iam` | Who can reach what: grants, groups, the built-in roles, your own effective permissions, and the policy file. | `flui iam --help` |
| `integration` | Connect GitHub for the installation and for your own account, and manage the token used to pull images. | [Integrations](/cli/integrations/) |
| `mail` | Connect mail providers, register sending domains, check what still blocks a message, send, and read delivery outcomes and suppressions. | `flui mail --help` |
| `migrate` | Move a database, an application, or both together, to another cluster — create, cut over, abort, destroy the source. | `flui migrate --help` |
| `node` | Add worker nodes, join a machine you already own, list them, remove them. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `operating-context` | Write down how this installation is run, so people and agents read it before acting. | `flui operating-context --help` |
| `repo` | Connect, list and disconnect the repositories this installation can deploy from. | [Integrations](/cli/integrations/) |
| `sandbox` | The guest areas of a demonstration installation: what is being held, and ending one now. | `flui sandbox --help` |
| `scaling` | What a cluster may buy for itself and where it must stop, what it decided, and what it would decide right now. | `flui scaling --help` |
| `server-types` | The machine sizes a provider offers. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `showcase` | Publish an application to the showcase — the short list this installation puts in front of other people — or take it back out. | `flui showcase --help` |
| `template` | Start a new repository from a Flui framework template. | [Templates](/cli/templates/) |
| `vault` | The passphrase that protects the credentials this CLI stores on your machine. | [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) |

Five commands sit at the top level, outside any topic:

| Command | What it does | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flui deploy` | Deploy an application from a `flui.yaml` manifest. | [Deploy](/cli/deploy/) |
| `flui reconcile` | Bring the CLI's local DNS state back in line with the API. | [Utilities](/cli/utilities/) |
| `flui ssh` | Open a shell on a cluster node. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `flui update` | Update the CLI itself. | [Utilities](/cli/utilities/) |
| `flui version` | The CLI version, and the platform release it pins. | [Utilities](/cli/utilities/) |

Where the "read more" column says `--help`, there is no
hand-written page for that topic yet. The command's own help
is the reference.

## Common conventions

A handful of flags recur across the CLI. Once you know them,
most commands behave the way you expect.

- **`-c, --cluster <name|id>`** — pick the target cluster on
  the commands that act on one. When the installation has a
  single cluster, it is detected for you.
- **`-o, --output <format>`** — switch between human and
  machine-readable output. The exact set varies by command,
  but `json` is there for scripting; the human format is
  `table` or `text` depending on the command's shape.
- **`--no-wait` / `--detach`** — on commands that start long
  work, return as soon as the job is queued instead of
  blocking until it finishes.
- **`-f, --force` / `-y, --yes`** — skip the confirmation on
  a destructive command.
- **`--dry-run`** — on a subset of commands, print what
  *would* happen and change nothing.

Commands that talk to the API print a short **context
banner** first — the active profile and the API URL — so it
is always clear which installation you are operating on.

## Profiles on disk

The CLI keeps each installation's state under
`~/.flui/profiles/<name>/`. A profile holds the API key, the
provider credentials, the SSH trust root used to reach
cluster nodes, and the local view of clusters, nodes,
firewalls and operations that installation knows about.
The active profile is named in `~/.flui/context`, and
`FLUI_PROFILE` overrides it for one command.

Credentials in a profile are protected by a **vault** at
`~/.flui/vault.json`. One vault covers every profile: you
choose the passphrase once with `flui vault init`, open it
for a session with `flui vault unlock`, and close it with
`flui vault lock`. Profiles still get their own derived
keys, so two accounts stay apart behind one passphrase.

Switching between installations is `flui context use <name>`
away; every command afterwards targets the new profile
without being told.

sections.title: Integrations and repositories
sections.body:
Source-built applications (`kind: Application`) need three things on a
fresh installation before the first deploy:

1. The **GitHub integration** configured on the installation — once by
   the operator. Two modes are supported: a **GitHub App** (recommended)
   or a **Personal Access Token**.
2. Your own **user connection** to GitHub — once per Flui user. In App
   mode you install the App on your account/org; in PAT mode you paste
   your own classic PAT.
3. The specific **repository** imported into your Flui account.

Two CLI topics cover it, and they answer different
questions.

**`flui integration …` — is Flui connected to GitHub?**
[`setup github`](#flui-integration-setup-github) and
[`reset github`](#flui-integration-reset-github) are the
operator's once-per-installation commands.
[`connect github`](#flui-integration-connect-github) is the
once-per-user one.
[`status github`](#flui-integration-status-github) and
[`list`](#flui-integration-list) say where you stand, and
[`ghcr-pat set|status|revoke`](#ghcr-pat-app-mode-only)
manages the credential that pulls the images Flui builds.

**`flui repo connect | list | disconnect` — which
repositories may be deployed?** This is a separate step, and
it is the one people forget. Connecting GitHub gives Flui
permission to see your repositories; it does not import any
of them. A repository has to be connected before
`flui deploy` will touch it, and disconnecting it stops
future deploys without touching anything on GitHub. Three
commands, no more: see [Repositories](#repositories).

The dashboard exposes the same flows under
*Apps → Repositories → GitHub setup*. CatalogApps (`kind: CatalogApp`)
skip every step — they pull a pre-built image from a public registry,
with no source repo on the install side.

## Choosing a mode

| | GitHub App | Personal Access Token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity used to talk to GitHub | Bot identity owned by the App | Your own user |
| Per-user setup | Install the App on your account / org | Paste a classic PAT |
| Can register webhooks | Yes, with the App | Yes, the PAT grants `admin:repo_hook` |
| Org policies that block PATs | Unaffected | May block the PAT entirely |
| Container registry (GHCR) | Needs a separate per-user PAT (see [GHCR PAT](#ghcr-pat-app-mode-only)) | The same PAT covers cloning *and* pulling images |
| Recommended for | Teams, multi-user installations | Single-user / self-hosted dev |

GitHub App is the recommended path. The PAT mode is an escape hatch
for solo deployments and environments where creating a GitHub App is
impractical.

One row on that table used to promise more than it does.
Webhooks are still registered, and this page used to call
that row "webhooks for deploy-on-push", as though having
them was what made a push go live. It is not, and it has not
been for a while — see
[A push does not redeploy on its own](#a-push-does-not-redeploy-on-its-own).

## A push does not redeploy on its own

The webhook itself has not changed. GitHub still calls Flui
back when a build finishes, in both App mode and PAT mode.
What changed is what Flui does with that call.

An application's **first** deploy is never affected by this
— it always goes live once the build succeeds, the same as
before.

For an application that is already running, a later push
only redeploys automatically if that application has
**auto-deploy on push** turned on. By default it does not.
Otherwise the finished build is recorded as an available
image and nothing rolls out. `flui app versions <app>`
marks that image `unreleased`, and you deploy it yourself
with `flui app redeploy <app> <target>` (a tag, a digest, or
`--build <id>`) — see
[Release management](/cli/applications/#release-management)
in the applications reference.

This is a per-application setting, not an installation-wide
one, and today there is no `flui` flag to turn it on or off
— it is set through the API. If you were relying on "push
means deploy" for an app that predates this change, it has
stopped, and the push is not silently failing: check
`flui app versions` for an unreleased build waiting on you.

## Setup (operator, once per installation)

### `flui integration setup github`

Interactive setup that walks the operator through either mode end to
end. Admin-only.

```bash
flui integration setup github
flui integration setup github --headless     # print URLs instead of opening a browser
```

If the integration is already configured the command asks before
overwriting — use `flui integration reset github` first if you want a
clean slate.

#### GitHub App branch (recommended)

The command builds a [GitHub App manifest](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/sharing-github-apps/registering-a-github-app-from-a-manifest),
opens GitHub with the App name and all the permissions pre-filled, and
waits for you to confirm. As soon as you click *Create*, GitHub
redirects back to the API, which exchanges the temporary code for the
final App credentials and stores them automatically.

You will be asked for:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| App name | Must be unique across GitHub. Defaults to `flui-<hostname>`. |
| Flui public URL | Base URL of this Flui API as reachable from `github.com`. Callback, manifest redirect and (if enabled) webhook URL are all derived from this. For local development behind a tunnel, use the tunnel URL. |
| Enable webhooks for deploy-on-push? | Off by default. Turn on if you want a push to trigger a deploy. |
| Allow install on other accounts / organizations? | Off by default (only the owner account can install). Turn on if Flui needs repos under multiple accounts or orgs. |

After confirmation the credentials (App ID, slug, Client ID, Client
Secret, Webhook Secret, private-key PEM) are persisted in Flui — no
copy-paste required.

#### Personal Access Token branch

The command opens GitHub's token-creation page pre-filled with the
required scopes, then validates the token against GitHub before saving
it. The validator surfaces missing scopes inline so you know exactly
what to re-check.

Scopes requested:

- `repo` — clone and push private repositories
- `workflow` — commit `.github/workflows/flui.yml` on first deploy
- `user:email` — identify the user
- `admin:repo_hook` — register webhooks for deploy-on-push
- `write:packages`, `read:packages`, `delete:packages` — push, pull,
  and clean up images on GHCR

The same token covers both the repository side and the GHCR side —
there is no separate GHCR step in PAT mode.

Classic PATs only — fine-grained PATs cannot grant `admin:repo_hook`
yet, which Flui needs to register webhooks.

### Equivalent dashboard flow

Open *Apps → Repositories → GitHub setup* in the dashboard for the
same two-card picker (App via manifest, or PAT). The dashboard polls
the API in the same way and the resulting configuration is identical.
A "I already have a GitHub App" disclosure under the App card lets you
plug in pre-existing App credentials instead of running the manifest
flow.

## User connection

### `flui integration connect github`

In App mode, opens the browser to install the Flui GitHub App on your
account or org and waits for the local callback. The same round-trip
also performs the OAuth grant your user needs to commit
`.github/workflows/flui.yml` on first deploy.

```bash
flui integration connect github
flui integration connect github --headless     # print URL instead of opening a browser
```

If the integration is not configured yet, the command exits with a
friendly hint pointing at `flui integration setup github` instead of
the raw API error.

In **PAT mode** this command currently targets the App install
endpoint and therefore reports the integration as not configured. The
operator's own PAT is saved at setup time; additional users in PAT
mode connect their token from the dashboard wizard
(*Apps → Repositories → GitHub setup* → PAT card).

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--headless` | Print the install URL instead of opening one. Useful over SSH. |

The callback uses the same port range as `flui auth login` (8899,
falling back through 8900–8910).

### `flui integration list`

Lists the third-party integrations configured for your account and
whether each is currently connected. Includes the GHCR PAT state in
App mode.

```bash
flui integration list
```

Only `github` is supported today; the topic is shaped to accept more
providers later.

## Status and health

### `flui integration status github`

Shows the active mode (App or PAT), runs a live health check against
GitHub, and prints your own user connection state.

```bash
flui integration status github
```

Sample output (App mode):

```
  Instance configuration
    Mode:          github_app
    App slug:      flui-acme
    Health:        ✔ App auth ok — 2 installations
```

Sample output (PAT mode):

```
  Instance configuration
    Mode:          pat
    Health:        ✔ PAT mode enabled (per-user credentials)

  Your connection
    Authenticated: @dawit-io
    Scopes:        repo user:email admin:repo_hook write:packages …
```

When the health check fails (App deleted on GitHub, credentials
revoked, network unreachable…) the output flags it and the dashboard
shows a banner with the same information.

## Reset

### `flui integration reset github`

Removes the instance-wide GitHub configuration plus every per-user
token and App installation Flui has on file. Useful when switching
modes (App ↔ PAT) or starting over after a bad registration. Admin-only.

```bash
flui integration reset github             # type "reset" to confirm
flui integration reset github --yes       # skip the confirmation (CI / scripts)
```

The App on `github.com` is **not** uninstalled — uninstall it there
separately if you want to clean up the GitHub side too.

After reset, run `flui integration setup github` to configure a fresh
integration. Users will need to reconnect.

## GHCR PAT (App mode only)

In App mode, the App's bot token cannot pull container packages from
`ghcr.io` (see
[community discussion #34084](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/34084)),
so each user stores a small classic PAT scoped only for packages.
In PAT mode this step is skipped — the main PAT already grants the
package scopes.

### `flui integration ghcr-pat set`

Saves (or replaces) the GHCR PAT for your user.

```bash
flui integration ghcr-pat set
flui integration ghcr-pat set --headless     # print the token-creation URL
```

The command opens GitHub's token-creation page pre-filled with
`read:packages` and `delete:packages`. Paste the token at the masked
prompt and pick an expiry — Flui warns 14 days before it expires.

### `flui integration ghcr-pat status`

Shows the stored token's login, scopes, days until expiry, and the
last health-check timestamp. Status values: `VALID`, `EXPIRING_SOON`,
`EXPIRED`, `INVALID`, `MISSING`.

```bash
flui integration ghcr-pat status
```

### `flui integration ghcr-pat revoke`

Deletes the stored PAT from Flui (does **not** revoke it on GitHub —
do that at `https://github.com/settings/tokens`). After revoking,
`flui deploy` refuses to run until a new PAT is set.

```bash
flui integration ghcr-pat revoke
flui integration ghcr-pat revoke --yes
```

## Admin diagnostics

### `flui integration installations`

Lists every GitHub App installation tracked by Flui — handy when
diagnosing a stale or duplicated record. Shows the numeric
`installationId` needed by `remove-installation`.

```bash
flui integration installations
```

### `flui integration remove-installation <installationId>`

Removes an installation record from the Flui database. This does
**not** uninstall the App on GitHub — uninstall it there first,
otherwise the next webhook will re-create the record.

```bash
flui integration remove-installation 12345678
flui integration remove-installation 12345678 --yes
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip the confirmation prompt. |

Get the ID from `flui integration installations`.

## Repositories

### `flui repo connect [<owner/repo>]`

Imports a repository into your Flui account so it can be deployed with
`flui deploy`. Pass the full `owner/repo` slug, or omit it for an
interactive picker over the repositories accessible through the
connected integration.

```bash
flui repo connect acme/my-app
flui repo connect                              # interactive picker
```

The repo must be visible to whichever side is connected: the GitHub
App installation in App mode, or the PAT's permissions in PAT mode. If
the picker doesn't show it, re-run `flui integration connect github`
(App mode — add the repo on the GitHub install page) or re-issue the
PAT with broader access (PAT mode). `flui deploy` on an un-imported
repo fails up front with `Repository "<owner>/<repo>" is not connected
to your account` — that is the signal to run this command.

### `flui repo list`

Lists the repositories already connected to your Flui account.

```bash
flui repo list
flui repo list --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-o, --output text\|json` | `text` | Output format. |

### `flui repo disconnect <owner/repo>`

Removes the repository from your Flui account. Requires admin
privileges and asks to confirm; pass `-y, --yes` to skip the prompt.
The repository on GitHub itself is untouched.

```bash
flui repo disconnect acme/my-app
flui repo disconnect acme/my-app --yes
```

A disconnected repo can no longer be deployed until it is connected
again with `flui repo connect`.

## First-deploy flow, end to end

For an `Application` repo on a fresh installation, by the operator:

```bash
flui auth login                              # OIDC against the installation
flui integration setup github                # one-time: configure App or PAT
```

Then by every user (in App mode):

```bash
flui auth login                              # OIDC, once per machine
flui integration connect github              # install the Flui App on your account
flui integration ghcr-pat set                # required for the cluster to pull built images
flui repo connect dawit-io/my-app            # import the repo
flui deploy                                  # build via GitHub Actions, roll out
```

In PAT mode the user steps collapse — the same PAT covers cloning and
GHCR pulls, and for a single-user install the operator is also the
user:

```bash
flui auth login
flui repo connect dawit-io/my-app
flui deploy
```

After the first deploy of a given repo, only `flui deploy` is needed
for subsequent rollouts. Rotate the GHCR PAT before its expiry with
another `flui integration ghcr-pat set` (App mode), or re-run
`flui integration setup github` to refresh the instance PAT (PAT mode).

sections.title: Profiles and config
sections.body:
The CLI keeps every piece of local state under `~/.flui/` and
exposes three related but distinct surfaces:

- **Profiles** (`context` topic) — each profile is one isolated
  Flui installation on this machine: its own API URL, its own
  credentials, its own local inventory of clusters/nodes/firewalls.
- **The vault** (`vault` topic) — one passphrase per machine that
  seals every stored credential, in every profile.
- **Configuration** (`config` topic) — a layered resolver that
  decides the value of each preference and stores provider
  credentials, always inside the active profile.

If you only ever run one installation from this machine, the
auto-created `default` profile is enough and the `context` topic is
something you can ignore. The `config` topic, on the other hand, is
the one you reach for any time you need to change an email, add a
provider credential, or troubleshoot "why does this preference have
this value". The vault you meet twice: once when you create it, and
once per session when you open it.

## Profiles

A profile is a directory `~/.flui/profiles/<name>/`. The CLI creates
`default` on first run and remembers the active one in
`~/.flui/context`. Switching profile is local-only — nothing in the
cluster cares; the CLI just retargets every subsequent command at a
different installation.

### Commands

```bash
flui context list                    # all profiles, active one marked
flui context show                    # active profile + its API URL
flui context create staging          # create a new profile
flui context create staging --switch # create and switch in one go
flui context use prod                # switch to an existing profile
flui context delete staging          # delete a profile (asks to confirm)
flui context delete staging --force  # skip confirmation
```

Profile names accept alphanumeric characters, hyphens, and
underscores.

## The vault

Stored credentials were always encrypted. The weakness was where
the key lived: in the profile directory, next to the data it
protected. Anyone who could read the folder could read both halves.

So the key now comes from a passphrase you know and this machine
does not keep. That is the **vault**, and there is one per
workstation, covering every profile.

```bash
flui vault init      # once per machine, before storing anything
flui vault unlock    # once per session
flui vault status    # is it open, and for how long
flui vault lock      # close it now
```

`flui vault init` creates the vault and asks for a passphrase
twice. It suggests a five-word one, because the passphrase is
never stored, cannot be derived back from anything, and cannot be
reset — losing it means losing every credential this machine has
sealed. Write it down at that moment. If a vault already exists,
`init` refuses to overwrite it rather than making every sealed
credential unreadable.

`flui vault unlock` asks for the passphrase once and then leaves a
small background helper holding the key for the session. That
helper is `flui vault agent`. It exists as a command only because
that is how the CLI starts a copy of itself — it is hidden from
help and you never run it by hand. It takes the passphrase down a
pipe rather than as an argument, so the passphrase never appears in
the process list.

**One passphrase, still one key per profile.** The vault does not
put every profile under the same key. Each profile gets its own,
derived from the passphrase and that profile's name, so a command
working in `staging` cannot open `prod`'s stored credentials.

**The session closes on its own.** After thirty minutes of
inactivity, and after eight hours regardless of how busy you were.
The first limit makes the vault comfortable; the second stops that
comfort becoming permanent. Both are in minutes and can be changed:

| Variable | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_VAULT_IDLE_MINUTES` | `30` |
| `FLUI_VAULT_MAX_MINUTES` | `480` |

Anything that is not a positive whole number falls back to the
default, so a typo cannot make a session permanent.

`flui vault status` tells you whether a vault exists, whether it is
open, and how long each of those two clocks has left. `--format
json` prints the same answer as `{ initialised, unlocked, location,
idleRemainingMs, lifeRemainingMs }`. It also warns you if the
helper's socket has become reachable by other users on this
machine, which is the one thing keeping them away from the key.

`flui vault lock` overwrites the key in memory and stops the
helper. On a machine where nothing is open, it says so and does
nothing.

**A locked vault is not an error on its own.** Most commands read a
preference or an API URL, both plain text, and never ask for
anything. Only a command that actually opens a stored credential
stops — and when it stops it says the vault is locked and names
`flui vault unlock`, rather than reporting a decryption failure
that would send you looking for corrupt data.

### An upgrade locks nobody out

A profile that still holds the older `.key` file keeps working
exactly as before, so updating the CLI does not strand credentials
you already have. The first `flui vault unlock` re-seals those
profiles under the vault and deletes the old key file. Each entry
is rewritten under the new key before the old one is removed, so an
interrupted move loses nothing, and it reports how many secrets it
moved. A profile it cannot move is left as it is, with a warning
naming it.

### Without a terminal

Both `flui vault init` and `flui vault unlock` take `--stdin` and
read the passphrase from standard input instead of prompting. That
is the scripted path; without a terminal, they refuse to prompt and
tell you to use it.

```bash
printf 'my passphrase' | flui vault init --stdin
printf 'my passphrase' | flui vault unlock --stdin
```

There is one more escape hatch, for callers that have no terminal
*and* no home directory that outlives the run — a provisioning
worker, for instance. Setting `FLUI_PROFILE_KEY` to 32 bytes of
base64 hands the CLI a profile key directly, and no vault is
consulted:

```bash
export FLUI_PROFILE_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
```

The key then lives only in whatever started the CLI. Anything the
run sealed stops being openable the moment that caller forgets it.
A value that is present but malformed is an error, never a quiet
fallback to something else.

## Layered configuration

`flui config` reads and writes preferences and credentials. Every
value goes through a cascade — the first layer that has a value
wins:

```
explicit CLI input  >  env var  >  user-global config.json (active profile)  >  schema default
```

`flui config show` prints every preference along with which layer
the current value came from — the fastest way to debug an
unexpected value:

```bash
flui config show
```

### Preferences

Four preferences are declared in the schema:

| Key | Env var | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `email` | `FLUI_EMAIL` | *(required)* | Contact email for Let's Encrypt and operational notifications. |
| `certificateMode` | `FLUI_CERTIFICATE_MODE` | `production` | Certificate issuance mode written into the dashboard config. One of `production`, `staging`, `preflight` — see [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/). |
| `apiPath` | `FLUI_API_PATH` | `.` | Path to the `flui-core` repo. Only relevant to Flui contributors using `env export-config` / `dev creds`. |
| `dashboardPath` | `FLUI_DASHBOARD_PATH` | `../flui-dashboard` | Path to the `flui-dashboard` repo. Same scope as `apiPath`. |

```bash
flui config set email you@example.com
flui config set certificateMode preflight
flui config get email                       # resolved value + source
```

Preferences are not secrets and are stored in plain text, so
reading or writing one never asks for the vault.

### Provider credentials

`flui config set <provider>` stores the credentials needed to talk
to a cloud provider's API. The shape is uniform across providers;
the only thing that changes is whether the credential is a single
token or a key+secret pair, which in turn decides whether it can be
passed inline or has to go through the interactive prompt:

| Provider | Credential | Input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hetzner` | Single API token (`apiKey`) | Inline accepted: `flui config set hetzner <TOKEN>` |
| `scaleway` | Access Key ID + Secret Key | **Interactive only**: `flui config set scaleway` prompts for both fields and live-validates them against the Scaleway IAM API before saving |

The list reflects what is supported today; the same `flui config set
<provider>` pattern extends to any future provider — single-token
ones will accept inline values, pair-credential ones will keep the
interactive contract.

This is the writing side of the vault, so it needs an unlocked one
— unless the profile still holds the old key file, in which case it
keeps working as it did before.
A value passed as an argument is visible to every process on the
machine through the process list, so `--stdin` is the safer way to
hand one over — and for a pair-credential provider it is the only
way to configure it without a terminal, as a JSON object of its
fields:

```bash
printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | flui config set hetzner --stdin
printf '{"accessKey":"…","secretKey":"…"}' | flui config set scaleway --stdin
```

Credentials are never printed back. `flui config list` shows which
providers have credentials stored but not their values; `flui config
get` works on preferences only, and says so if you ask it for a
provider.

```bash
flui config set hetzner <YOUR_API_TOKEN>
flui config set scaleway                    # interactive prompt
flui config list                            # everything in the active profile
flui config list --tokens                   # provider credentials only
flui config list --preferences              # preferences only
flui config remove hetzner                  # asks to confirm by retyping the key
flui config remove scaleway --force         # skip the confirmation
```

### System keys

`api-url` is the one system-level key today: the URL of the Flui API
the active profile talks to. It is set automatically by `flui env
create` (and on the joining side by importing the export-config
output), and only rarely needs manual editing.

## What lives in a profile, and how it is stored

One file sits above the profiles:

- `~/.flui/vault.json` — the vault header: the salt and a value
  that proves a passphrase is right. It holds no credential, and
  nothing in it helps anyone who does not know the passphrase.

A profile directory contains:

- `config.json` — preferences (plain) and provider credentials
  (sealed under the vault).
- `.key` — the pre-vault key file. Present only on a profile that
  has not been moved across yet; the first `flui vault unlock`
  removes it.
- `ca/` — the SSH CA used to authenticate to cluster nodes
  (encrypted).
- `clusters.json`, `nodes.json`, `firewalls.json`, `vnets.json`,
  `operations.json` — local inventory cached from the API; safe to
  delete, will be repopulated on the next command that needs them.

## Examples

```bash
# Set the machine up once
flui vault init
flui vault unlock

# Create a staging workspace on Hetzner
flui context create staging --switch
flui config set email staging@example.com
flui config set hetzner <staging-token>
flui config set certificateMode staging
flui env create

# Same on Scaleway — interactive prompt for the key pair
flui context create staging-scw --switch
flui config set email staging@example.com
flui config set scaleway
flui env create --provider scaleway

# Debug where a preference is coming from
flui config show
flui config get certificateMode

# Remove a provider's credentials
flui config remove scaleway --force

# Finish for the day
flui vault lock
```

Why the vault works this way — one passphrase over many
installations, and what it does and does not defend against — is
covered in [Multi-context CLI](/concepts/07-multi-context-cli/).

sections.title: Templates
sections.body:
The `template` topic exists to close the gap between "I want to start
a new application in framework X" and "I have a repository the
platform can build and deploy". One command produces a fresh
repository, pre-wired with the Dockerfile, `flui.yaml`, healthcheck,
and build pipeline a Flui-compatible repo needs — see [Framework
templates](/concepts/19-framework-templates/) for the conceptual
model.

## `flui template use <framework> <name>`

Creates a new repository copied from the framework's template and, by
default, imports it into Flui so the application appears on the
dashboard side immediately.

```bash
flui template use <framework> my-app                   # private repo, default org
flui template use <framework> my-app --public          # public repo
flui template use <framework> my-api --org my-org      # under a specific org
flui template use <framework> my-svc -d "Internal microservice"
flui template use <framework> my-app --no-import       # skip the Flui-side import
```

| Argument / Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<framework>` | Template name. Run `flui template use --help` for the list available today. |
| `<name>` | Name for the new repository (required). |
| `--org <name>` | Organisation or user to create the repo under. Default: your account. |
| `-d, --description <s>` | Repository description. |
| `--public` | Create as public. Default: private. |
| `--no-import` | Create the repository on GitHub but skip the Flui-side import. |

## Prerequisites

- `flui auth login` must have been run — the command uses the active
  profile's API key.
- Your linked GitHub account needs permission to create a repository
  in the destination organisation. If the target is your personal
  account this is implicit; for an org, you (or the linked
  installation) must have repository-create rights there.

sections.title: Utilities
sections.body:
A handful of commands that do not belong to a single operational
topic and live at the top level of the CLI.

## `flui version`

Prints the CLI version and the **platform release it pins** — the
component image tags and the bootstrap revision a fresh `flui env
create` would install. Handy when debugging an install or confirming
which release a machine is on. See [Creating a
cluster](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) for what release pinning
means.

```bash
flui version
flui version --latest   # show what `env create --latest` would resolve to
flui version --json
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--latest` | Show the rolling development tags (bootstrap `master`, `:latest` images) that `flui env create --latest` resolves to, instead of the pinned release. |
| `--json` | Machine-readable output. |

## `flui update`

Checks `npm` for a newer published version of `@flui-cloud/cli` and,
if there is one, reinstalls the CLI globally after asking for
confirmation.

```bash
flui update
```

The reinstall uses `npm install -g @flui-cloud/cli@<latest>` under
the hood. If you originally installed the CLI with `pnpm` or `yarn`
the command still works, but it produces a mixed install on the
local Node setup; reinstall manually with your package manager of
choice if that matters.

## `flui reconcile`

Reconciles the CLI's local state with what the API knows. Today it
covers the **DNS configuration** only — useful after manual edits to
DNS records or to the provider zone, to line the two views back up.

```bash
flui reconcile
flui reconcile --type dns
flui reconcile --dry-run
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-t, --type <kind>` | `all` | Reconciliation kind. Available today: `dns`, `all`. Repeatable. |
| `--api-url <url>` | from profile | Override the API URL for this run. |
| `--dry-run` | — | Show what would be reconciled without applying changes. |

## DNS

The `dns` topic is bigger than one command now. This page
owns the low-level, one-off one: cleaning up leftover
records. For the everyday DNS work — assigning a zone to a
cluster, publishing the wildcard record that covers every
application on it, and adding a second provider for
redundancy — see [Put an application on the
internet](/tasks/put-an-application-on-the-internet/), which
covers `flui dns zone`, `flui dns wildcard` and `flui dns
replica` end to end, CLI and dashboard both.

### `flui dns cleanup`

Deletes every `A` record in the named zone on **Hetzner
DNS**. Typically used after destroying a batch of test
clusters that left their hostnames behind.

```bash
flui dns cleanup --domain example.com --dry-run    # preview first
flui dns cleanup --domain example.com
flui dns cleanup --domain example.com --force      # skip confirmation
```

| Flag | Required | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--domain <name>` | yes | Zone name on Hetzner DNS. |
| `-f, --force` | no | Skip confirmation. |
| `--dry-run` | no | Preview the records that would be deleted. |

> ⚠️ **Destructive and irreversible.** Always run `--dry-run` first;
> the command does not look at which records belong to active
> clusters, it removes every `A` record in the zone.
